# *The Back Goes Backwards*

## Book I: *Medical Foundations*

Michael Seiler and Katherine E. Gallardo, MD

First-draft manuscript

July 2026

# Introduction — A mechanical history

Move an object from one support to another and carry it across a room. The task can be trivial or demanding. The object can be a cup, a suitcase, a box, a tool, or something held with another person. The route can be level or uneven. The person can stand, sit, use an assistive device, pause, change hands, ask for help, or arrange the environment so that the task requires less effort. There is no single correct solution hiding inside the example.

Yet every successful solution has a mechanical history. The object exchanges force with the hand or another point of contact. The person exchanges force with a chair, floor, device, or helper. Joint geometry changes as the task unfolds. Muscle generates force. Tendons transmit it. Bones and joint surfaces provide changing routes. Ligaments restrain some motions while permitting others. Deformable tissues receive contact, slide, bend, expand, and recover. Pressure participates in support. Sensation and motor control alter the next moment before the previous one is over.

That history is not separate from biology. It occurs through living structures whose behavior depends on development, tissue composition, inflammation, hydration, fatigue, pain, prior exposure, sleep, illness, training, medication, expectation, attention, and recovery. The same task can be uneventful one day and difficult another. The same external weight can be distributed differently by two people or by the same person at two times. A mechanical description that ignores the living state is incomplete. A biological description that treats material demand as irrelevant is incomplete in a different way.

This book begins from that common ground.

> The human body is a living biomechanical system. Its tissues and structures continuously receive, distribute, transform, transmit, and dissipate forces and moments while managing pressure and deformation over time. Clinical reasoning can improve when load history, load distribution, and body-wide load routing are considered alongside biological, psychological, social, developmental, and environmental factors.

The argument is substantial, but it is not a claim that mechanics explains every illness. It does not require one ideal posture, one correct way to move, or one force path that every body should reproduce. It does not ask the reader to replace diagnosis, medication, surgery, rehabilitation, psychology, public health, or social analysis with biomechanics. It asks a narrower and often neglected sequence of questions: What demand entered the system? What structures and relations carried it? Where did it become concentrated, interrupted, or redirected? What changed through repetition and time? What did the receiving tissue or person have the capacity to tolerate and recover from? What alternatives could explain the same finding or symptom?

Those questions can matter before they provide a diagnosis. They can reveal a missing measurement, an untested assumption, a plausible exposure, a compensatory strategy, a limit of an analogy, or a reason that two observations should not yet be joined. A mechanical narrative becomes useful not when it is confident, but when its links can be inspected.

## Mechanics is already part of medicine

This book is not premised on the idea that medicine forgot the body is physical. Mechanical reasoning is explicit wherever care concerns fracture stability, joint contact, ventilation, blood pressure, conduit patency, pressure injury, prosthetic interfaces, movement, balance, assistive support, or surgical reconstruction. Biomechanics, orthopedics, rehabilitation, cardiopulmonary medicine, occupational health, movement science, and many other fields already contain deep mechanical knowledge.

The proposed addition is one of organization and continuity. Mechanical questions are often answered within a region, specialty, procedure, or immediate endpoint. That local precision is necessary. It does not always reconstruct the longer path by which a demand reached the structure now under consideration, how neighboring regions shared or redirected it, what strategy preserved function in the meantime, or how the distribution changed before a discrete injury or finding became visible.

The phrase *load routing* gives that broader inquiry a name. A load path is not a hidden pipe running through the body, and load is not a substance that travels intact from one end to the other. A path is a bounded model of how a defined demand is partitioned among candidate carriers in a declared task and period. It can branch, change phase, recruit a new contact, use active force, exchange energy, involve pressure, or become indeterminate with the available measurements. Several internal arrangements can produce a similar external result. A useful path model therefore names what is known, what is calculated, what is inferred, and what remains unobserved.

The word *load* will sometimes remain a convenient umbrella. When the distinction carries the argument, the book will replace it with the actual quantity or relation: force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, displacement, excursion, work, power, repetition, rate, or recovery. A visible posture is not a stress field. A joint moment is not an individual muscle force. A narrowed space is not yet a diagnosis. A changed symptom is not by itself a reconstruction of origin. The discipline of the book lies in refusing those substitutions while continuing to ask the larger question.

## A division of mechanical labor

One compact intuition organizes the early chapters:

> Load wants to travel through the hard body so that the soft body can remain soft.

The sentence is deliberately physical and deliberately provisional. It does not mean that bone alone should bear force or that tissues conventionally called soft should remain unloaded. Tendon can carry high tensile force. Muscle can stiffen an assembly through activation. Ligament can guide and restrain. Cartilage can deform while a fluid–solid structure supports contact. A pressurized cavity can contribute to a comparatively shape-preserving job. Bone itself deforms.

Here, *hard* and *soft* name roles rather than tissue classes. A hard role is relatively shape-preserving, path-establishing, constraining, or structurally resolving in the direction, scale, phase, and task under discussion. A soft role is relatively form-receiving and shape-conforming. It yields to its surroundings while remaining available to glide, contain, expand, buffer, respond to pressure, or change local shape. Softness is not weakness. It is a functional capacity to receive form without being forced to impose the gross geometry of the task. Either role can transmit substantial force; transmission alone does not decide the role.

The polarity is motivated by traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts. Book I develops a flexible mechanical translation of that motivation. It does not claim that the traditional and mechanical categories are definitionally identical, that a channel map has already been established, or that a traditional correspondence proves a biomechanical proposition. Those stronger questions belong later in the series. The present distinction must earn its value through mechanical clarity: whether it identifies a useful relation, predicts a role exchange, preserves a necessary freedom, or explains something that ordinary stiffness, contact, pressure, activation, and load-sharing language does not already explain as well.

This is a division of labor, not a moral hierarchy. A form-receiving structure performs essential work. Yielding, gliding, containment, expansion, and local deformation are not failures to be eliminated. A shape-preserving route is useful only relative to a task and a receiver whose freedom matters. The same structure can perform both roles at once in different directions or exchange them as contact, activation, pressure, rate, or phase changes.

## Why the posterior body matters

The posterior chain is the book's first sustained anatomical example. The label can be used too loosely, as if the back of the body were one cable or one movement pattern. This book uses it more carefully: as a scope-declared grouping of posterior structures whose boundaries and contribution depend on the question.

That grouping is not imaginary. The feet and posterior legs, hamstrings, gluteal region, pelvis, spinal extensors, thoracolumbar relations, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, shoulder girdle, and posterior neck contain large and mechanically consequential structures. They participate in stance, gait, propulsion, lifting, reaching, braking, balance, transfer, and recovery from perturbation. Their cooperation with bones, joints, active control, pressure, anterior and lateral structures, external support, and the environment changes from one phase to the next.

The anatomical fact earns attention without settling priority. The posterior chain is not the whole body. A task can depend visibly on anterior, lateral, deep, compliant, pressure-mediated, or external support. Strong posterior activity does not by itself identify an efficient or preferred organization. The first book therefore makes the affirmative case that posterior anatomy is substantial and functionally important while leaving the stronger directional proposition open.

That boundary is central to the series title. *The Back Goes Backwards* can first be read as a reminder that the back is not merely a surface that follows the front or a region noticed only after pain. Posterior structures have their own architecture, capacity, timing, and mechanical jobs. The title also points toward a stronger hypothesis developed in Book II: that human anatomy may possess a preferred body-wide organization involving three signed generalized modes and necessary but insufficient posterior participation. Book I names that research program honestly. None of its foundational claims depends on the result.

## From demand to medical meaning

A mechanical account becomes medically consequential only through intermediate links. The recurring chain in this book is:

> task and environment → body state and configuration → available paths and internal distribution → local force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, or excursion → tissue response over time → function, findings, possible symptoms, and clinical interpretation

The arrows are not decoration. Each is a proposition with its own scale, timing, evidence, and alternatives. A task can alter configuration without producing a harmful local exposure. A local exposure can occur without causing a symptom. A tissue finding can precede symptoms, follow them, coexist without them, or be incidental to the present problem. Pain, inflammation, fear, fatigue, illness, and environmental constraint can change movement and load distribution rather than merely result from them. Treatment response can establish that something changed without proving what originally caused the condition.

Capacity and recovery enter throughout the chain. A peak value is not a complete dose. Direction, rate, repetition, duration, variability, sequence, material state, and time between exposures can change the receiving condition. So can development, disability, training, age, illness, assistance, work organization, sleep, and access to care. A strategy that appears inefficient in one narrow model may be the solution that preserves balance, confidence, participation, or a painful region. Calling it compensation does not make it a defect. The first question is what, if anything, it preserved.

The book will use six recurring families to describe adverse mechanical organization: global or regional redistribution; local concentration; segmental or task-specific instability; timing, coordination, or handoff failure; constraint-maintained deformation or lost excursion; and compensatory rerouting. These are not diagnoses. They are ways of making a proposed exposure more specific. They can coexist, remain asymptomatic, reverse, protect function, or prove irrelevant in a particular case. Scale transition is an additional analytical question rather than a seventh family: it asks what evidence connects a local, regional, task-level, or wider change across a new system boundary.

## What the worked narratives are for

The examples in Part V do not function as rhetorical votes for the framework. They are stress tests. Each must declare its system boundary, task, chronology, candidate carriers, quantities, biological bridges, competing explanations, missing observations, and disfavoring results.

The first follows a change in geometry toward a candidate local strain field without treating alignment as a verdict. The second studies a thoracic-outlet context in which a compliant structure can remain deformed because an ongoing relation maintains that deformation. The consequential object is not narrowing alone, but the load, contact, pressure, excursion, wall behavior, or strain that produces and sustains the changed relation. The third examines instability and repeated demand under changing capacity. The fourth uses a mixed chronic presentation in which a mechanical history may be informative but cannot plausibly stand alone.

These narratives stop before individualized treatment. They do not teach a home test, corrective posture, drill, breathing protocol, or diagnostic score. Their immediate contribution is a better sequence of comparisons: which relation is observed, which exposure is proposed, what else could produce it, what would need to be measured, and what result would leave the hypothesis unsupported.

## The movement of the book

The six Parts are cumulative.

Part I establishes the mechanical foundations of living structure. It begins with embodiment, distinguishes the quantities hidden inside the word *load*, introduces the hard/soft division of labor, and places those roles within three-dimensional configurations and changing paths.

Part II gives the abstractions an anatomy. Bones and joints, active muscle, tendons, ligaments, fasciae, sliding interfaces, compliant structures, fluids, cavities, pressure, and neural control cooperate. The posterior chain then provides a large-scale example whose anatomy, ordinary functions, variability, and limits can be examined without assuming a universal route.

Part III asks what happens when a viable relation is lost, narrowed, overloaded, poorly timed, repeatedly substituted for, or preserved at a growing cost. Its purpose is not to generate a list of bad postures. It is to distinguish mechanisms that are often collapsed: a global geometric change from a local concentration, instability from maintained constraint, a failed handoff from a successful but costly substitution, and immediate protection from delayed consequence.

Part IV connects mechanical organization to medical meaning. It begins with mechanics already used in medicine, defines longitudinal load routing as the proposed addition, follows exposure into tissue response, compares different compliant and pressure-bearing systems, establishes the whole-person causal boundary, and asks how the lens could enter professional reasoning without becoming a diagnosis or a competing medical system.

Part V applies the full chain to four contrasting narratives. Their value lies as much in the arrows they cannot complete as in those they can.

Part VI turns the framework into bounded questions for reasoning, education, environmental design, research, measurement, therapeutic development, implementation, and health-system development. Those programs do not mature as one package. A useful educational vocabulary does not establish a diagnostic test. A reliable measurement does not guarantee decision value. A therapeutic effect does not automatically prove the proposed mechanism. Successful implementation does not create benefit.

The final chapter returns to the title and separates three levels: the durable Book I foundation, the posterior organizing lens, and the preferred-configuration hypothesis that the later series will test. It includes a real rejection condition. If the stronger configuration, coordinate, traditional, breath, or practice programs fail, the mechanical history developed here must still be worth tracing.

## How to read the claims

The prose will often distinguish what was observed, measured, calculated, modeled, inferred, reconstructed, hypothesized, or reported through experience. These are not ranks from worthless to true. They are different relations to evidence. A model can answer a question a direct measurement cannot. An embodied observation can identify a phenomenon worth defining. A traditional system can preserve a structured body of experience. None should borrow the evidentiary status of another without the intervening work.

The same rule applies to disagreement. A broad review that finds no consistent relation between a general posture category and pain does not automatically test every narrower load-routing hypothesis. Nor does a narrower hypothesis survive by redefining itself whenever evidence is unfavorable. The tested construct and the proposed construct must be compared directly. A negative result can retire one arrow while leaving another question open.

Figures in this development draft are text-native models rather than final anatomical art. They state boundaries, variables, evidence states, and text alternatives so that the reasoning can be reviewed before visual polish makes it persuasive. Citations identify the exact work a source performs and, where important, what it did not measure. External specialist, medical-coauthor, traditional-language, accessibility, rights, bibliography, and final-art reviews remain necessary before publication.

The reader is not being asked to choose between mechanics and the whole person. A person is mechanically embodied and also biological, psychological, social, developmental, historical, and situated in an environment. The question is not which vocabulary gets the whole explanation. It is whether the mechanical history has been traced carefully enough to know what it adds.

We begin with the simplest part of that history: a living body cannot opt out of mechanics.

# Part I — Mechanical foundations of living structure

Calling the body mechanical can sound either trivial or reductive. It is trivial if the word means only that bodies have mass and occupy space. It is reductive if a living person is treated as a passive machine whose behavior follows from a few levers and material constants. Part I develops the useful position between those extremes.

Living structures carry force, sustain pressure, deform, move, maintain contact, and recover. They also activate, sense, regulate, grow, remodel, fatigue, heal, and change their behavior with context. The mechanical description is therefore indispensable but incomplete. Its job is to make material relationships inspectable without pretending that those relationships exhaust biology or experience.

The four chapters move from broad fact to working model. Chapter 1 establishes mechanics as one dimension of embodied life and places it inside a whole-person account. Chapter 2 opens the word *load* into the quantities and timescales it can conceal. Chapter 3 introduces hard and soft as changing mechanical roles: comparative shape preservation and form reception rather than permanent tissue classes. Chapter 4 places those roles inside three-dimensional configuration and develops a bounded meaning of load path.

One ordinary object transfer accompanies the progression. At first it shows only that material demand must be managed. It then acquires forces, moments, contacts, boundaries, rates, and phases. Different structures take on different jobs, and the available paths change with geometry, activation, support, and time. The example prescribes no technique. It teaches a method: declare the system before explaining what happened inside it.

By the end of Part I, a mechanical question should be more precise and less certain than it first appeared. That is progress. The reader will be able to distinguish external demand from internal distribution, force from stress, deformation from damage, visible posture from configuration, and a candidate path from a proven route. Part II can then ask which anatomical systems perform the work those distinctions describe.

# Chapter 1 — The mechanical dimension of life

An ordinary object rests on a table. A person makes contact with it, takes its weight, moves it away from the support, carries it several steps, and places it on another surface. This is an ordinary observation, not a demonstration of correct technique. The object might be a box, a basket, or a bag. The person might use two hands, one hand, an assistive device, another person’s help, or a surface that lets the object slide. The details change the task, but none of the versions is mechanically empty.

Gravity acts before the first touch. Contact changes when the object leaves the table. The person generates force, accepts force, changes speed, redirects the object, exchanges support with the floor, and eventually gives the object’s weight to a new surface. Joints move, tissues deform, pressure changes, and active control varies from one phase to the next. At the same time, this is not a passive structure executing a diagram. Sensation informs action. Circulation and breathing continue. Prior fatigue, pain, confidence, attention, skill, and expectation can alter what the person does. The room, the available space, the object’s handles, the height of the supports, and the availability of assistance can change which solutions are possible.

The mechanical and living descriptions do not take turns. They describe the same event from different positions. That fact is the beginning of this book.

It is not yet an explanation of an injury, a symptom, or a disease. It does not tell us that one way of moving the object is best, that one internal route carried the demand, or that a later complaint began here. It gives us a more useful question: what would we need to observe, measure, or model before deciding whether the mechanical history of this event mattered to a selected outcome?

## A body cannot opt out of mechanics

The human body is a materially embodied, actively regulated biomechanical system. Its tissues and structures continuously receive, generate, distribute, transform, transmit, oppose, and balance mechanical demand while storing, returning, or dissipating mechanical energy and managing pressure, contact, motion, and deformation over time.

The statement is broad because it comes before any particular theory of health. A body has mass. External contacts act through surfaces. Weight must be supported or accompanied by acceleration. Joint geometry changes how interactions are redirected. Lung expansion occurs through changing volume and pressure in relation to surrounding structures. Blood moves within deformable vessels. Tissues stretch, shorten, shear, bend, compress, slide, and recoil while cells remain biologically active. Mechanical stresses can arise from processes within living tissue as well as from forces imposed from outside it.[^01-01]

None of this makes the body merely a machine. A machine analogy can isolate a useful relation: a lever can clarify a moment, a pressure vessel can clarify a wall–pressure interaction, and a free-body diagram can clarify which contacts cross a chosen boundary. But living materials are built, maintained, sensed, altered, and sometimes repaired by living processes. Cells generate internal forces. Neural activity changes muscle action. Hydration, inflammation, healing, development, age, and prior exposure can change material behavior. The system also has a history. Its properties cannot be treated as fixed values stamped onto passive parts.

Three claims must therefore remain separate.

*Mechanical presence* means that material relations involving force, pressure, contact, motion, and deformation are present. *Mechanical explanation* means that a defined mechanical relation helps account for the particular state or outcome we have selected. *Mechanical priority* means that this relation explains more of that selected question than plausible alternatives do. Material embodiment establishes the first. It does not automatically establish the second or third.

This distinction prevents a simple fact from becoming an unlimited claim. Mechanics may be central to a question about whether the moving object remained supported during departure from the table. It may be one contributor to a question about fatigue after many transfers. It may add very little to an account of why performance changed during an acute systemic illness. The body remains material in all three questions. What changes is the explanatory job we are asking mechanics to perform.

The same restraint applies when the body is healthy and comfortable. Mechanical conditions are not only adverse exposures waiting to become injuries. A joint redirecting force, a tendon changing tension, a vessel wall changing shape, or a pressure-bearing space changing volume can be part of ordinary function. Whether a given mechanical state is supportive, inconsequential, demanding, or harmful requires a defined task, receiver, duration, comparison, and outcome. The word *mechanical* supplies none of those judgments by itself.

Calling the body a system adds another restraint. It means that skeletal contact, active muscle, tendon and ligament, compliant tissue, sliding interfaces, pressure-bearing spaces, vessels, nerves, and sensory control coexist and interact. It does not mean that every local event recruits the whole body in a consequential way, or that one network governs all the others. A local change can remain local. Several structures can share one task. The carrier that matters can change with direction and phase. Sometimes the most useful boundary is the whole person; sometimes it is one segment, interface, or patch of tissue. “One system” is an instruction to account for relevant interactions, not permission to infer a body-wide cascade.

> initial support   object rests on surface        sensation and anticipation     support height, space
> acceptance        hand/object contact changes    active force and timing        grip options, assistance
> departure         support transfers; motion      balance and ongoing physiology object form, task goal
> carry             contacts and direction vary    repeated control and sensation path, terrain, fatigue
> placement         object decelerates; support    controlled release             second support, time
>                   transfers again
>

>

>
> **Text alternative.** A five-phase table follows an object from its first support through contact, departure, carrying, and placement. Each phase pairs a material event with living regulation and contextual conditions. A final line states that these descriptions do not determine local exposure or outcome.

The useful starting position is therefore neither “mechanics explains the body” nor “mechanics is only relevant after injury.” It is that embodied function always has a mechanical dimension, and that the importance of this dimension must be earned for each question.

## Mechanics and biology change one another

Separating mechanical presence from priority does not separate mechanics from biology. Living tissue is a relation between material organization and biological activity. In soft connective tissues, resident cells sense features of the extracellular matrix and participate in depositing, rearranging, removing, and organizing that matrix. The matrix in turn supplies mechanical and biochemical surroundings that affect cellular behavior. Even a tissue described as being in a steady state can therefore be dynamically maintained.[^01-02]

One older experiment makes the direction from mechanical conditions to biological behavior concrete. Researchers grew rabbit aortic medial cells on elastin membranes and subjected the membranes to repeated elongation and relaxation. Under that protocol, the stretched preparations showed higher synthesis rates for several matrix components than stationary or agitated comparison preparations. The finding is specific: a defined mechanical history altered defined cellular outputs in an in-vitro preparation.[^01-03]

It does not show that stretching is generally beneficial. It does not establish a response in an intact artery, much less a whole person. Change the cell type, substrate, direction, magnitude, rate, duration, or measured endpoint, and the result may change. The experiment matters here because it demonstrates one controlled arrow: mechanical conditions can alter biological behavior.

The reverse arrow is equally important. In another experiment, bovine cartilage explants were exposed to the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1 beta. The exposure was associated with matrix catabolism and changes in measured stiffness and stress-relaxation behavior. The experiment was designed principally to study lithium chloride, but its comparison groups demonstrate the narrower relation needed here: a changed biological environment and associated matrix state changed the measured mechanical behavior of the explants.[^01-04]

Again, the boundary matters. These were bovine tissue samples maintained and tested in vitro. The study does not establish what a person feels, whether a joint is diseased, what caused a clinical presentation, or how anyone should be treated. It shows why an externally similar task cannot be assumed to meet the same mechanical receiver when tissue state has changed.

The two arrows are reciprocal, not symmetrical. They need not have equal strength, equal speed, or matching endpoints. Some responses are rapid; others develop across longer intervals. Some mechanical changes are sensed without producing a consequential response for the question at hand. Some biological changes alter material behavior profoundly; others do not. Feedback can maintain a usable range, contribute to remodeling, participate in injury or repair, or be negligible in a selected outcome. *Response* is the broad term. Adaptation, recovery, damage, healing, and degeneration are more specific results that must each be demonstrated rather than presumed.

This reciprocity also blocks a false choice. A mechanical explanation does not become less mechanical because inflammation changed the material receiving the demand. A biological explanation does not become less biological because pressure, contact, or deformation participated in the signal. The serious question is not which domain owns the event. It is which relation is being proposed, at what scale, with what evidence, and with what competing account.

## One event, several non-equivalent scales

Return to the object leaving the table. From across the room, we can observe the task: the object starts on one support and ends on another. We can describe the environment, the visible contacts, the sequence, and perhaps the motion. This is a whole-event description.

Move the analytic boundary inward and the questions change. Around the person and object together, the hand–object contact is internal to the selected system. Around the person alone, it is an external contact. Around an arm segment, interactions at neighboring joints and tissues enter the accounting. At a joint, geometry, active forces, and distributed contact matter. At a patch of tissue, the relevant description may involve local stress, strain, pressure, deformation, or sliding. At a cell, the question changes again to the way a particular local history interacts with receptors, cytoskeleton, matrix, and signaling.

These levels are connected, but they are not magnified copies of one another. The object’s weight does not uniquely determine a joint force. A joint resultant does not uniquely determine a contact-pressure distribution. Visible position does not uniquely determine a tissue stress field. A local mechanical exposure does not uniquely determine a cellular response, and a cellular response does not by itself determine pain, participation, diagnosis, or recovery. Multiscale models exist precisely because relations at tissue and cellular levels require different representations and explicit coupling assumptions.[^01-05]

At each transition, new information is needed. Moving from the task to segment forces requires a system boundary, contacts, motion, geometry, and assumptions about active action. Moving from a segment resultant to an interface distribution requires the contact geometry and boundary conditions. Moving from an interface to local stress or strain requires material behavior and a reference state. Moving from a mechanical field to biological response requires evidence appropriate to the tissue, state, dose, and time. Moving from response to what the person can do or feel requires still more observation and allows still more alternatives.

The status of the information changes as well. We can observe that the object left the table. An instrument might measure motion or the force at an external contact. A calculation can combine those measurements within a declared model. An internal force distribution may then be inferred rather than directly observed. A local tissue field may depend on material and boundary assumptions that are uncertain. A later biological or experiential response requires its own observation. Calling all of these results “what happened” would conceal how each entered the account.

The distinction matters even when two transfers look alike. The same visible object path can coexist with different hand contacts, active forces, joint resultants, or tissue distributions. Conversely, two visibly different strategies can satisfy the same external task without one being mechanically deficient. Appearance is evidence about geometry and motion at the scale actually seen. It becomes evidence about an internal exposure only through the additional observations and model that connect them.

This is not an argument for impossible completeness. Every useful model omits detail. The point is to make the omission visible enough to know what a conclusion depends on. A whole-person account can be appropriate for one question while being too coarse for another. A cell experiment can establish a cellular mechanism while remaining insufficient for a clinical outcome. The error occurs when fluency hides the change of scale.

Physical setting, assistance, illness, fatigue, attention, pain, experience, work, care demands, and resources enter named task, receiver, strategy, report, participation, or consequence nodes as candidates to test. A final branch either retains the mechanical history for demonstrated incremental value or returns a low-priority or null result.

The scale problem gives the book its method. Rather than moving directly from an appearance to a health conclusion, we will ask what happened between the levels—and whether the missing links can actually be observed or tested.

## Mechanics inside a whole-person account

A person does not arrive at the object transfer as an interchangeable material specimen. Potentially relevant conditions include development, anatomy, genetics, current illness, inflammation, medication, sleep, nutrition, training, previous injury, and healing. Attention, expectation, fear, confidence, experience, and the meaning of the task may also belong in the account, as may work organization, caregiving, resources, transportation, social demands, tools, terrain, and access to assistance. Their presence does not establish a causal pathway. It identifies candidate differences in receiving state, task choice, timing, effort, sensation, reporting, available options, exposure history, or consequence that must be observed or supported for the question at hand.

This is not a ceremonial list of things that “also matter.” Each factor earns a place only when evidence or observation connects it to a named part of the account.

Some entries follow directly from the task description: an assistive device becomes part of the selected system and adds contacts; a narrow workspace or a support at a fixed height limits the configurations physically available; a documented schedule locates repetitions and rest in time. Others remain candidate pathways. Did acute illness or prior fatigue change the state receiving the next event? Did expectation or pain change movement strategy or the experience reported afterward? Did access to help alter the feasible strategy, or did employment and caregiving make task failure more consequential? The model becomes more discriminating when a relevant condition enters at a named node with an appropriate observation rather than through assumption.

The World Health Organization’s International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health places body structure and function in relation to activity, participation, and environmental factors. It offers a framework for describing functioning and disability in context.[^01-06] It is not an etiological verdict, and it does not say that all domains have equal importance in every case. Its value here is to prevent a local material description from silently standing in for the person’s complete situation.

Whole-person reasoning also preserves causal direction. Suppose pain appears before a new movement pattern. The pattern may be a response to pain rather than its source. Suppose inflammation changes tissue mechanics and also makes a task feel harder. The biological state may be a common influence on both the mechanical observation and the experience. Suppose a person uses an asymmetrical strategy because the environment leaves only one workable approach. The visible arrangement may reflect access and task constraint rather than an intrinsic deficit. Each alternative changes the mechanical question; none requires mechanics to disappear.

Time can change the role of the same factor. Assistance may reduce one external demand while making a valued task possible. A protective movement may be useful during one phase of recovery and become the starting configuration for later tasks. A symptom that first followed an exposure may later alter behavior, sleep, participation, and future exposure. A work constraint can shape the original task, the opportunity for recovery, and which outcomes matter. The account is therefore a dated set of relations, not a timeless inventory of personal traits.

This matters because *mechanical* is sometimes treated as a synonym for objective, while psychological or social is treated as subjective background. That division is unhelpful. External forces can be unmeasured. Internal stress can be model-dependent. Pain and confidence can be reported with specificity. Work schedules and support access can be documented. Different kinds of evidence answer different questions. They should not be ranked merely by domain.

Nor does a plural account require causal dilution. If a mechanical relation is proposed, it can still be examined specifically: which demand, which configuration, which tissue, which time, which response? The surrounding factors make that proposal more discriminating. They identify why two apparently similar tasks may not be equivalent, why the same tissue state may have different functional consequences, or why a coherent mechanical description may not explain the selected outcome.

The practical result is a change in posture toward evidence. We do not begin by assigning permanent causal rank to mechanics, biology, psychology, or context. We select a question and follow the relations that could answer it. A mechanical contribution can be important without being exclusive. It can also be present yet secondary, consequential, incidental, or unsupported.

## From obvious injury to upstream context

Some mechanical histories are comparatively easy to recognize. A person experiences a discrete impact and a fracture is identified in close, documented relation to it. The lesion develops during the mechanical event even if it is confirmed afterward. Biology influences the material that fractured and the response that follows, but the close chronology gives the event an evident place in the account. Fracture itself is a multiscale process, and living-tissue failure can involve stresses arising internally or externally as well as tissue state.[^01-01]

Many histories are less tidy. A task repeats across days or years. The demand changes with tools, environment, fatigue, or assistance. The body finds ways to continue. One region changes its participation while another takes on more work. Capacity and recovery vary. The first symptom has no single memorable beginning, or the initiating event has passed while a changed strategy remains. In these situations, the present state cannot reveal the entire history by inspection.

The wider inquiry of this book begins here. Mechanical organization may sometimes help explain tissue state, function, symptoms, risk, or recovery before a discrete lesion is visible, after an initiating event has passed, or in a problem not conventionally framed as mechanical. That is an organizing hypothesis, not a conclusion smuggled out of material embodiment.

To support it in any particular setting, a chain must be built rather than assumed. What task and environment imposed the demand? What was the body’s state and configuration? Which contacts and structures distributed it? What local force, stress, strain, pressure, deformation, or loss of motion occurred? How did the relevant tissue or system respond over time? Did that response correspond to function, findings, or experience? What else could produce the same observations, and what result would lower the priority of the mechanical account?

The chain can fail at any link. A visible configuration may coexist with several internal distributions. A proposed local exposure may not be present. An exposure may occur without the expected response. A biological response may not correspond to a symptom or functional limitation. The same finding may arise from a different process. A present mechanical pattern may be a consequence of illness, pain, treatment, fatigue, or altered participation rather than an initiating event.

History introduces another evidentiary boundary. We may know the current configuration and a few dated events without having observed the interval between them. Repeated demand, compensation, or declining reserve can be a plausible reconstruction, but plausibility is not observation. A responsible reconstruction states which endpoints are documented, which transitions are inferred, and which other histories remain possible. Prospective measurement may support one route, reveal several routes, or show that the proposed mechanical history does not improve explanation over a simpler account.

Consider a hypothetical comparison. The same person moves the same object on two days. On the second day, an acute systemic illness is chiefly responsible for markedly reduced energy and task performance. Mechanical demand is still present, and the illness may change speed, active force, support, or distribution. But for the question “Why is performance reduced today?” tracing the internal mechanical route may add little beyond the illness account. For the narrower question “How was the object supported during departure?” mechanics may again be central. Priority belongs to a selected question and outcome, not to the body in the abstract.

This low-priority result is not an embarrassment to the framework. It is one of the results the framework must be able to return. A method that always discovers its preferred cause is not tracing; it is relabeling.

The upstream question nevertheless deserves to remain visible. Obvious injuries do not exhaust the ways material history can matter. Repetition, direction, rate, duration, variability, changing capacity, compensation, and recovery create mechanically intelligible questions even when their clinical importance is unresolved. Later chapters will separate these features, identify possible modes of failed distribution or transfer, and ask what evidence is required to connect them to tissue response and medical meaning. The opening chapter only establishes why that inquiry belongs inside a serious account of embodied life.

## What we have earned

Return once more to the object between the two supports. It is a mechanical event because forces, contacts, motion, pressure, and deformation are unavoidable. It is a living event because active regulation, biological state, sensation, history, and context are present at the same time. Neither description is complete by itself, and neither receives automatic priority for every later question.

This chapter has established a starting position, not a hidden route through the body. Living function has a mechanical dimension. Mechanical state and biological state can alter one another. Descriptions at different scales require explicit bridges. Context changes the demand, the available solutions, the receiving state, and the meaning of the outcome. A mechanical history can prove important, mixed, consequential, or low priority when those relations are traced.

But we have repeatedly used one word that is too broad for the work ahead: *load*. The object’s weight, the turning effect at a joint, pressure at an interface, stress inside a tissue, deformation through time, and the capacity to repeat the task are not the same thing. Before we can ask how demand travels through living structure, we need to choose the system and name the quantity. That is the work of Chapter 2.

# Chapter 2 — A working language of load

Place an ordinary object on a table, lift it, carry it across a room, and set it down somewhere else. Nothing about the task seems mysterious. The object has weight. The hands support it. The feet meet the floor. Muscles work, joints turn, and tissues change shape. We can reasonably say that the body is *under load*.

That sentence is useful, but it is not yet precise. The object's weight is a force. Holding it farther from the trunk changes a moment. Contact between hand and object is distributed over an area. A joint may be represented by a resultant force and moment, while the contact within it has a pressure distribution. A tendon can develop internal stress and change length. Repeating the task creates a history that no single peak value describes. These quantities are related, but they are not interchangeable. They do not even have the same units.[^02-01]

The word *load* will remain useful throughout this book. We will use it as an umbrella for mechanical demand when the exact internal quantity is not yet known or does not yet matter. Whenever an argument bears weight, however, the umbrella must open. We must ask what kind of demand is present, where it acts, how it is distributed, what changes through time, and what has actually been observed rather than calculated, modeled, or inferred.

The first question is simpler still: what system are we talking about?

## Choose the system before describing the force

Imagine the object halfway between the two tables. If the system includes both person and object, the forces exchanged between the hands and the object are internal interactions. They do not cross the chosen boundary. Gravity acts on the combined system, the floor acts through the feet, and the surrounding environment may add other contacts.

Redraw the boundary around the person alone. The object is now part of the environment. Its contact with the hands crosses the boundary and must appear in the external force inventory. Redraw again around one forearm, and interactions at the hand and elbow become external to that segment. Draw the boundary through a tendon, and the traction across the cut becomes part of the local accounting. The event did not change. The mechanical question did.

This is the plain-language use of a free-body diagram: select a body or subsystem, separate it conceptually from its surroundings, and inventory the interactions that cross the boundary. A force is not permanently internal or external. Its status depends on what has been included.[^02-02]

The boundary need not follow the skin or the edge of an anatomical structure. It can be drawn around a person and an assistive device, through a joint, across a patch of tissue, or around a fluid-filled region. The choice follows the question. If we want the force exchanged between hand and object, they must lie on opposite sides of the boundary. If we want the balance of the person–object pair, they can be grouped together. If we want local wall stress in a vessel, the whole-person boundary is too coarse even though it remains mechanically valid for another purpose.

Every boundary also creates a responsibility. We must account for what crosses it. A diagram that shows gravity but omits the supporting contact cannot balance. A segment diagram that includes a joint reaction but silently omits muscle and other soft-tissue actions may be a useful simplification only if those omitted actions are represented in the resultant or explicitly left unknown. Drawing a smaller boundary does not automatically make the description more accurate; it creates a more detailed question with more unknowns.

The time and phase matter as well. During a quiet hold, the object's acceleration may be negligible, so a quasi-static approximation can be useful. During lift-off, carrying, braking, or placement, momentum changes. The general balance is not “all forces cancel,” but that the sum of external forces equals the rate of change of linear momentum. Likewise, when the moment is taken about a fixed point *O* in an inertial frame, the sum of external moments about *O* equals the rate of change of angular momentum about *O*. Static equilibrium is one case of those balances, not the definition of a free-body diagram.[^02-02]

This method immediately exposes a common shortcut. Knowing the object's weight and the ground reaction does not tell us the force in a particular muscle, the contact distribution within a joint, or the stress in a tendon. Whole-body balance constrains the possibilities. Moving inward requires geometry, segment dynamics, active-force estimates, contact assumptions, material behavior, and sometimes an inverse model. In human movement analysis, many useful internal quantities are inferred from measured motion and external forces rather than observed directly.[^02-03]

> **Figure 2.1 — One task, several system boundaries [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> SAME EVENT: object held during transfer
>
> [person + object]       [person]             [forearm]             [tissue region]
> gravity on both         body weight          hand contact          surface traction
> floor contacts          floor contacts       elbow interaction     local deformation
> air/contact if needed   object at hands      gravity               material response
> hand-object exchange    hand-object force    muscle/tendon action  internal field
> is internal             is external          crosses boundary      requires a model
>
> HOLD: acceleration approximately zero     MOVE/BRAKE: acceleration retained
> STATUS: qualitative model inventory; no force value is presented as measured
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Redrawing the boundary changes which interactions are external and which quantities can be determined. It does not change the event, reveal local tissue stress, or identify a unique internal route.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four views of the same object-transfer phase progress from person plus object to person, forearm, and tissue region. Each smaller boundary adds interactions that were internal at the larger scale. A final contrast separates a quasi-static hold from an accelerating or braking phase.

Once the system is explicit, we can name its mechanical quantities without making them do one another's jobs.

## Force, moment, and pressure answer different questions

A force is a directed interaction. It has magnitude, direction, and a point or region of application. Its SI unit is the newton. When we replace a distributed interaction by a resultant force, we have compressed the description for a particular balance calculation. The resultant does not preserve every local detail of the distribution.

For rigid-body balance, a distributed contact is generally replaced by an equivalent resultant force *and* an equivalent resultant moment about a stated point. Matching the total force alone is not enough. Two contact patterns can push with the same net force while producing different turning effects; two patterns can share both resultant force and moment while still differing locally. This is the first example of a theme that will recur throughout the book: a valid coarse description constrains a finer one without uniquely determining it.

A moment describes the turning tendency of a force about a selected point or axis. If a force **F** acts at position **r** relative to point *O*, its moment about that point is

```text
M_O = r × F
```

The cross product fixes both the magnitude and direction of the moment. In a simple planar case, its magnitude is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from *O* to the force's line of action. That distance is the moment arm.

This is why the same backpack can create a different demand when it hangs close to the trunk or is held behind the body. Its weight may be unchanged, but its line of action has moved relative to a selected joint or segment. The corresponding external moment changes. We will use *moment* as the default technical term. *Torque* is common and often useful, especially for an applied couple or rotation about an axis, but it is not a separate substance hiding inside the body.

A couple makes the distinction especially clear. Two equal and opposite forces separated in space can produce no net force but still produce a nonzero moment. That turning action cannot be represented by pretending that one force follows a line through the anatomy. Conversely, a force's line of action tells us its moment arm about a selected point; it does not tell us where internal stress will be largest or which tissues will participate.

Moment is measured in newton metres. Work and energy can also be expressed in newton metres, conventionally called joules. Identical dimensions do not make moment and energy the same mechanical object. A moment is a directed turning effect about a point or axis; energy is a scalar accounting quantity.[^02-01]

Pressure answers another question. Contact between the hand and object, cartilage surfaces, the foot and floor, or a fluid and a wall is distributed. Surface traction is force per area with both normal and tangential components. At a solid interface, *contact pressure* refers to the compressive normal part of that distribution. It is a field over a stated surface, not merely a force divided by any convenient area. Dividing a normal resultant by area gives an average under stated assumptions; it can hide a strongly nonuniform distribution.

Fluid pressure is also measured in pascals, but it describes a scalar field within a fluid. A pressure difference may contribute to flow, and pressure acting on a surface produces a force, but pressure is neither flow nor force by itself. We must name the location, reference, boundary, and area before moving among them. In later chapters this distinction will matter wherever a solid contact, a pressure-bearing space, and a deformable conduit interact.

Consider a flexible tube. Its internal pressure, the pressure outside it, the difference between them, the wall geometry, wall stress, cross-sectional shape, resistance to flow, and volumetric flow rate are related but separate. A smaller lumen can alter flow conditions, while an external constraint can maintain the deformation that created the smaller lumen. Saying only that the tube is “under pressure” hides the direction of the pressure difference, the state of the wall, and the causal order. The tube will return later as an analogy, but the vocabulary already prevents the analogy from doing more than its mechanics allows.

None of these quantities is inherently supportive or harmful. That judgment requires a material, a configuration, a duration, a response, and a criterion. Here they are descriptions.

## Stress, strain, and deformation move the question inside the material

Now replace the body with an idealized strip. Pull its end through a distributed traction. The traction integrates to a resultant force, but the same resultant can produce different local fields if the strip's geometry, constraints, material directions, or contact conditions change. External force does not specify internal stress.

Stress describes the local intensity and orientation of internal mechanical interaction. In a continuum, the stress tensor at a point determines the traction acting across every possible plane through that point. Both stress and pressure have units of pascals, but one is a tensorial description of internal interaction and the other is a scalar field or scalar part of a contact description. The distinction is not pedantry; it determines which directions and surfaces the model can represent.[^02-04]

Deformation describes how material points change their relative positions. Displacement describes how a point moves relative to a chosen reference. Strain is a defined measure of relative deformation. A photograph can show a change in gross shape or position, but it does not by itself reveal the full strain field. Nor does a visible deformation reveal the stress that produced or maintains it.

Return to the idealized strip. If every point translates and rotates together without changing the distances among material points, the strip has moved but has not strained. If one end moves farther than the other, relative geometry changes. Even then, a single change in length captures only one component of a possibly nonuniform, multiaxial field. A narrow region, a change in cross-section, a contact, or a fixed edge can concentrate the deformation. Equal end displacement need not imply equal local strain; equal local strain need not imply equal stress when the material relation differs.

The reference state must be named. A living tissue observed at rest may already carry active tension, residual stress, fluid pressure, or constraint from surrounding structures. Its visible baseline is not necessarily unloaded or stress-free. When that state is unknown, the honest term is an observed baseline or a model reference—not zero stress.

Tension, compression, shear, bending, and torsion are useful components or loading descriptions. Real structures commonly experience several at once. A tendon can carry tensile stress while also bending around a surface. A vessel wall can experience multiaxial stress as pressure, axial tethering, flow, and surrounding contact change. A joint surface can carry compressive contact pressure alongside tangential traction. Assigning one word to the whole state may be useful shorthand, but it is not a complete field description.

Nor is strain a synonym for injury. Deformation is ordinary and necessary in living tissue. Whether a particular strain is accommodated, sensed, remodeled around, associated with fatigue, or linked to damage depends on its magnitude, direction, rate, duration, repetition, spatial distribution, material state, and biological context. Those bridges belong to later chapters and tissue-specific evidence. Here the important rule is narrower: first describe the deformation correctly; then ask what response follows.

Rate also belongs to the description. The same nominal change in length applied slowly or rapidly is not mechanically identical. Living tissues are heterogeneous, anisotropic, nonlinear, often viscoelastic or poroelastic, and actively maintained; their behavior can depend on direction, rate, history, hydration, activation, and timescale.[^02-05] These properties do not erase ordinary balance laws. They tell us that the relation between stress and strain requires a constitutive model and boundary conditions appropriate to the tissue and question.

This is also why local stress in living tissue is often model-dependent. Motion, geometry, external force, pressure, or deformation may be measured with an instrument, while an internal field is reconstructed from those observations through assumptions and inverse calculations. Methods for estimating tissue stress can be powerful, but they are not assumption-free and no method fits every scale or tissue.[^02-06]

The figures will use a compact provenance key. **OBS** marks a direct observation, **MEAS** an instrument-derived measurement, **CALC** a calculation from stated inputs, **INF** a nonunique inference, **MOD** a forward model or constructed schematic, **HYP** a proposed relation, and **EMB** an embodied report. These labels describe how a quantity entered the account; they do not rank its importance or make a measurement assumption-free.

>           |                         |                      |                       |

## Stiffness is not strength, and neither is capacity

When a structure is pushed, pulled, or rotated, stiffness relates a change in applied demand to a change in displacement or rotation over a stated range. Compliance describes the corresponding tendency to yield. For a simple one-dimensional relation, translational stiffness might be expressed in newtons per metre and compliance in metres per newton. In a joint, sheet, or tissue with several coupled directions, the relation may require a matrix or more complete constitutive model.

Stiffness depends on more than the material. Geometry, boundary conditions, direction, operating point, loading rate, and history all matter. An elastic modulus relates stress to strain for a stated material model; structural stiffness relates generalized demand to displacement for a structure. They are not synonyms.

More importantly for this book, stiff and compliant are not permanent moral or anatomical identities. A structure can be relatively stiff in one direction and compliant in another. Muscle activation can change the effective stiffness of an assembly without changing the passive material into a different tissue. A pressurized space can receive form in one phase and contribute structural support in another. A tendon can transmit substantial tension while bending or sliding relative to its surroundings.

Strength names a failure-associated value only after the material, geometry, loading mode, rate, and endpoint have been defined. Tolerance likewise requires an endpoint: material failure, fatigue, pain, physiological disturbance, loss of task performance, or something else. These outcomes cannot be exchanged silently.

Capacity is broader and more contextual. It is the present ability of a tissue, assembly, or person to meet a defined task or exposure criterion. Active control, fatigue, prior exposure, tissue state, pain, skill, sleep, recovery, assistance, and environment may all change it. Capacity is therefore not one material constant attached permanently to a person.

The object transfer makes this concrete. A person may complete the same external task before and after fatigue while changing speed, grip, stance, assistance, or internal distribution. The endpoint “object moved successfully” does not show that the same structures carried the same demand. Conversely, a different movement solution does not by itself show diminished capacity; it may be a deliberate, efficient, protective, learned, or merely available alternative. Capacity has to be defined against an endpoint, not inferred from visual conformity.

This is also where the mechanical terms *stiff* and *compliant* must remain separate from the later hard/soft vocabulary. Stiffness and compliance are measured relations under specified conditions. Hard and soft will name relative jobs within an organization: preserving or resolving form versus receiving or conforming to it. A structure can be mechanically stiff in a tested direction while performing a form-receiving role at another scale, or compliant in one mode while helping stabilize an assembly in another.

A reserve can be discussed only when demand and capacity are expressed in comparable terms. Subtracting a force from a duration or a modeled strain from a person's confidence does not create a mechanical margin. Those observations may all matter, but they belong in a structured account rather than an invented common unit.

## Mechanical exposure has a history

“Too much load” often compresses several different claims. Was the peak large? Was the direction unusual for the selected tissue? Was the application rapid? Was the deformation sustained? Did the event repeat with little rest? Did the sequence vary, or did the same region receive the same demand every time? What was the system's state before the exposure, and what recovery occurred afterward?

A useful mechanical history can therefore include magnitude, direction, rate, duration, repetition, frequency, sequence, variability, rest intervals, and recovery context. This list is not a formula. The entries have different units and cannot simply be added. Their relevance depends on the tissue, task, state, timescale, and response being studied.[^02-07]

Sometimes one summary measure is enough. Peak force may answer a bounded structural question. Impulse may matter when the time integral of force is relevant. Cycle count may help in a fatigue model. Work or energy may clarify storage and dissipation. But each summary retains some features and discards others. A richer descriptor earns its place only if it improves explanation or prediction over a simpler one.

Biological meaning enters only after the history has been defined. In controlled bone-loading research, for example, local response depends not merely on an externally applied force but on strain magnitude and other loading parameters, with distinct adaptive and injury-associated outcomes in the studied models.[^02-08] That is useful evidence for the importance of exposure structure in one tissue and experimental context. It is not a universal dose equation for cartilage, tendon, nerve, vessel, muscle, or a whole person.

The same restraint applies to variability and rest. Either can be useful, neutral, or adverse depending on the system. We should not turn “variation is good” or “repetition is bad” into a mechanical law. The correct result may be that a peak value dominates, that several history features interact, or that the proposed descriptor adds no explanatory value.

Sequence can matter even when totals match. Ten repetitions followed by rest do not necessarily produce the same state as the same ten repetitions interleaved with another task. A rapid demand applied after fatigue may meet a different active and material state than the same demand applied first. Recovery is therefore not a force to subtract from exposure. It is a change in the system receiving the next event. Later chapters will ask how that state changes; this chapter only requires that the timeline remain visible.

>
> **Text alternative.** Five time series on identical axes contrast short and sustained exposure, repetition, variable sequencing with rest, and rapid application. A separate layer lists starting state, prior exposure, recovery, and the response window rather than combining them into the curves.

## Work, energy, and the paths of transfer

Work and energy add another useful view. Mechanical work is energy transferred when a force acts through displacement or a moment acts through rotation. Power is the rate of that transfer. A muscle–tendon unit may generate, store, return, or dissipate mechanical energy; an external task may involve different energy accounts depending on the system boundary. Net joint power does not, by itself, tell us the work of every individual muscle or tissue.[^02-03]

Energy is not a substance that must travel along one anatomical line. Nor is lower mechanical or metabolic cost automatically healthier. A whole-body claim about efficiency requires an objective, a comparison class, a task, and an account of what costs are being included. Those questions matter to the wider series, but they are not settled by naming work and power.

This brings us to *load path*. In ordinary structural teaching, a load path links an applied load to the forces that bring a structure into equilibrium.[^02-09] That is a useful starting point. Living systems require a broader, explicitly declared representation. A load path may describe how a defined demand is distributed, transferred, opposed, and ultimately balanced through skeletal contact, joint resultants, tensile structures, active muscle, pressure-mediated support, sliding interfaces, or several carriers at once.

A defensible path must therefore begin and end. A force-and-moment route begins with a stated interaction crossing a boundary and ends in reactions, momentum-rate or inertial terms, or another explicitly bounded mechanical interaction. A separate work-and-energy account can track transfer, storage, return, and dissipation through the same task. The two accounts can inform one another, but they do not conserve or trace the same object. Between endpoints, any path must preserve the mechanical object it claims to follow. A force cannot silently become pressure, then sensation, then health merely because arrows connect the words. Each change of description needs its own relation and evidence.

The path need not be a single line. It may be a branching graph, a contact network, a distributed stress field, or a time-varying relation. It has no unit of its own. Each edge, arrow, or region must say what it represents: force, moment, pressure, traction, stress, deformation, or another defined quantity. It must also say whether that quantity was measured, calculated, inferred, modeled, hypothesized, or reported as an embodied experience.

Several paths can be mechanically compatible with the same external task. Active forces can redistribute resultants. Contact can migrate. Pressure can change which boundaries contribute support. A structure can participate strongly in one phase and little in another. Nonuniqueness is not a failure of the idea; it is a property the model must represent. A single path earns priority only through a declared criterion and discriminating evidence, not through the visual smoothness of a line.

Three related expressions deserve especially careful separation.

First, the **line of action** of a specified force is a geometric line through its point of application and parallel to the force. It lets us calculate a moment arm. It does not show how the demand is distributed inside the body. A pure couple has no line of action, and a general three-dimensional contact may require both a resultant force and a resultant moment.

Second, an **inferred internal force line** is a project term for a proposed relation among regions or carriers during a task. The relation may be mechanically coherent and useful while remaining nonunique. To become a testable mechanical claim, it needs a system boundary, quantity, scale, phase, candidate carriers, balance or compatibility check, and observations capable of distinguishing it from diffuse or alternative paths.

Third, an **embodied force line** describes a felt continuity or internal connection. Such an experience can be specific, repeatable, and important without already being a measured resultant or anatomical cable. Its immediate evidence is phenomenological: who reported it, during which task, on which side, in which phase, and with what repeatability. It can then motivate a mechanical hypothesis and a search for correlates. Mechanical underdetermination does not require erasing the observation; experiential precision does not remove the need for measurement.

The three meanings can refer to aspects of the same event. They cannot inherit one another's evidentiary status. A force's external line of action does not prove an internal route. A modeled route is not directly measured because its diagram looks anatomical. A felt connection is not a force in newtons until an operational relation earns that interpretation.

> **Figure 2.5 — Three meanings of force line [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Sense | Representation | Provenance status | What is known | What remains open |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | External line of action | Solid force arrow with a thin geometric extension | `MEAS` when instrumentally measured; `CALC` when derived from stated inputs | Specified force, application point or region, and frame | Internal distribution |
> | Inferred internal relation | Dashed branching network among named carriers | `INF` for an inference from observations; `MOD` for a declared model; `HYP` while proposed for testing | Task, boundary, quantities, assumptions, and evidence used | Uniqueness, exact carriers, validation, alternatives |
> | Embodied continuity | Distinct perceptual annotation tied to reporter and phase | `EMB` for the report; `OBS` only for separately observed task features | Reported experience, context, and repeatability | Mechanical quantity, anatomical correlate, causal role |
>
> **Caption.** Similar language does not make these objects identical. The embodied sense may generate a mechanical question; the inferred sense may organize a model; only the external sense is the ordinary geometric line of a stated force.
>
> **Text alternative.** A three-row comparison contrasts an external force line, a branching inferred internal relation, and an embodied report. Each row separates what is directly specified from the mechanical or anatomical questions that remain open.

## From an object in the hands to mechanical organization

We can now describe the original transfer without asking the word *load* to do everything.

The object and the ground apply external forces to the person. Their effects depend on the task phase, acceleration, points of contact, geometry, and selected frame. At a segment, these interactions contribute to resultants and moments. Within a joint or tissue region, active forces, contact, pressure, material behavior, and boundary conditions shape a distribution that may be measured in part and modeled in part. Stress and strain describe local material states; displacement and visible geometry do not substitute for them. Repetition adds a history whose relevant features depend on the receiver and endpoint. A load path organizes this transfer only when its quantities, carriers, scale, time, and provenance are visible.

This language gives us discipline, not destiny. It does not tell us that one configuration is best, that one route is universal, or that a measured exposure necessarily produces injury, recovery, comfort, or disease. It tells us how to state those stronger questions so they can be investigated rather than implied.

One question now becomes unavoidable. If a living system can distribute demand through structures that preserve geometry, structures that actively generate and transmit force, structures that slide or conform, and spaces that bear pressure, how is the mechanical labor divided among them?

The next chapter introduces a compact answer: relatively shape-preserving and structurally resolving roles work with relatively form-receiving and shape-conforming roles. That distinction is motivated by traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts, while its mechanical use here remains a flexible translation rather than an exact identity. The quantities in this chapter do not decide that division of labor. They make it possible to inspect.
