# Chapter 3 — Hard and soft mechanical roles

The object is halfway between one support and the next. Its weight no longer rests on the table. The hands contact it, the feet contact the floor, and the person continues to breathe, balance, and move. This is the same ordinary, non-prescriptive object transfer used in the first two chapters. Chapter 2 gave us several ways to describe it. We can draw an external force, calculate a moment, represent joint resultants, discuss pressure at a contact, and ask how stress, strain, deformation, and energy change through time. None of those quantities, by itself, tells us how the structures involved divide the work.

Some relationships must remain organized well enough for the object to be supported. Others must change. Joints rotate. Muscle length and activation change. Tendons carry tension and may change length or course. Cartilage deforms at contact. Pressure-bearing spaces change state. Skin conforms to the object. The same event requires both persistence and accommodation, often in the same structure at different scales or in different directions.

This book proposes a compact way to name that division:

> Load wants to travel through the hard body so that the soft body can remain soft.

The wording is intentionally direct. It is also easy to misunderstand. It is not a law of motion, a claim that force literally wants anything, or a division between bone and everything else. *Load* remains umbrella language until a technical application names the force, moment, pressure, stress, deformation, or other quantity at issue. *Hard* and *soft* name relative mechanical roles.

The distinction is **motivated by** traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts. That origin is part of the project and should be stated rather than hidden. Book I makes a flexible mechanical translation of the motivating polarity. It does not claim that the translation is historically exact, that every traditional use reduces to mechanics, or that correspondence with a traditional category validates a mechanical proposition.

The mechanical question can therefore stand on its own: under a specified demand, which relationships preserve enough shape and continuity to establish or resolve a path, and which structures need to remain available to receive form and change?

## Support requires both persistence and change

A body that preserved every relation perfectly could not reach, breathe, circulate, absorb contact, or place the object down. A body that preserved no usable relation could not support the object or direct it toward the next surface. Living support depends on selected persistence amid selected change.

We use *hard role* for behavior that is comparatively shape-preserving, path-establishing, constraining, or structurally resolving under declared conditions. We use *soft role* for behavior that is comparatively form-receiving and shape-conforming: a structure yields rather than imposing the gross geometry of the selected assembly, while remaining available for the deformation, glide, containment, expansion, recoil, or other change required for its function.

Both definitions are relational. They require a system, scale, direction, task, phase, state, reference, and timescale. The hand can preserve its relation to one face of the object while the skin and subcutaneous tissues conform locally to the contact. A joint assembly can preserve a useful relation in one direction while permitting rotation in another. An entire limb can establish a comparatively firm route even though every one of its tissues deforms.

Neither role is a substance. Hard does not mean perfectly rigid. Soft does not mean weak, passive, unloaded, or mechanically unimportant. Force transmission alone does not make a structure hard, because a form-receiving structure can transmit substantial force. Deformation alone does not make a structure soft, because every material body deforms under demand. The useful distinction is the job performed by a selected relation: what must remain organized, and what must remain available to change?

> **Figure 3.1 — One task, changing mechanical roles [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Selected relation | Declared conditions | Comparatively shape-preserving job | Comparatively form-receiving job | Status and limit |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Hand–object contact | Hand and contact scale; normal and tangential directions; supported phase; active state; seconds | Multi-structure hand assembly maintains contact and directs the object | Skin and other local interfaces conform to object geometry | Constructed model; no unique internal route or ideal grip |
> | Tendon in a selected transfer phase | Named tendon region; longitudinal versus transverse or bending directions; loaded state; event timescale | Longitudinal tension can help preserve a tensile relation | Transverse compression, bending, and sliding can change local form | Ordinary mechanics with tissue-specific evidence; no universal tendon assignment |
> | Articular contact while configuration changes | Local interface inside a joint; surface-normal and tangential directions; fluid-saturated state; task interval | Joint assembly retains a usable larger-scale relation | Cartilage deforms while the fluid–solid system shares contact demand | Bounded tissue model; no inference about every joint or disease |
> | Active or pressure-supported assembly | Declared region; perturbation and volume-change directions; before and during demand; activation or pressure specified; event timescale | Activation or pressure can make a deformable assembly comparatively firm | The same assembly can change length, volume, or shape in another phase | Comparative hypothesis until the selected system is measured |
>
> **Caption.** Hard and soft are attached to relations, directions, phases, states, scales, and timescales rather than permanently to tissues. The vocabulary is motivated by TCM hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts, but these mechanical roles neither define nor validate the traditional categories. Substantial force or deformation can occur in either role. The figure does not establish one preferred object-transfer strategy or a body-wide route.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows show simultaneous and changing roles during an ordinary object transfer. Each row declares its scale, direction, phase, state, and timescale. A hand assembly preserves contact while local tissues conform; tendon transmits longitudinal tension while bending or sliding transversely; cartilage deforms inside a larger joint relation; and active or pressure-supported assemblies can become comparatively firm while remaining deformable. The assignments are conditional rather than fixed tissue labels, and the stated TCM motivation is not presented as mechanical evidence.

## Hard is not the same as rigid

Bone is the easiest introductory example of a hard role because its geometry and material properties often contribute strongly to shape preservation, leverage, contact, and transmission. But even this example is relative. Bone is elastic, anisotropic, heterogeneous, and organized across scales. Its whole-structure behavior depends not only on tissue material but also on geometry, orientation, support, and the way demand is applied.[^03-01] Calling bone comparatively shape-preserving does not mean that it does not deform. It means that, for a declared relation and timescale, its deformation is compatible with maintaining the larger job.

This separation between material and structural behavior matters. A material test may report a stress–strain relation in a particular specimen and direction. A joint, limb, or whole-body assembly includes geometry, contact, active forces, restraints, and boundary conditions. The stiffness measured in one experiment is not a portable label for everything the tissue or assembly will do. Even the phrase *joint stiffness* can refer to different components, methods, and levels of description unless the system and procedure are specified.[^03-02]

A hard role can therefore be performed by structures that anatomy classifies as soft tissue. A tensioned tendon or ligament can help preserve a relation between its attachments. Active muscle can change the demand–displacement behavior of an assembly. Coactivation can increase resistance to a perturbation, although its relation to stability, movement, and cost depends on the task and model; more activation is not automatically better.[^03-03] Several individually deformable elements can also create a comparatively shape-preserving whole.

Pressure gives an especially clean counterexample to bone-only thinking. Hydrostatic skeletons use internal pressure, tensioned walls, muscle, and approximately volume-conserving contents to support and transmit force without rigid skeletal elements.[^03-04] They do not show that any particular human cavity functions in the same way. They show something more basic: shape-preserving support is an assembly-level mechanical job, not the exclusive property of a mineralized material.

Hard is also not a synonym for strong, high-capacity, healthy, or beneficial. A comparatively firm route can be poorly oriented for the task, under-capacity for the imposed demand, energetically costly, or too restrictive of another needed freedom. A high-capacity structure can receive form. A low-capacity structure can temporarily establish a path. Strength describes a defined endpoint, capacity describes present ability relative to a task or exposure, and the hard role describes how a relation is being organized. None can be inferred from either of the others.

The hard role is therefore modest but useful. It asks us to identify the relation being preserved and the combination of geometry, contact, active force, tension, pressure, or external support that preserves it. If we cannot name that relation, *hard* has become atmosphere rather than analysis.

## Softness is a positive capacity

The word *soft* is often heard as a deficit: less stiff, less strong, less stable, or less capable. That is not its job here. A soft role receives form. It permits a structure to accommodate surrounding geometry and demand without having to determine the gross geometry of the assembly. Its yielding can permit a course change, relative motion, volume change, contact distribution, containment, recoil, or reversible accommodation. These expressions differ mechanically, but each depends on some freedom to change.

Form reception can occur under substantial load. Tendon is anatomically soft tissue and can carry large longitudinal tension. Tendons and aponeuroses can store and return energy, attenuate power, or alter how muscle work reaches the skeleton; they are not passive cords that merely pass a force packet onward.[^03-05] In a study of porcine wrap-around tendons, the measured response varied by region and among tensile, compressive, and combined multiaxial loading.[^03-06] Separate equine experiments found function-related differences at fascicular interfaces, including greater sliding in the tested energy-storing tendon.[^03-13] These findings do not establish a universal human route. They do show why one label cannot capture every direction and interface. A tendon can participate in a comparatively shape-preserving tensile relation along its length while receiving form where it bends, compresses, or slides.

Articular cartilage provides a different counterexample. It is deformable and fluid-saturated. Under studied contact conditions, interstitial fluid pressurization and the solid matrix share load over time; deformation and pressure-mediated support coexist.[^03-07] Cartilage may therefore receive local contact form while contributing to a larger joint relation that remains organized. Calling this a soft role does not mean that the tissue carries little demand. Calling the larger assembly hard does not mean that one rigid component carries everything.

Ligaments likewise resist simple classification. Their mechanical response is nonlinear, anisotropic, and time-dependent, and their contribution to joint restraint changes with the ligament, direction, configuration, and loading condition.[^03-08] A selected ligament can remain comparatively accommodating through part of a range and become a substantial restraint in another part. The change is not a moral transition from soft to good. It is a change in mechanical role under changed conditions.

Muscle can change length while active and transmitting force. Fascia can deform, slide, tension, or participate in local transfer. Neither observation assigns a permanent role. They protect the central meaning: softness is the capacity to receive form under stated conditions, not the absence of force or agency.

This positive definition also supplies a necessary limit. More softness is not automatically better. Unbounded deformation, inadequate restraint, or insufficient structural resolution may prevent a task. The proposition is not that every structure should yield as much as possible. It is that form-receiving functions need enough freedom for the declared job while the surrounding organization resolves gross demand. *Enough* must eventually become a measured comparison, not a preferred look.

## A candidate handoff from accommodation to resolution

A more specific intuition is nested inside the general polarity: fascia or muscle gathers, actuates, accommodates, or directs demand; tendon or ligament transfers or constrains it; bone or joint geometry resolves it through a more shape-preserving route. This pattern is proposed as a first-order anatomical hypothesis. It does not define hard and soft, and it is not a universal conveyor belt.

Return to the object while it is supported in the hands. Active muscle force contributes to the hand's contact with the object. Tendons connect muscle action to skeletal attachments. Bones and joint contacts contribute geometry and transmit resultants. Ligaments can restrain or guide particular relations. Other muscles act in parallel, external contacts complete the support problem, and pressure and compliant interfaces participate. The event is not a single serial chain even when a muscle–tendon–bone sequence is mechanically important.

The attachment between tendon or ligament and bone makes the idea of *handoff* more precise. Many attachments—especially fibrocartilaginous entheses—are regionally graded rather than sharp borders between two uniform materials. Neighboring tissues and changing fiber or mineral organization help distribute demand across a mechanically dissimilar transition.[^03-09] The anatomy makes transfer into bone concrete while correcting the picture of a force packet crossing an abrupt soft–hard boundary.

Fascia requires the same discipline. Anatomical continuities exist, and experimental literature supports some force transmission across adjacent myofascial structures. A systematic review also found important methodological limits and uncertainty about functional magnitude and body-wide significance.[^03-10] A named fascial attachment or interface can enter a bounded path. Morphological continuity alone does not prove one dominant whole-body chain, a traditional channel, or a preferred posterior route.

> selected phase: object supported in the hands
>
> object–hand contact [external interaction]
>            |
>            v
> active muscle and compliant interfaces [actuation / accommodation]
>            |
>            +------ parallel active structures ------+
>            v                                         |
> tendon or task-relevant restraint [tensile transfer] |
>            |                                         |
>      graded attachment                               |
>            v                                         v
> bone, joint contact, and geometry [structural resolution]
>            |
>            +---- pressure, fascia, ligament, and other contacts
>                  enter only where named and mechanically relevant
>
> status: candidate bounded hypothesis, not a measured unique route
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The proposed handoff preserves a recurring muscle/fascia–tendon/ligament–bone/joint intuition while showing graded interfaces, branches, and parallel carriers. Each arrow must name its mechanical quantity in a technical application. The figure does not establish a mandatory sequence, route dominance, health effect, or technique.
>
> **Text alternative.** An object–hand interaction leads into active muscle and compliant interfaces, then into a task-relevant tensile carrier and a graded attachment, and finally into bone and joint contact. A large parallel branch returns other active structures to the skeletal relation, while pressure, fascia, ligament, and other contacts are shown as conditional contributors rather than required stages. The entire diagram is labeled a bounded hypothesis rather than a measured unique route.

The candidate pattern is useful when it produces better questions. Did the named tensile structure participate in the selected phase? Did the joint geometry actually resolve the resultant being discussed? Did another path carry a substantial share? Did a form-receiving interface retain the movement or deformation its function required? If the answers differ from the proposed sequence, the sequence must change. The body is not obligated to preserve the diagram.

Later chapters test a possible adverse case: a structure that needs to receive form may become a maintained substitute boundary when another shape-preserving relation is unavailable or unrecruited. Chapter 3 does not assume that substitution has occurred; it establishes the roles and observations needed to ask the question.

## Roles change with direction, state, scale, and phase

The object transfer is not one mechanical instant. Contact begins, the object leaves its support, the person may accelerate or carry it, and a new surface eventually accepts it. The demand, active state, contact geometry, and available supports change across those phases. A defensible role assignment can change with them.

During initial contact, local conformation helps the hand meet the object's surface while the larger hand assembly establishes a usable relation. As the table ceases to support the object, active and tensile structures contribute to the new demand, while joint contacts and skeletal geometry participate in transmitting it toward the person's supports. During steady carrying, the external acceleration may be small while active force and internal distribution remain substantial. At placement, the receiving surface progressively takes back the object's weight and the previous route becomes less important. This sequence is a constructed description, not an instruction about how to lift. Its point is that the same tissue name does not carry one role unchanged from first touch to release.

Nor does a visible change identify the switch by itself. A different joint angle may accompany a different role assignment, but geometry alone does not reveal active force, contact distribution, tissue stress, or route dominance. The comparison becomes mechanical only when the proposed carrier, receiving freedom, and observable are stated for both phases. Two visibly different transfers may preserve the same functional division through different carriers; two similar-looking transfers may divide the work differently.

Direction is often the easiest switch to see. Tendon can resist longitudinal tension while accommodating transverse compression or bending. Bone and joint geometry can preserve one relation while allowing rotation in another. A fascial plane can transmit tension in one direction while permitting relative movement at an adjacent interface. Saying that a tissue is hard or soft without a direction loses the distinction the model was meant to create.

State can change the same assembly. Activation alters muscle force and the resistance of a joint relation to displacement. Internal pressure and wall tension can change the firmness of a deformable compartment. Ligament recruitment changes with joint configuration. Material response can also depend on rate and history. The role at the start of a task need not be the role during a perturbation or after sustained demand.

Scale adds another reversal. Cartilage can receive form locally while the joint assembly remains comparatively shape-preserving. Individual bones deform while a skeletal relation persists. Several compliant components can create a firm pressure-supported whole. Conversely, a tissue that is stiff in a specimen test may belong to an assembly that changes gross shape. The role belongs to the selected system, not to the smallest named material.

These switches make the proposal observable in principle. A role claim should identify:

1. the selected system and boundary;
2. the relation proposed to remain organized;
3. the form-receiving structure and the freedom its job requires;
4. the demand, direction, phase, state, and timescale;
5. the candidate carriers and parallel paths; and
6. what was observed or measured, what was calculated or modeled, and what remains inferred.

Possible observations include relative displacement, rotation, shape retention, contact migration, active force, pressure, load share, local deformation, excursion, glide, and recovery after a perturbation. None is a universal hard/soft meter. Stress inside a living tissue, in particular, is often inferred through models or specialized methods rather than read directly from visible shape; the distinction among observed deformation, measured force, and model-dependent stress must remain explicit.[^03-11]

A role switch should be predicted before the outcome is known. If activation is proposed to make an assembly more shape-preserving, a declared perturbation and response can be compared across activation states. If a tendon is proposed to exchange roles by direction, longitudinal and transverse observables should differ in a specified way. If a form-receiving interface is said to need glide, that excursion and its task relevance must be examined separately. A label applied only after every result cannot discriminate anything.

## The model must add something to ordinary mechanics

Hard and soft do not replace established mechanical descriptions. Their value depends on whether the paired questions—what relation remains organized, and what neighboring freedom remains available—add something useful to a bounded analysis.

The comparison can be made explicitly:

| Conventional description | What it can establish | What a hard/soft claim would still need to add |
|---|---|---|
| Material class | Tissue composition and conventional anatomy | Why that tissue or assembly performs a particular role in this direction and phase |
| Stiffness or compliance | A stated demand–displacement relation around a defined condition | Which gross relation is being preserved and which neighboring change must remain available |
| Strength or capacity | A failure, tolerance, or task endpoint under declared conditions | How the work is divided before that endpoint is reached |
| Impedance or stability | Dynamic response, resistance to motion, or return under a chosen criterion | Whether preserving that response retains or suppresses the receiver's required freedom |
| Load share | The fraction of a defined resultant or contact demand carried by a component | Why a large or small share corresponds to one role rather than simply to participation |
| Prestress or tensegrity-like organization | How internal tension, compression, and geometry cooperate | A task-specific role assignment and a test that does not depend on visual resemblance |

Material class tells us what a tissue is conventionally called. It cannot settle the role because anatomically soft tissues transmit major forces and bone deforms. Stiffness and compliance describe a force–displacement, moment–rotation, pressure–volume, or related response under specified conditions. They can help measure a role, but they do not automatically identify which form-changing freedom matters to the task. Strength describes a failure or performance endpoint. Capacity adds present state and task context. Neither identifies the division of labor.

Impedance can organize dynamic relations among force and motion. Stability can describe a bounded response or return criterion. Load share can estimate how much of a defined resultant or contact demand a component carries. Prestress and tensegrity-like models can describe cooperation among tension, compression, and geometry. These are possible competitors or complements, not synonyms. The hard/soft vocabulary earns a distinct scientific place only if it improves comparison, prediction, or measurement beyond the simpler description.[^03-12]

The strongest null result is straightforward: a conventional account of geometry, stiffness, contact, activation, pressure, and load share may explain the selected event just as well. In that case, hard and soft may remain a useful heuristic and an honest record of the project's intellectual provenance, but they have not added a separate mechanical explanation.

The best opportunity for added value lies in the pairing. A model focused only on preserving one angle or increasing one stiffness can miss the cost imposed on a neighboring structure's necessary movement. A model focused only on local deformation can miss the larger relation that makes that deformation useful. The hard/soft proposal asks for both at once. In the object transfer, for example, maintaining contact is not enough if the arrangement prevents the changes needed to take or release the object; local compliance is not enough if the assembly cannot support and redirect it. Whether this paired description predicts anything beyond a conventional multivariable model remains an empirical question.

The model is also weakened when:

- the roles cannot be assigned until after the outcome is known;
- the proposed shape-preserving carrier does not measurably participate in the selected demand;
- the proposed form-receiving structure does not exhibit or require the named freedom;
- changing direction, activation, pressure, support, or phase does not produce the predicted role change;
- every heavily loaded structure is redefined as hard and every yielding one as soft after the fact; or
- an ordinary mechanical model predicts the same result with fewer assumptions.

These are not apologies for the proposition. They make it a proposition rather than an aesthetic preference. A flexible vocabulary becomes scientifically useful by accepting the possibility that it will add value in some systems, remain descriptive in others, and fail in still others.

## A visible traditional provenance

The hard/soft vocabulary did not arise here from a neutral search through mechanics textbooks. It was motivated by TCM hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts and by an embodied sense of a yielding, internally connective organization that can receive and coordinate force without becoming a rigid external strut. Naming that motivation protects the actual research program. It prevents a later mechanical translation from being mistaken for the whole origin of the idea.

It also establishes a boundary. An embodied force line, as Chapter 2 described it, is first evidence of a reported experience in a task and phase. It can motivate a proposed internal relation. It is not thereby a measured resultant or an anatomical cable. In the same way, a traditional distinction can motivate a mechanical hypothesis without supplying mechanical evidence for it.

Book I owns only the general translation: relative shape preservation and structural resolution paired with relative form reception and shape conformation. It does not reconstruct the historical meanings of hard, soft, Yin, or Yang; map channels or Six Divisions; assign signed body coordinates; or prove that the mechanical and traditional objects are equivalent. Those later questions require their own textual, historical, anatomical, embodied, and empirical work.

The evidence paths remain separate. Traditional sources must support a historical claim. A reported experience must retain its embodied provenance. Mechanical measurements and models must support the mechanical claim. Agreement among the three can become a question worth investigating, but resemblance is not validation by correspondence.

## From roles to paths

Return to the object between the supports. We can now ask more than which tissues are loaded. We can ask which relations preserve a usable route under the selected demand and which structures need to remain available to conform, move, contain, or change. The answer will not divide the body permanently. It will change with direction, activation, pressure, task phase, scale, and time.

Ordinary biomechanics already establishes the essential counterexamples: bone deforms; tendon and ligament can carry substantial tension; muscle and pressure can make an assembly comparatively firm; cartilage can deform while sharing load; and several paths can cooperate. The proposal developed here is a synthesis placed over that common ground. Hard names relative shape preservation and structural resolution. Soft names relative form reception. The candidate tissue handoff preserves one important anatomical intuition, but it remains narrower than the polarity and open to branches, parallel carriers, and disconfirmation.

What remains unresolved is whether this paired language improves observation or prediction in any selected system beyond established variables. That question cannot be answered by making the definitions more flexible. It requires predeclared roles, measurements, comparators, and results that can favor the simpler account.

Roles alone are not yet paths. To locate a shape-preserving relation or a form-receiving freedom, we need a three-dimensional configuration, a reference frame, directions, contacts, and a way to represent several simultaneous or changing routes. Chapter 4 takes up that spatial problem: how do mechanical roles become organized within one or more load paths through a living body?

# Chapter 4 — Three-dimensional configuration and load paths

The object has left the table and is moving toward a shelf. Its weight acts toward the floor. The hands contact it at separated surfaces. The person changes the object's speed and direction while remaining supported through the feet. This is still the ordinary, non-prescriptive transfer used throughout Part I, but it now exposes a problem that a list of mechanical quantities cannot solve by itself: where, and through what arrangement, is the demand being carried?

From across the room, the event may look like a single object moving upward and forward. At the hands, it is a changing contact problem. At an elbow, it includes forces and moments expressed relative to the forearm or upper arm. Along a curved tendon, the useful directions may follow and cross the tissue rather than the walls of the room. Inside a joint, the relevant description may be a distributed contact stress rather than one visible line. All of these descriptions can concern the same event without being interchangeable.

Chapter 3 gave us two relative mechanical roles. Some relations are comparatively shape-preserving and path-establishing; others are comparatively form-receiving and shape-conforming. Roles alone, however, do not locate anything. To turn them into a mechanical account, we need to state the system boundary, describe its three-dimensional configuration, choose one or more reference frames, identify contacts and constraints, and say what quantity a proposed path carries.

That requirement is more than technical housekeeping. A direction that is obvious in the room may not be the direction that matters at a joint or along a tissue. A posture that looks unchanged may conceal a different distribution of active force or pressure. A line that correctly represents an external resultant may say little about the several internal carriers that balance it. Conversely, a full three-dimensional model can add detail without improving the answer if the omitted dimension was never consequential.

The aim of this chapter is therefore disciplined description, not maximal complexity. We will ask when a plane is enough, when it is not, what belongs in a configuration, how load paths can branch or change, and how four different kinds of three-direction description can be kept separate. The result is a spatial grammar for the rest of the book. It does not yet identify one preferred organization of the body.

## One transfer, several descriptions

Begin with the object alone. Draw a boundary around it during the carrying phase. Gravity acts on its mass, the hands exert contact forces and perhaps contact moments, and its changing motion determines the balance those external interactions must satisfy. This is a free-body description. It can be expressed in a room-fixed frame whose vertical axis follows gravity, in an object-fixed frame that turns with the object, or in another declared basis suited to the task. The physical interactions do not change merely because their components are written in a different basis.[^04-01]

Now move the boundary. Include the hands and forearms with the object. The hand–object forces that were external to the object-only system become internal interactions within the enlarged system. Forces at the elbows and the same gravitational and inertial accounting enter the new boundary problem. Enlarge it again to include the whole person, and the contacts with the floor become especially important. This is not another view of the same free body. It is a different free body, with a different boundary and a different set of external interactions.

The distinction is basic:

- a **change of frame** changes the coordinates used to describe a physical quantity; and
- a **change of boundary** changes which interactions count as external and which remain internal to the selected system.

Confusing them creates false disagreements. Two analysts may report different numerical components because one uses the room and the other the forearm as a basis. Their vectors can still represent the same physical interaction. Or they may draw identical-looking arrows while analyzing different boundaries, in which case the arrows do different mechanical jobs.

Time supplies another difference. During a quiet hold, the object's acceleration may be small even though the hands continue to support it. During departure from the table or arrival at the shelf, acceleration and changing contact alter the balance. A single still image does not identify those phases. The useful description must therefore name not only the boundary and frame but also the time or task phase to which it applies.

> **Figure 4.1 — One event, several frames and boundaries [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> ROOM / TASK FRAME                 OBJECT FRAME
> vertical follows gravity         axes turn with the object
>          ↑ z                              ↑ z_o
>          |                                |____ x_o
>       [object]  → x                    [object]
>        /     \
>     hand     hand
>
> OBJECT-ONLY BOUNDARY              OBJECT + ARMS BOUNDARY
> hand contacts are external        hand contacts are internal
> gravity is external               elbow interactions are external
>
> LOCAL CURVED FRAME ALONG A CARRIER
> tangent follows the selected centerline;
> transverse directions must be constructed and declared
> ```
>
> **Caption.** A change of basis re-expresses the same physical quantity, while a change of system boundary changes the free-body problem. A local moving frame can follow a curved structure, but its transverse directions are modeling choices rather than hidden anatomical facts.
>
> **Text alternative.** The diagram compares a room frame, an object-fixed frame, two different system boundaries, and a local frame along a curved carrier. It emphasizes that coordinates may change without changing the physical vector, whereas enlarging the boundary changes which contacts are external.

The same discipline applies to every later use of *load path*. Before asking where a path goes, we must know which system is under study, which interaction starts the accounting, which support or boundary completes it, which phase is being represented, and which frame makes the stated direction meaningful.

## Frames are chosen, not discovered

A reference frame gives an origin and a set of directions from which positions, orientations, vectors, and tensor components can be reported. Biomechanics commonly uses standardized segment and joint coordinate systems so that measurements can be compared, but even a standard remains a declared convention. Reporting recommendations exist precisely because apparently simple words such as flexion, rotation, force, and moment can become ambiguous when the segment, origin, axes, sign, or expression frame is left unstated.[^04-02]

Different questions favor different frames. A room or task frame is useful for gravity, a shelf, a floor, or the motion of the carried object. A segment frame can follow the forearm or pelvis. A joint or surface frame can describe contact relative to an articular geometry. A tissue frame can follow fibers, a centerline, or a local material direction. None is universally primary. The best choice is the one that makes the relevant boundary conditions and comparison inspectable without hiding important components.

Suppose a force vector is resolved into three room-fixed components. If the analyst rotates the basis, the component values change according to the transformation between frames, while the geometric vector does not. The same is true of a moment, although the point about which the moment is taken must also be stated. Stress and strain require tensor transformations rather than the transformation for a single vector. Carrying a familiar axis label from one kind of object to another does not carry the transformation law with it.

Local frames become more delicate when a structure curves. A centerline supplies a tangent direction at each regular point, but it does not automatically supply two unique transverse directions. The classical tangent–normal–binormal frame can become undefined where curvature vanishes and can rotate abruptly in ways that are unhelpful for some applications. A rotation-minimizing or Bishop frame offers another construction, but it too requires an initial orientation and an explicit transport rule.[^04-03] The lesson is not that one construction is correct for every tissue. It is that a moving frame must be built and documented.

Cylindrical language can be useful around a clear axis. An axial direction can run along that axis, a radial direction can point away from it, and a circumferential direction can be tangent to circles around it. But bodies and tissues are not globally cylindrical. The outward normal of a local surface need not point radially from the spine or from any other chosen axis. A direction tangent to a bone surface need not be circumferential around the body. *Outward*, *radial*, *normal*, *lateral*, and *transverse* therefore cannot be substituted for one another without a defined geometry.

This matters for the series' later coordinate work. Book II will investigate axial, opening or rotational, and expansive organization as a candidate whole-system model. Chapter 4 does not assign signs, preferred directions, or traditional correspondences to those modes. It establishes what that later model will owe the reader: a declared frame, a measurable coordinate for each mode, transformation rules between local and global descriptions, and an explanation of where the chosen coordinates cease to be useful.

## When a planar model is enough

Three-dimensional reality does not require every useful model to be three-dimensional. The familiar sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes provide useful views and starting conventions, provided that the analyst states which physical terms have been projected or omitted. A side-view free-body diagram may answer a sagittal-plane question cleanly. A cross-section may isolate a pressure or contact problem. A planar linkage may reveal how a moment arm changes. Reducing dimension is often good modeling because it removes variables that do not materially affect the conclusion.

The reduction becomes a problem when the omitted direction contains an interaction on which the conclusion depends. An apparently sagittal object transfer may include asymmetric hand contacts, lateral displacement, axial rotation, or a support reaction outside the chosen plane. A transverse section may conceal an important change along the length of a structure. A planar joint model may reproduce the visible motion while missing a substantial out-of-plane moment or contact shift.

A practical planar-reduction test has four steps:

1. **Declare the plane and frame.** State the origin, axes, system boundary, phase, and quantity being modeled.
2. **Inspect the omitted terms.** Ask what out-of-plane forces, moments, contacts, displacements, rotations, or gradients are assumed negligible, constrained, or symmetric.
3. **Bound or compare them.** Use measurement, sensitivity analysis, a three-dimensional subset, or a defensible symmetry argument to estimate whether the omitted terms could change the result.
4. **Withdraw the reduction when necessary.** If a plausible omitted term changes the sign, ranking, route, or interpretation that matters, the planar model is not adequate for that question.

This test does not require every small component to be zero. It requires the simplifying assumption to be visible and proportionate to the claim. A planar description that predicts an external resultant within a declared tolerance may be adequate even if it does not recover every internal stress. The same description would be inadequate if used to assert that no meaningful out-of-plane carrier exists.

Dimensional sufficiency is thus claim-specific. “Two dimensions are enough” and “the body is three-dimensional” are both incomplete sentences. Enough for what quantity, at what scale, during which phase, and within what tolerance? The answer determines whether added dimensions clarify the problem or merely decorate it.

## Configuration is more than posture

Geometry changes mechanics before any tissue property is changed. If a force **F** acts at a position **r** measured from a point *O*, its moment about that point is

\[
\mathbf{M}_O = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}.
\]

Here **M** is the moment about *O*, **r** runs from *O* to the force's line of application, and **F** is the force, all expressed in a common declared frame. In SI units, force is measured in newtons, position in metres, and moment in newton metres. The relation's job here is narrow: it shows that changing the relative position or direction of the same force can change the moment it produces.[^04-04]

In the object transfer, moving the object farther from an elbow can change the moment about that elbow even if the object's weight is unchanged. Separating or shifting the hand contacts can change the moments applied to the object. Changing a joint angle can alter moment arms, contact geometry, muscle lengths, and the set of structures positioned to contribute. Geometry is not an ornamental description laid over the forces; it helps determine the mechanical problem they form.

Compare two transfers of the same object to the same shelf. In one, the object remains near the body and both hands maintain separated contacts; in another, it travels farther from the body or laterally while the contacts are rearranged. Either configuration may be viable. They need not produce the same moments, contact resultants, or candidate internal distributions, and this chapter does not rank them.

Yet visible geometry is not the whole configuration. For this book, a **configuration** is the minimum declared arrangement and state needed to determine the interactions and available changes relevant to a question. Depending on the question, that record can include:

- the geometry and orientation of selected bodies or regions;
- contacts, supports, attachments, and constraints;
- active forces, preloads, pressures, and external devices;
- material state, including history or rate dependence where relevant;
- stress, strain, deformation, or flow fields when those are the objects of study;
- the motions or deformations currently available; and
- the reference phase, measurement method, and provenance of each entry.

This is an accounting record, not a proposed universal state vector for the human body. A simple rigid-body question may require only geometry, mass properties, contacts, and motion. A tissue question may need direction-dependent constitutive behavior, pressure, activation, or time history. Configuration expands only as the claim requires.

The distinction from posture is especially important. Posture usually names an observed arrangement of body segments at an instant or over an interval. Two people can present a similar observed posture while differing in muscle activation, contact force, pressure, fatigue, tissue properties, or recent loading history. One person can reproduce a similar silhouette through a different combination of internal actions. Conversely, visibly different postures can satisfy the same external task through different configurations. Observation constrains the candidate models; it does not uniquely reveal the internal distribution.[^04-05]

Mass distribution adds another configuration-dependent term. Resistance to angular acceleration is represented by a moment of inertia or, in three dimensions, an inertia tensor defined for a selected body, point, and frame. Moving the object or a body segment changes the mass distribution relative to a joint or other reference point. It is not valid to treat “inertia” as a generic internal tension or to use one scalar rotational equation without checking whether the body, axis, and frame support that simplification.[^04-06]

> **Figure 4.2 — From observed transfer to candidate internal paths [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> OBSERVED AND MEASURED
> object motion + segment geometry + named contacts
>                    |
>                    v
> CONFIGURATION RECORD
> boundary + frames + phase + constraints + active state
> + pressure/material history where the question requires them
>                    |
>                    v
> EXTERNAL BALANCE
> measured and calculated resultants and moments
>                    |
>          does not uniquely determine
>                    v
> CANDIDATE INTERNAL MODELS
> skeletal contact | muscle/tendon | ligament/fascia
> pressure | sliding interfaces | external support
>                    |
>                    v
> DISCRIMINATING OBSERVATIONS
> force, motion, pressure, deformation, activation, or sensitivity
> ```
>
> **Caption.** An observed posture and external balance constrain internal models but do not uniquely select one. A configuration record makes assumptions visible, and additional measurements or model comparisons can discriminate among candidate carriers.
>
> **Text alternative.** A vertical flow starts with observed object motion, segment geometry, and contacts; adds the boundary, frames, phase, constraints, active state, and any needed pressure or material history; computes an external balance; then branches into several candidate internal carrier models. The final step lists observations that could distinguish those models.

A configuration claim becomes useful when it predicts a difference. If changing a contact, orientation, activation state, pressure, or support is proposed to reroute demand, the model should state which measured force, deformation, pressure, movement, or sensitivity is expected to change. Without such a comparison, configuration can become a long description that explains every outcome after it occurs.

## Load paths can branch and change

A line of action is a geometric property of a force: the line through its point of application in the force's direction. It is valuable in a free-body diagram because it helps determine moments. An internal load path is a different construct. It proposes how a declared mechanical demand is carried through named structures, contacts, or fields between selected boundaries. A correct external line of action does not establish a unique internal route.

The object illustrates the difference. Its weight has a line of action through its center of mass in the gravitational direction. While the object is held, two hands may share contact, and each contact may include distributed pressure, friction, and a resultant. Within the person, muscle forces, tendon tensions, joint contacts, ligament or fascial contributions, pressure-supported regions, sliding interfaces, and external supports may participate as carriers or contacts. Segment mass and acceleration remain part of the dynamic balance, but inertia is not an anatomical carrier. External balance constrains the combined effect; it rarely identifies every contribution uniquely.

Calling a proposed route a **multicarrier load path** means that the representation permits parallel and serial contributions from more than one kind of carrier. It does not mean that all possible tissues are substantially active in every event. Each retained carrier should earn its place through anatomy, measurement, calculation, or a clearly labeled hypothesis. A model that names everything explains nothing unless it also states how contributions could be compared or excluded.

Different representations serve different path questions:

- A **line of action** can represent a defined force; a **force-and-moment resultant** can summarize a more general interaction at a boundary.
- A **graph** can name structures or regions as nodes and their interactions as edges.
- A **field** can represent distributed stress, strain, deformation, pressure, or velocity through a region.
- A **time-varying network** can show routes appearing, disappearing, or changing share as contacts, configuration, and activation change.

These representations are not successive levels of truth. A line may be sufficient for an external balance while a field is needed for a local tissue question. A graph can preserve anatomical branching that a single line hides, but it may still omit the distribution within each node. The model should be no richer than the inference it has to support.

A defensible path statement therefore names the system boundary, mechanical quantity and unit, frame, scale, phase, proposed carriers, and status of the supporting evidence. It should satisfy the relevant balance laws, show plausible alternative routes, and state which measurements or sensitivity tests could change the proposed distribution.

Chapter 3's hard/soft polarity enters here as a description of roles within paths. That polarity is **motivated by** traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts, while Book I's mechanical translation remains deliberately non-identical to the traditional categories. A comparatively shape-preserving relation may establish or resolve part of a path; a comparatively form-receiving structure may conform, slide, contain, expand, or otherwise change while carrying substantial demand. Role and path are not synonyms. The same path can include both roles, and the same structure can change roles with direction, phase, or scale.

The project's phrase **force line** can also be retained if its level is stated. In a free-body diagram, it can refer to a force's line of action. In an embodied or anatomical hypothesis, it may refer to a felt or proposed internal connection across several structures. The second sense is potentially useful, especially for later questions about internal coordination, but it is not converted into a measured force vector by being drawn as a line. It must be translated into candidate carriers, boundaries, directions, and observables before it can function as a mechanical explanation.

Load paths can fail to remain simple even in ordinary tasks. When the object leaves the table, a support path through the table disappears and the hands assume the full external interaction. If one hand releases, the remaining contact and the object's configuration change. If the shelf accepts part of the weight, another branch appears. Internal contributions can change without any dramatic visible posture change as activation, pressure, fatigue, or contact distribution evolves. A path is therefore a phase-bound model of transmission and support, not a permanent cable hidden in the body.

This is also where later accounts of load mismanagement will begin. A mechanically intelligible adverse condition need not be described merely as “less space.” The relevant question may be what maintained geometry, contact, or constraint is imposing deformation or pressure on a form-receiving structure, how that changes the structure's internal state or function, and which shape-preserving relation is carrying or redirecting the demand. Book I does not turn that narrative into a diagnosis or universal causal chain. It establishes the vocabulary needed to investigate it without reducing every consequence to visible posture or local narrowing.

## Four descriptions that happen to use three directions

The series contains several three-part descriptions. They can illuminate one another, but the shared number three does not make them the same coordinate system. Four distinctions are especially important: spatial frames, generalized modes, material-symmetry frames, and principal-stress directions.

> **Figure 4.3 — Four different three-direction descriptions [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Description | What its directions describe | How they are determined | State dependence | What cannot be inferred from the number three |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Spatial frame | Components of position, force, moment, motion, or tensors | Declared origin and basis; global, segmental, surface, or local | May be fixed or move by a declared rule | No preferred direction, tissue property, or mode follows automatically |
> | Generalized coordinates and loads | Selected independent or coupled changes, such as axial displacement, opening angle, or expansive measure | Model definition plus units, signs, constraints, and virtual-work pairing | Depends on configuration and chosen model | A circumferential tangent is not itself an opening mode or moment |
> | Material-symmetry frame | Directions used in a constitutive approximation for a specified material or region | Experiment, microstructure, anatomy, or fitted constitutive model | Depends on tissue, region, scale, state, and model purpose | Local orthotropy does not make the whole body one orthotropic solid |
> | Principal-stress frame | Directions in which the current stress tensor has no shear components | Eigenvectors of the stress tensor at a point | Changes with the stress state; may be non-unique | Principal directions are not permanent anatomical channels or force lines |
>
> **Caption.** Each row can contain three directions, but the mathematical object, units, construction, and dependence differ. Any proposed correspondence must supply transformations and predictions rather than rely on a shared count.
>
> **Text alternative.** A five-column table compares spatial frames, generalized modes, material-symmetry frames, and principal-stress frames. It states what each describes, how its directions are chosen, whether they change with state, and why three directions in one row do not prove equivalence with three directions in another.

### Spatial frames

A spatial frame supplies a basis and origin. Force components may be expressed left–right, forward–back, and up–down in the room; relative to a bone; or along and across a local surface. The axes answer *where and in what direction?* They do not by themselves answer what kind of change is permitted, how a material responds, or which direction a current stress state selects.

### Generalized modes

A generalized coordinate is a chosen variable that describes a permitted or modeled change. Its conjugate generalized load is defined through the work associated with an infinitesimal change in that coordinate. Translation pairs with force, angle with moment, and a volume-like measure can pair with pressure, but more complex coordinates require their own dimensional accounting.[^04-07]

This is the most promising home for the series' axial, opening or rotational, and expansive language. An axial coordinate might be a length or displacement along a declared axis. An opening coordinate might be an angle between selected segments or surfaces, with a corresponding moment. An expansive coordinate might be a width, perimeter, cross-sectional area, volume, or surface-normal displacement. These are not interchangeable. Their units differ, and a change in one may contribute to but cannot simply be renamed as a change in another.

The rib cage makes the distinction concrete. Rib rotations at the costovertebral joints can contribute to three-dimensional changes in thoracic dimensions and volume, but a rib angle, a transverse width, an anteroposterior dimension, and a volume are distinct observables.[^04-08] Calling the whole event “expansion” may be adequate in ordinary prose. A model must state which measure is meant and how the other changes are coupled to it.

The pelvis requires even more care. A scissors analogy can represent a relative angular relation or a composite change among pelvic structures. It should not suggest that the intact sacroiliac joints undergo a large literal opening. Coordinate choices alter how their small, coupled translations and rotations are reported, and available cadaveric measurements under physiological loading are on sub-degree and sub-millimetre scales.[^04-09] The analogy can survive as a mode hypothesis if its hinge, segments, coordinate, expected magnitude, and observation are declared.

The distinction between a direction and a mode is crucial. A circumferential tangent around an axis is a spatial direction. Opening is a change in an angle and is paired mechanically with a moment. Expansion is a change in a length, area, perimeter, volume, or other declared measure and has a corresponding generalized load. A rib may move partly along a circumferential direction while contributing to an expansive change, but that does not make circumferential direction, rotation, and expansion three names for one object.

### Material-symmetry frames

A constitutive model describes how a selected material relates quantities such as stress and strain under stated conditions. An isotropic model treats material response as direction-independent. An orthotropic elastic approximation assigns three mutually orthogonal material-symmetry directions and different response parameters along and between them. That structure can be valuable when a tissue or engineered material has an appropriate directional organization.[^04-10]

Orthotropy is therefore available to this project as a local constitutive approximation, not as a premise that the entire body is one orthotropic material. Cortical bone, cartilage, myocardium, and other tissues can show direction-dependent behavior, but their useful material frames, symmetries, nonlinearities, active properties, and scales differ.[^04-11] Bilateral body organization and the practical usefulness of three spatial directions do not by themselves derive three orthogonal material-symmetry planes for a whole-body model.

This demotion is constructive. If a later calculation concerns a region whose response is reasonably approximated as orthotropic, the model can state the region, tissue, scale, state, axes, parameters, and validation range. If the purpose is instead to describe whole-body geometry or a coordinated mode, spatial or generalized coordinates may be the more honest objects. The project does not have to make one mathematical structure perform all three jobs.

### Principal-stress directions

At a point in a continuum, the stress state can be represented by a tensor. Its principal directions are directions in which the traction has no shear component; mathematically, they are eigenvector directions of the current stress tensor. They change when the stress state changes. When principal stresses are repeated, the corresponding directions may not be unique.[^04-12]

Principal directions can reveal locally important patterns. They do not automatically follow a visible anatomical axis, a material-symmetry direction, or a proposed internal force line. Under particular conditions those directions may align, but the alignment is a result to establish, not a definition. A material frame describes a constitutive approximation; a principal frame describes a current state. One may remain anatomically anchored while the other rotates as loading changes.

Keeping the four descriptions separate does not prevent a future synthesis. It makes one possible. Book II can propose generalized coordinates, relate them to local and global spatial frames, select constitutive assumptions where needed, and predict how stress or other observables change. It can also investigate the stronger possibility that some coordination is more mechanically efficient or more reliably organizes demand than alternatives. None of those later steps is required for Book I's argument that configuration and multicarrier load paths improve mechanical reasoning. The foundational claim remains standing even if a proposed correspondence or preference is revised.

## From spatial organization to anatomy

We can now describe the object transfer without pretending that one picture contains the whole event. A declared boundary identifies external interactions. A declared frame locates their components. A configuration record adds the contacts, constraints, active state, pressure, material history, and available changes that the question requires. A planar model is accepted or rejected according to the terms it omits. A load-path model names its quantity and carriers, allows branches and phase changes, and separates an external line of action from internal distribution.

We can also keep several uses of three directions in productive tension. Spatial axes locate components. Generalized coordinates describe selected changes. Material frames organize a constitutive approximation. Principal directions describe a current stress state. Their correspondences remain hypotheses until transformations, units, observations, and discriminating predictions are supplied.

What remains is to place these abstractions into actual anatomy. Which structures and systems establish, guide, tension, cushion, contain, pressurize, and change these paths in an actual living body? Chapter 5 begins with the skeleton and joints, while Chapter 6 adds the active, tensile, compliant, sliding, and pressure-bearing systems that make skeletal possibilities function.

## Part I synthesis — From embodiment to paths

Part I began with a fact: life takes place through material structures under demand. It ends with a disciplined way to describe that fact.

The word *load* now separates into forces, moments, pressures, stresses, strains, deformations, rates, repetitions, work, power, and exposure over time. Each quantity belongs to a declared system, scale, frame, reference, task, and phase. None can be inferred in full from appearance alone. A whole-body motion, a joint resultant, a tissue field, and a cellular response can describe the same event at different levels without becoming interchangeable.

The hard/soft polarity adds a relational question. Which structures or relations comparatively preserve shape, establish a path, constrain motion, or resolve gross geometry while transmitting demand? Which must remain able to receive form, yield, glide, contain, expand, or change local shape? A structure can answer both questions in different directions or phases, and force transmission alone assigns neither role. The vocabulary is useful only when it sharpens an observable division of labor rather than recoloring anatomy after the result is known.

Configuration then gathers geometry, contact, activation, pressure, material state, and available motion into a changing whole. A load path is one model of how a defined demand is partitioned within that configuration. The path can branch, recruit, disappear, reverse, or remain indeterminate. Similar external success can conceal different internal solutions.

These distinctions do not yet tell us what the body's structures actually do. They establish the questions anatomy must answer. Part II begins with the skeleton and joints, then restores active, tensile, compliant, sliding, pressure-bearing, and control systems around them. Only after that cooperation is visible can the posterior chain be examined as a real anatomical and functional system rather than assumed as a line on a diagram.

# Part II — The architecture of support

A body does not support itself through one material or one kind of force. Bones preserve useful geometry while deforming. Joints redirect demand while moving. Muscle acts through changing length, velocity, leverage, and activation. Tendons and ligaments transmit, store, guide, and restrain. Cartilage receives contact through a fluid–solid structure. Fasciae and sliding interfaces connect, separate, contain, and permit relative movement. Cavities and pressure can contribute to support. Sensation and control continually alter the distribution.

Part II turns Part I's abstract roles into this cooperative anatomy. Chapter 5 begins with bones and joints because their geometry provides the clearest shape-preserving routes. It also shows why the skeleton cannot be understood as a rigid frame acting alone. Chapter 6 adds the active, tensile, compliant, gliding, pressure-bearing, and distributed systems that make skeletal paths usable and adaptable. It tests broad network and tensegrity representations without asking a model to prove a medical effect.

Chapters 7–9 then take up the posterior body. Chapter 7 maps what the phrase *posterior chain* can legitimately include and where continuity remains anatomical, inferred, variable, or unmeasured. Chapter 8 follows posterior participation through ordinary functions such as walking, lifting, propulsion, braking, balance, and recovery. Chapter 9 returns those functions to whole-body variation across development, training, pregnancy, pain, illness, disability, assistance, and aging.

The sequence matters. Posterior anatomy appears only after the reader has seen that support is shared. This prevents a large and consequential system from becoming either invisible or total. The questions are affirmative but bounded: What posterior structures exist? What do they contribute in a declared task? With what other systems do they cooperate? What changes with phase, capacity, and context? The stronger claim that posterior participation belongs to a preferred body-wide organization remains a later hypothesis rather than an answer built into the anatomy.

# Chapter 5 — Skeleton, joints, and shape-preserving paths

The object is leaving its first support. A moment earlier, the table carried most of its weight. Now the hands are accepting the contact, the object is accelerating, and the person's contacts with the floor help complete the external balance. This is phase 2—departure—in the ordinary, non-prescriptive transfer that has followed us through Part I.

Chapter 4 ended by asking which anatomical structures make a three-dimensional load path possible. The skeleton is the clearest place to begin. Bones preserve gross relations more readily than many neighboring tissues over the timescale of an ordinary task. Joint surfaces let one bone move relative to another while still exchanging force. Ligaments and capsules constrain which relations remain available. Together, these structures supply geometry through which demand can be organized.

But the word *skeleton* can encourage two opposite mistakes. One is to picture an inert rack on which the active body hangs. The other is to treat visible skeletal arrangement as a complete code for mechanical quality. Neither picture survives the object transfer. Bone deforms. Joint contact moves. Ligaments are recruited differently as configuration changes. Muscle, tendon, pressure, cartilage, sensory control, and external support all help determine whether any proposed skeletal route exists. A still image does not tell us how those contributions are shared.

We will therefore begin with a deliberately skeletal-first graph. For gross gravitational and externally applied structural demand, we first represent the skeleton and external contacts, then ask which active, tensile, pressure-mediated, compliant, and external-support terms are needed to close the balance. This is an accounting order, not the formal skeletal-primary routing assumption developed in Book II and not a conclusion that every internal force travels through bone or that other tissues are secondary. It earns its place only when the representation clarifies the contacts, moments, and candidate distributions in a defined task. Mass and acceleration must remain in dynamic accounting.

This chapter follows the object from hand to ground at several boundaries. Its question is not which posture is correct. It is how bones, joints, and recruited restraints create relatively shape-preserving possibilities in a body that must keep moving.

## Geometry establishes possibilities, not solutions

A bone's length, curve, cross-section, orientation, and relation to neighboring structures affect what can happen around it. Articular surfaces determine where contact can occur. The distance from an external force's line of action to a joint reference changes the external moment about that joint. A curve or change in cross-section changes how a simplified beam model represents bending or torsion. A surface orientation changes its normal direction and, together with the contact model, the tractions that the interface can support. These are mechanical constraints, but they do not select one response by themselves.

Consider the object during departure. Its position relative to the hands and upper limbs helps set external moment arms. The relative positions of the hands, forearms, upper arms, trunk, pelvis, and feet establish a linked geometry. Yet many internal solutions can remain compatible with the same visible arrangement. Muscle forces can differ. Contact can be shared differently between two hands or two feet. A table edge, rail, mobility aid, or another person's assistance can add an external support. Acceleration can differ even when two images look similar. Geometry defines a feasible set; contact, active state, material state, and time select among the possibilities.

The same distinction applies locally. A joint surface may permit a range of rotations and translations, but muscles, ligaments, capsule, pressure, contact, and the applied task determine which part of that range is used. A long bone may be represented as a rigid segment for one whole-body calculation, but that simplification does not turn the living bone into a rigid material. A planar linkage may answer a question about one external moment while being inadequate for an out-of-plane contact question.

This is the anatomical form of Chapter 4's configuration rule. Skeletal geometry is part of configuration, not a substitute for it. It tells us which contacts, moment arms, and movements are possible under a declared frame and phase. It does not tell us which force-sharing solution occurred, what the local tissue stress was, or whether the result was desirable.

Thinking in terms of a feasible set changes what an anatomical explanation should try to do. It should not begin by naming one position as the answer. It should first identify the contacts and movements that the anatomy permits, the external interactions that must be reconciled, and the alternatives still compatible with those facts. Only then can a model ask whether one configuration changes a moment, brings a restraint into tension, relocates contact, or removes an available route. The observation becomes informative through the difference it predicts.

The skeletal-first graph is useful at this stage because it offers a tractable first accounting pass. Bones become segments or deformable structural members; joints become changing interfaces; external supports become boundary contacts. If that graph helps close the selected force-and-moment balance and predicts a change that can be observed, it has done real work. If the same result follows from a simpler free-body diagram, or if an omitted active, pressure, or support term reverses the conclusion, the skeletal graph should be weakened or set aside for that question. First in the analysis does not mean primary in the body.

Nor does a first graph have to be a unique graph. One analyst might divide the upper limb into hand, forearm, and upper arm; another might combine the hand and object or isolate one joint interface. Both can be valid if their boundaries answer different questions and the transitions between them are explicit. The danger is not simplification. It is allowing a convenient anatomical line to acquire conclusions that its boundary and measurements cannot support.

> |---|---|---|---|
> | Object during departure | Object position, hand-contact locations, support contact ending | Gravity, contact resultants, acceleration, contact moments where relevant | How the person produces the hand forces |
> | Forearm segment during redirection | Segment orientation, elbow and hand locations | Neighboring resultants, active/tensile forces, segment mass and acceleration | Individual muscle force or tissue stress |
> | Joint interface during one configuration | Articular geometry and candidate contact region | Distributed contact, cartilage state, restraint, active force | Pressure field, material strain, pain, or damage |
> | Person plus object during carry | Whole-body geometry and ground contacts | Gravity, ground interaction, acceleration, any retained external support | A unique internal skeletal or soft-tissue route |
