> **Text alternative.** A schematic places an object at a perpendicular distance from a declared trunk or pelvic moment point or axis inside a selected system boundary. Gravity acts on the object, the hand and feet provide contacts, and posterior, nonposterior, and pressure-mediated contributors share the resulting requirement. The figure labels internal sharing as unresolved by the external moment alone.

The cart changes the question more clearly. Once the object is supported by the cart, the wheels, handle, and floor enter the load path. The unaided body is no longer the entire carrier between the two tables. An exoskeleton, handrail, second person, shelf edge, or mobility aid changes the system in the same general sense. In a small lifting study, altering active lumbar-and-hip exoskeleton support changed modeled active moments and spinal loading while higher support could also restrict motion or feel obstructive.[^08-02] Assistance can reduce one modeled requirement, add contact elsewhere, constrain movement, or introduce another cost. It is a real boundary condition, neither proof of failure nor proof of universal improvement.

## Energy has several destinations

The phrase *absorbs load* often conceals several different mechanical events. Force and energy are not synonyms. Work is the transfer of energy by force through displacement, while power describes the rate of that transfer. A muscle–tendon unit can generate positive work, perform negative work while controlling motion, store recoverable strain energy, return some of that energy, dissipate some, or pass energy across the boundary chosen for analysis. The correct verb depends on what is measured and where the boundary is drawn.

Posterior muscle–tendon systems demonstrate the distinction vividly. During walking or running, plantar-flexor muscles and the Achilles tendon operate as a coupled system. In-vivo estimates based on motion, ground reaction, ultrasound, and subject-specific tendon properties have found substantial Achilles loading and recoverable strain-energy release during propulsion, with behavior changing by gait and speed.[^08-03] Constrained hopping studies likewise distinguish work by muscle fascicles from tendon work and relate tendon behavior to the apparent efficiency of that particular task.[^08-04] These findings establish a meaningful energy-management role. They do not turn the posterior body into one spring or make maximum recoil desirable in every circumstance.

Lowering the object shows why. While the person controls descent, active muscle may lengthen under force and perform negative work. A tendon may deform and temporarily store energy. Some stored energy may later return; some may be dissipated by tissue behavior, active control, friction, impact, or other processes. When the object contacts the destination, energy also crosses from the person–object system into the shelf and surrounding environment. Placement is not departure played backward.

Nor is redirection the same as dissipation. A force can change the direction of momentum without eliminating all mechanical energy. Energy can move between translation and rotation, between body segments, between active and elastic components, or across a contact. A tendon can delay or redistribute power even when it returns much of the energy it received. A posterior muscle can contribute to braking in one phase and propulsion in another. Words such as *absorption*, *spring*, and *shock* are therefore starting points for an account, not final explanations.

Even *efficiency* requires a denominator. Mechanical efficiency may compare external work with metabolic energy under a specified convention. A device may reduce muscle activation in one region while adding mass or restricting motion. Elastic return may reduce active work in one phase while demanding force and control elsewhere. A strategy may be efficient for speed, repeatability, precision, heat management, or recovery, and those objectives need not rank it identically. Book II's proposed global efficiency measure must therefore be constructed rather than smuggled in through an appealing energy metaphor.

> **Figure 8.2 — Energy verbs require separate accounts [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Event in one transfer | Possible mechanical description | Evidence still required |
> |---|---|---|
> | Object rises or gains speed | positive net work increases the selected object's mechanical energy | contributing forces, displacements, boundary, and timing |
> | Motion is controlled during lowering | active structures may perform negative work | muscle–tendon state and the system over which work is calculated |
> | Tendon deforms and later recoils | strain energy may be stored and partly returned | tendon force–length behavior and losses |
> | Contact or tissue behavior reduces recoverable energy | dissipation may occur | destination, rate, material behavior, and measurement |
> | Shelf progressively accepts the object | energy and support cross the person–object boundary | contact history and chosen system boundary |
>
> **Caption.** Positive work, negative work, storage, return, dissipation, redirection, and boundary crossing can coexist. “Absorption” alone does not say which occurred, and none of the rows establishes injury prevention.
>
> **Text alternative.** Five rows distinguish raising or gaining speed, controlled lowering, tendon deformation and recoil, dissipation, and transfer to a shelf. Each row names the additional evidence needed before the event can be assigned a precise energy meaning.

This vocabulary protects the positive posterior thesis from exaggeration. Posterior structures do not become less important when their functions are separated. The separation reveals more of what they can do: produce work, resist an external moment, control a descent, store and return energy, redirect motion, and change the timing of demand. It also prevents one desirable performance result from becoming an unsupported health conclusion.

## Standing and sitting are histories of support

Standing is often treated as a shape. Mechanically, it is an evolving relation among body mass, skeletal geometry, foot–floor contact, small movements, active and passive forces, attention, and any support supplied by the surroundings. The center of pressure moves within the contact region. The body does not need to be motionless to remain upright; slight motion is part of the ordinary event.

Posterior structures participate in that event, but their contribution is not fixed by the outline of the back. Skeletal alignment can reduce or redirect active requirements in some configurations. Calf, hip, and trunk muscles can respond to small changes or perturbations. Passive tissues and pressure-mediated relations can contribute. Placing a hand on a counter adds another contact and can change the balance without requiring a large visible postural change.

Sitting adds a seat and may add a backrest, armrests, foot support, or a work surface. These contacts accept portions of demand that would otherwise be resolved elsewhere. An upright unsupported sitting configuration, a reclined back-supported configuration, and a forward-leaning configuration therefore describe different support systems, not merely different spinal shapes. Duration, task, attention, recent history, and freedom to change relation matter alongside geometry.

A randomized study of asymptomatic adults compared twenty minutes of slouched, upright, and back-supported sitting. Muscle activity differed, but the investigators did not find an immediate or short-term group change in the selected pain, range-of-motion, or proprioceptive outcomes after those brief exposures.[^08-05] The result does not show that sitting never matters or that all durations and populations are equivalent. It shows why posture label, measured activity, exposure history, symptoms, and clinical consequence must not be collapsed.

The same restraint applies in the other direction. A configuration that reduces active demand at one moment need not be globally better; a configuration that asks more of posterior structures need not be harmful. Leaning on a counter may be an efficient use of external support, an accommodation to fatigue, a way to perform another task, or an incidental preference. Standing without support may require more of a selected capacity, but the visible choice does not identify its meaning.

The sit-to-stand transition makes posterior participation easier to see. External contacts change as seat support diminishes, the feet accept more of the support demand, and whole-body momentum changes. Hip and knee moments change; trunk geometry affects those demands; hands or armrests can add carriers; posterior muscles can contribute substantially. Yet two people can rise successfully through different combinations of forward momentum, foot placement, hand support, speed, and joint sharing. Once again, a strong contribution does not imply one mandatory strategy.

Time turns each posture into an exposure rather than a photograph. Ten seconds, twenty minutes, and a workday are not interchangeable; neither are an uninterrupted interval and the same nominal duration broken by other tasks. A person may retain the same outline while muscle activity, contact pressure, attention, or comfort changes. Another may change shape frequently while preserving similar average demand at a selected structure. The chapter does not assume that variability is always beneficial. It insists only that duration, sequence, and support belong in the observation before a posture is interpreted.

> **Figure 8.3 — Posture becomes a support history [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Situation | Contacts and changing boundary | Posterior question | What shape alone cannot answer |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Quiet standing | two feet, floor, possible hand support | which posterior structures contribute, when, and to what quantity? | individual forces, fatigue, comfort, or health |
> | Unsupported sitting | seat and feet, with active balance | how are trunk and pelvic demands shared? | whether visible uprightness means one internal route |
> | Back-supported sitting | seat, backrest, feet, perhaps arms | what demand has moved into the chair? | whether reduced activity is beneficial or adverse |
> | Sit-to-stand | seat contact falls while foot contact and momentum change | how do posterior and other contributors share the transition? | one correct strategy or outcome |
>
> **Caption.** Standing and sitting are time-varying contact systems. Posterior participation can be measured within them, but a silhouette cannot reveal the unique internal load path or its consequence.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows compare quiet standing, unsupported sitting, back-supported sitting, and rising. Each row names the contacts, a posterior mechanical question, and what visible shape alone cannot establish about internal force, fatigue, comfort, or health.

This framing removes moral judgment without removing mechanical stakes. Sustained, repetitive, constrained, or poorly matched exposures can matter; Part III will examine dose, capacity, failed handoff, and retained strain. Chapter 8 supplies the necessary positive baseline: support can be shared in several viable ways, and the relevant comparison begins with contacts, time, task, geometry, and measured demand rather than a posture label.

## Walking makes posterior participation unmistakable

Walking provides one of the strongest positive cases for posterior function because its phases can be measured and modeled. During stance, the body must be supported while forward progression continues. During late stance, propulsion and transfer toward the next step become important. The swing limb must be advanced and then prepared for contact. Balance must be maintained in three dimensions while each foot alternately leaves the ground.

Three-dimensional simulations of eight children with unimpaired gait walking at several speeds identified important contributions from gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, soleus, and vasti to support and progression. The estimated contribution changed by speed and phase; at slower speeds, skeletal alignment supplied more early-stance support in the model.[^08-06] That finding is not a dilution of the posterior case. It shows how large posterior contributions coexist with anterior and lateral muscles and with geometry itself.

Forward-dynamics work offers a complementary view. A model using groups of timed muscle excitations assigned a plantar-flexor group major roles in support and propulsion and a hamstring group roles in late-swing energy absorption and early-stance energy addition.[^08-07] The modules are a useful representation of phase-specific coordination, not proof that every nervous system uses five literal fixed commands. Their value here is functional: the same broad posterior system can support, propel, brake, and exchange energy at different times.

Muscle names do not remove the need for geometry and timing. Experimental stimulation during walking has produced different effects for gastrocnemius and soleus on vertical support, forward acceleration, and center-of-pressure progression.[^08-08] Both muscles can contribute to plantar flexion, but one is biarticular and their anatomical relations differ. The result reinforces a general rule: sharing one joint action does not make two structures mechanically interchangeable at the whole-body level.

The ground-to-body relation also changes throughout stance. Foot contact and its pressure distribution change as the center of pressure shifts. The ankle–foot complex, plantar flexors, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk participate in converting those changing external contacts into support and progression. The Achilles tendon can carry high tension while the foot and ankle geometry change the relation between muscle force, joint moment, and motion. None of this means a literal unit of “ground force” travels intact up one posterior cable. It means that a linked series of contacts and active–tensile relations makes posterior participation both anatomically plausible and experimentally measurable.

The upper body remains part of walking. Arm swing and trunk rotation can affect angular momentum and energy transfer. Lateral hip muscles, foot placement, frontal-plane ankle action, and sensory control matter for balance. Pressure is redistributed across the foot. The pelvis and trunk move in three dimensions. Calling gait a posterior-chain function is defensible only if the phrase means that posterior structures make major, phase-specific contributions inside this wider organization. It is misleading if it turns walking into a sagittal animation with the rest of the system erased.

The word *extension* also needs care. A posterior muscle can contribute to an extension moment while the joint is moving into flexion, moving into extension, or moving very little. It can perform positive or negative work depending on the relation between moment and angular velocity. Conversely, an observed extension motion does not identify the force source. Region, motion, moment, tissue role, and later Yang sign remain distinct concepts.

This distinction matters for the series boundary. Book II asks whether posterior participation is necessary but insufficient within a preferred whole-body organization. Chapter 8 establishes a premise that makes the question serious: posterior structures are not incidental decorations on upright life. It does not yet establish necessity across every task or define the efficiency measure by which configurations would be compared.

## Recovery from disturbance is a repertoire

A stable task is not one with no movement. Stability is the maintenance or recovery of task-usable relations under a declared disturbance. The relevant relation might be continued upright progression, preservation of a hand contact, containment of the center of mass relative to available support, or successful completion of a step. Different definitions can produce different rankings of the same response.

During perturbed walking, people can change foot placement, ankle action, push-off, trunk motion, step timing, or use an external support. In an overground study that perturbed one foot of healthy adults, recovery varied with perturbation direction and included changes in step width, ankle inversion or eversion, push-off, trunk sway, and erector-spinae activity. Foot placement was prominent in that experimental setup, while ankle and trunk strategies also contributed.[^08-09]

The posterior system is plainly involved: spinal extensors, hip muscles, hamstrings, and plantar flexors can contribute to maintaining or recovering the task. But the involvement does not translate into the instruction to “engage the posterior chain.” The measured response was coordinated across planes and contacts. A handhold, cane, slower step, wider step, reach, or another person's support could become part of a different viable system.

Coactivation illustrates the tradeoff. Increasing simultaneous activity around a joint may increase resistance to a perturbation in one model or phase. It can also increase internal contact force or metabolic cost, and maximal rigidity can interfere with the movement needed for recovery. More motion is not automatically instability, just as less motion is not automatically control. The account needs a perturbation, an endpoint, a time window, and the costs that matter.

> **Figure 8.4 — Balance recovery is three-dimensional [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> perturbation
>      |
>      +--> foot placement / step timing ------+
>      +--> ankle and foot action --------------+--> task relation recovered or lost
>      +--> hip and posterior contribution -----+
>      +--> trunk and arm angular momentum -----+
>      +--> reach, handhold, aid, or assistance -+
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Posterior structures can be prominent during balance recovery without constituting a solitary strategy. The relative contribution of stepping, ankle, hip, trunk, arm, and environmental responses—and their selection and timing through sensory information—depends on the perturbation, person, phase, and endpoint.
>
> **Text alternative.** One perturbation branches into foot placement, ankle and foot action, hip and posterior contribution, trunk and arm movement, and external support. Sensory information changes the selection and timing of these mechanical responses rather than acting as another force carrier. The branches reconverge on whether a defined task relation was recovered.

The repertoire is mechanically important beyond balance research. It demonstrates that redundancy can be useful. Several combinations may satisfy the external task while producing different local exposures, energy costs, or recovery margins. Chapter 10 will make those time-dependent differences explicit. For now, the central point is that posterior support works as part of an adaptable whole, not as one fixed command.

Sensory information is part of that whole without becoming another carrier of load. Vision, vestibular information, proprioception, touch, expectation, and prior experience can alter timing and strategy. They help determine which mechanical relations are created in response to a disturbance; they do not themselves balance an external force. This separation is important whenever a mechanical account meets a control account. Information changes the selection of forces and contacts, while forces and contacts perform the mechanical work.

## The object transfer, completed

The object transfer has accompanied the book's mechanical vocabulary long enough to become a complete event. It began with the object supported by the first table. The person approached and established contact. During acceptance, hand forces rose while the table continued to carry part of the weight. Departure occurred as that support fell away. The object was redirected and carried. Placement created a new contact with the shelf. During release and aftermath, the shelf became the principal external support while active force and local deformation changed on their own timescales.

Across those phases, posterior structures can contribute at several regions. Lower-limb and hip extensors can help redirect and raise the combined system. Spinal and hip muscles can resist or generate moments created by object position and segment geometry. Posterior shoulder-girdle structures can contribute to hand and arm positioning. Plantar flexors and the Achilles tendon can participate as foot contact changes. During placement, these same broad systems may control descent, stabilize relations, or redirect energy.

No single posterior line carries one unchanged packet from hand to floor. Demand branches through both arms, multiple joints, active and passive structures, pressure-mediated relations, skeletal contacts, feet, and the environment. The division changes whenever a contact appears or disappears. A hand retained on the first table, an object slid rather than fully lifted, or a second person holding one side changes the system before any tissue property changes.

The three variants now expose what the recurring example was designed to teach. Where possible, the alternatives grouped in one row below are compared one at a time rather than combined into a single movement.

| Variant | Changed condition | Defensible mechanical statement | Open question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nearer, two-handed transfer with substantial leg participation | distance, contact, base, and segment geometry | external moments and candidate sharing differ from a farther transfer | individual tissue force, cost, comfort, and long-term response |
| Farther, faster, laterally displaced, or rotational transfer | moment arm, acceleration, direction, and base change | lateral and rotational demands and modeled trunk sharing may change | whether the difference is meaningful for the selected person and outcome |
| Cart, shelf slide, second person, hand support, or exoskeleton | an external carrier enters or remains in the system | part of the force or moment is accepted through a different boundary | local redistribution, device cost, accessibility, preference, and later response |

These are comparisons, not instructions. The near transfer is not colored green; the farther transfer is not colored red. A farther reach may be required by the task, may distribute demand usefully, or may be trivial at the chosen dose and capacity. A cart can be liberating, inconvenient, energetically costly, or mechanically helpful depending on the comparison. Mechanics clarifies what changed before medicine asks what it meant.

> **Figure 8.5 — The recurring transfer, completed [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> initial support -> approach/contact -> acceptance -> departure
>        -> redirection/carry -> placement -> release/aftermath
>
> Variant A: two hands + nearer object + changing foot support
> Variant B: farther/lateral object + changed base + rotation
> Variant C: cart/shelf/person/device adds an external carrier
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The seven phases complete the recurring transfer. Three variants reach a comparable endpoint through different contacts, geometry, rates, and carriers. The figure makes no technique recommendation and does not identify a unique internal path from visible movement.
>
> **Text alternative.** Seven phases run from the object's initial table support through contact, acceptance, departure, carrying, placement, and release. Beneath them, two unassisted variants and one assisted variant show different boundaries that can produce the same task result.

With this comparison, the full transfer retires. Later chapters can recall a phase—repetition in Chapter 10, handoff in Chapter 11, concentration or constraint in Chapters 12 and 13—but they need not replay the entire scene. Its final lesson is redistribution: successful function is produced by changing relations among the body, object, and environment, with major posterior participation available but never readable from shape alone.

## Five outcomes are not one ladder

Posterior function is often described through a chain of apparently obvious conclusions: more posterior capacity improves performance, reduced fatigue improves stability, and improved stability prevents injury. Each link is possible under defined conditions. None follows merely because the preceding word sounds favorable.

Performance is a task output. It may be measured as work, power, speed, accuracy, endurance, or successful completion. Fatigue can refer to a reported experience, while performance fatigability refers to a decline in an objective measure over a specified task. The two can relate without being identical, and laboratory fatigability does not automatically predict real-world performance.[^08-10] Stability is the maintenance or recovery of a declared relation under a disturbance. Injury exposure is a tissue- and history-specific mechanical estimate. Injury is a biological or clinical outcome. These objects occupy different columns.

| Question | Candidate measure | What the answer can establish | What it cannot replace |
|---|---|---|---|
| Did performance change? | work, power, speed, accuracy, endurance, completion | a defined output differed under stated conditions | health, comfort, stability, or injury outcome |
| Did fatigue change? | perceived fatigue or a decline in force, power, timing, or output | a reported state or measured fatigability response | tissue damage or chain failure |
| Was the task stable? | perturbation response, step result, usable configuration, recovery time | a selected relation was maintained or recovered | maximal stiffness, symmetry, or absence of movement |
| Did exposure change? | local force, stress, strain, rate, repetition, or recovery history | a candidate mechanical history differed | injury occurrence, risk magnitude, or prevention |
| Did injury or health change? | defined clinical, imaging, functional, or epidemiological outcome | the measured outcome changed in the studied context | the mechanism, unless separately tested |

A posterior training intervention might increase force or power without changing injury incidence. A person may preserve task output while internal sharing or perceived effort changes. Greater coactivation may improve one perturbation measure while raising another cost. An assistive device may reduce a modeled lumbar quantity without improving comfort or reducing exposure at another site. These are not reasons to abandon the questions. They are reasons to design the studies that connect them.

The connecting study must match the arrow it claims. To move from posterior force capacity to performance, measure both under a defined task and account for competing contributors. To move from a modeled tissue exposure to injury, establish that the estimate is valid, that chronology is correct, and that the outcome occurs more often or changes when the exposure changes. To move from a symptom response to a mechanism, test alternatives rather than treating improvement as proof of the favored path. A single experiment can rarely close every bridge, but a coherent research program can accumulate them.

The distinctions also permit a stronger negative-load program later. If a proposed interruption, concentration, or constraint is said to matter, the account can specify whether it predicts performance loss, faster fatigability, altered stability, a particular tissue exposure, a biological response, symptoms, or an injury outcome. “Load mismanagement” then becomes a family of testable relations rather than a synonym for any disliked movement.

## Evolution makes posterior specialization a serious question

Human anatomy did not appear without history. Bipedal walking, running, carrying, climbing, throwing, tool use, endurance, development, and environmental variation all provide possible contexts in which posterior structures acquired or retained their present proportions and functions. The large gluteal muscles, long Achilles tendon, spinal and pelvic organization, and posterior muscular architecture make evolutionary interpretation both tempting and legitimate.

The strongest accounts separate several steps. First identify a trait. Then propose a candidate function. Next distinguish evidence from living biomechanics, comparative anatomy, fossils, development, physiology, and ecology. Then consider multifunctionality, phylogenetic inheritance, developmental constraint, tradeoffs, and competing tasks. Only after that should a modern functional prediction be made.

Comparative and fossil arguments have proposed that endurance running contributed to the evolution of *Homo*.[^08-11] Experimental work comparing gluteus-maximus activity during walking and running found a larger role during running and interpreted that result as consistent with a running-related evolutionary hypothesis.[^08-12] These are meaningful lines of evidence. They do not prove that the entire posterior chain is the universal primary route, that every modern person should run, or that one standing posture is natural.

Evolution selects across reproductive and ecological consequences, not toward a single engineering optimum defined by the present book. A trait can serve several jobs. A structure advantageous in one activity may carry a cost in another. Current environments and lifespans differ from past ones. Development, sex, body proportions, disability, illness, training, and technology shape what a given anatomy can do. “Evolved for” is therefore usually too simple for a whole system.

A productive evolutionary hypothesis yields comparisons. It might predict that a structure's activity, architecture, or elastic behavior changes especially during one task relative to another; that a human trait differs in a specified way from a comparative sample; or that a fossil feature is consistent with a bounded range of functions. Competing accounts should predict something different. If the hypothesis explains every posterior feature after the fact and risks no contrary observation, evolutionary language has added narrative rather than evidence.

> **Figure 8.6 — Evolutionary claims need intermediate steps [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> specified trait
>      -> candidate function
>      -> evidence class and comparison
>      -> alternatives, multifunctionality, and tradeoffs
>      -> bounded prediction in a named modern task
>
>      -/-> correct posture, universal route, or health conclusion
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Evolutionary history can motivate a testable posterior-function program. It cannot bypass the mechanical, comparative, developmental, and outcome-specific steps needed to infer a modern preferred configuration.
>
> **Text alternative.** A sequence runs from a named trait through candidate function, evidence, alternatives, and a bounded modern prediction. A blocked arrow prevents the sequence from jumping directly to correct posture, a universal route, or health.

What this evolutionary evidence establishes at this stage is a reason to prioritize the question. Posterior specialization deserves direct study because multiple named structures make substantial contributions to upright support, propulsion, braking, balance, and energy exchange. Book II can ask whether these contributions participate necessarily, though not sufficiently, in a preferred organization and whether an explicit efficiency metric can distinguish that organization from alternatives. The answer cannot be assumed from ancestry.

## A substantial system inside a larger one

The posterior chain is mechanically consequential. This chapter has shown that claim in the places where it is strongest. Posterior muscles can make large contributions to the moments of object transfer. Posterior muscle–tendon systems can generate work, brake motion, store and return energy, redirect demand, and change the time course of power. Gluteal, hamstring, calf, Achilles, and spinal structures contribute to support, progression, swing control, and recovery from perturbation. These functions are ordinary, measurable, and central to upright life.

Their importance remains conditional because living mechanics is relational. A contribution belongs to a task, phase, boundary, quantity, geometry, state, and model. An external balance does not uniquely reveal internal sharing. Standing and sitting are support histories rather than moralized shapes. Walking is three-dimensional. Stability can use movement and external assistance. Performance, fatigue, stability, exposure, injury, and health require different observations.

This conclusion is neither posterior exclusivity nor the neutral claim that every tissue matters equally. It says that the posterior system warrants special attention and that its role can be stated with precision. Anterior, lateral, deep, sensory, pressure-mediated, and environmental partners do not cancel posterior importance; they describe the whole in which that importance operates.

The next chapter expands the view across the body and lifespan. It asks how posterior participation changes with development, pregnancy, illness, disability, aging, assistance, environment, and individual anatomy, and how nonposterior partners keep the system viable. That whole-body account will preserve three separate propositions: the existence of a posterior system, the usefulness of an anterior–posterior comparison under defined conditions, and the later hypothesis that posterior participation is necessary but not sufficient within a preferred organization. Only the first two carry Book I's present argument.

# Chapter 9 — Posterior support across the whole body and lifespan

The object is already being carried. The full transfer ended in Chapter 8, so there is no need to lift it again. Keep only one frame: a person moving with the object in the hands while the feet exchange contact with the ground. The posterior overlay remains important—calf and Achilles, hamstrings and gluteal structures, axial muscles, latissimus, trapezius, and their broader connective relations are all available to participate.

Now widen the frame. Add the abdominal wall and thorax, lateral hip and ankle relations, deep segmental structures, skeletal contacts, pressure-bearing boundaries, sensory information, the object's shape and grip, the floor, and any device, furniture, or person supplying support. None of these additions makes the posterior structures less substantial. They show the system in which posterior contribution becomes possible and measurable.

Widen the frame once more, this time through time. The person did not arrive as a completed adult mechanism. Anatomy, proportions, control, experience, confidence, tasks, and environment have histories. Pregnancy can change mass distribution and the assumptions used in a model. Injury, pain, and illness can change the state in which a task begins. Disability and assistance can change available contacts and goals. Training may alter one capacity without altering another. Aging can change margins, strategies, and recovery without placing everyone on one decline curve.

Posterior support remains a major theme across those histories. Its anatomy persists, its available contribution changes, and its meaning depends on the body, task, phase, environment, and support actually present. The purpose of this chapter is to keep all three statements true at once: posterior anatomy is mechanically significant; it operates within a larger whole; and the larger series asks a stronger question about preferred organization that Book I does not need to answer.

> **Figure 9.1 — Widen the familiar task, then retire it [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Boundary | What enters the carry frame | What the frame can establish |
> |---|---|---|
> | Posterior overlay | selected posterior muscles, tendons, fasciae, joints, and junctions | structures available to participate |
> | Whole-body overlay | anterior, lateral, deep, skeletal, pressure-bearing, sensory, and control relations | cooperating contributors and candidate internal partitions |
> | Person–environment overlay | object, ground, furniture, rail, device, helper, space, and task goal | external contacts, constraints, assistance, and a complete task boundary |
>
> **Caption.** The final callback to the object transfer widens one carry phase from a posterior overlay to a whole person–environment system. Measured external contacts remain distinct from modeled or inferred internal sharing. The recurring transfer ends here.
>
> **Text alternative.** Three rows progressively add posterior anatomy, whole-body partners, and environmental or assistive supports to one carry frame. Each row states the limited conclusion supplied by that boundary; no row ranks a technique or infers a unique internal route.

## A major participant inside a whole-body system

Whole-body cooperation does not mean that all structures contribute equally. It means that the contribution under discussion belongs to a closed question. Posterior muscles may generate or resist moments, propel, brake, suspend, or redirect. Anterior structures may actively brake, guide, contain, or change pressure relations. Lateral structures can help manage side-to-side demands and foot placement. Deep structures can alter segmental relation. Bones, joints, passive restraints, pressure boundaries, sensory control, and external contacts change the available solution. The partition can be unequal and still be cooperative.

This distinction separates three claims that are easy to compress into one. An anatomical system can be substantial because of its scale, arrangement, and connections. It can have considerable capacity under selected conditions. It can nevertheless contribute little to a particular output during a particular phase. Conversely, a comparatively small structure, a contact with the environment, or a modest pressure change can be decisive when the geometry gives it the relevant leverage. Anatomical significance, available capacity, and participation in the selected task are related questions, not interchangeable answers.

The output matters just as much as the contributor. A structure can oppose a joint moment while doing little positive work. It can receive load while another relation controls motion. It can help stabilize a segment while an external contact carries much of the resultant demand. A pressure-bearing boundary can support shape without replacing the skeleton, and the skeleton can transmit a substantial resultant without explaining how the person maintained balance. “What carried the load?” is therefore unfinished until *load*, carrier, boundary, direction, phase, and outcome have been named.

Walking makes this specificity visible. In simulations based on eight participants, estimated contributions of gluteal, hamstring, plantar-flexor, vasti, and skeletal-alignment relations changed with walking speed and phase.[^09-01] The result is model-dependent, but its central lesson is secure: “posterior participation in walking” is not one constant number. Support and progression are changing outputs, and muscles that contribute strongly in one phase need not do the same work in another.

Balance recovery changes the partition again. In an overground perturbation study of fifteen healthy adults, recovery strategies varied with the direction of the disturbance and included different combinations of stepping and segmental response.[^09-02] A posterior hip or ankle contribution can be substantial without becoming the universal recovery strategy. Arms, lateral foot placement, visual and vestibular information, a rail, or assistance may change what happens next. Information influences the selection of forces and contacts; it is not itself an anatomical carrier of load.

External support makes the boundary change especially clear. In an eight-participant lifting study, varying the lumbar-to-hip support ratio of an active exoskeleton changed modeled spinal loading and lumbar motion.[^09-03] The device did not become part of the person's anatomy. It added contact, force, geometry, mass, and control relations to the task. Whether such a change is useful depends on the endpoint—modeled loading, freedom of motion, comfort, effort, performance, access, or another outcome. The chapter uses the experiment only to establish that an external carrier can reorganize the mechanical solution.

The same logic applies to ordinary assistance. A hand on a counter, an object resting against a shelf, a cane, a cart, an orthosis, a second person, or permission to sit changes the boundary. Removing that support from a model does not reveal the body's pure mechanics. It analyzes a different task.

Posterior importance is therefore compatible with several kinds of variation. A task may rely heavily on posterior work in one phase and mostly on contact or skeletal geometry in another. A person may use an external support to reduce one requirement while increasing upper-limb or control demands. Another may use a distinct but stable asymmetric strategy. The mechanical question is not whether posterior participation is maximized. It is what contributes, to which output, under which boundary, and with what alternatives.

This is a stronger posterior account than a simple inventory. It allows posterior contribution to be large without requiring it to be visually obvious, and it allows a visible posterior motion to occur without assuming posterior tissues carry every important demand. It also makes comparison possible. A study can ask whether posterior participation changes when object position, pace, support, fatigue, or task phase changes, while preserving the other contributors needed to interpret the result. The posterior system becomes a tractable object inside whole-body mechanics rather than either a universal explanation or an isolated chain.

> **Figure 9.2 — Whole-body load sharing changes with the boundary [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Task and phase | Selected output | Posterior participation | Cooperating relations | Boundary that can change the account |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Carry at steady speed | object support and trunk moment balance | posterior trunk, hip, and lower-limb structures may contribute actively or passively | abdominal and pressure relations, lateral balance, skeleton, grip, ground contact | object position, pace, fatigue, device, or help |
> | Place an object | deceleration and final contact | selected posterior structures may brake or change leverage | knee extensors, upper limb, feet, target support, sensory guidance | target height, leaning contact, assistance, confidence |
> | Recover from a perturbation | regain a viable base | ankle, hip, trunk, or stepping contribution varies with direction and timing | lateral foot action, arms, vision, vestibular and somatosensory information | surface, footwear, rail, helper, predictability |
> | Walk with external support | progression under changed contacts | posterior work may be reduced, displaced, or retained in another phase | device, upper limb, contralateral limb, trunk, ground, user control | design, fit, comfort, goal, and permitted contact |
>
> **Caption.** Posterior contribution remains a serious object of measurement, but every row needs a task, phase, selected output, cooperating relations, and boundary. The table does not imply equal contribution, symmetry, or one preferred solution.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows compare carrying, placement, perturbation recovery, and assisted walking. Columns name the output, posterior contribution, other cooperating systems, and the boundary condition that could change the result.

## Region, domain, role, and sign are different questions

Several project terms often appear together because the larger theory proposes a systematic relationship among them. They cannot be made synonymous at the definition stage.

**Region** asks where a structure lies relative to a declared anatomical frame: posterior thigh, anterior abdominal wall, lateral hip, or deep spinal region. **Relative domain** asks what lies outside or inside a selected boundary: skin relative to viscera, a cavity wall relative to its contents, or a superficial layer relative to a deep compartment. The answer changes with the boundary. Exterior is not automatically posterior, and interior is not automatically anterior.

**Mechanical role** asks what a selected structure or assembly does in a direction, task, state, and timescale. The hard/soft language developed earlier is motivated by traditional Chinese medicine, but in Book I it names relative shape-preserving and form-receiving roles. A posterior muscle can be active while lengthening and receiving form. A tendon can transmit substantial tension while deforming. An anterior or lateral pressure-supported boundary can preserve a larger shape. A bone can cease to carry a dominant path when contact changes. No region or tissue owns one role.

**Proposed sign or traditional relation** asks a later question about Yin, Yang, and the coordinate families developed in Books II and III. Those categories may prove to correspond systematically with region, domain, or role. They are not yet validated mechanical variables, and the correspondence cannot be installed by labeling posterior structures Yang in advance.

> **Figure 9.3 — Four columns that must not collapse [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Column | Question | Example | Not identical to |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Region | Where is it in a declared anatomical frame? | posterior thigh; anterior abdomen; lateral hip; deep spine | force direction, role, or sign |
> | Relative domain | What is outside or inside a selected boundary? | cavity wall relative to contents; superficial relative to deep | posterior or anterior region |
> | Mechanical role | Is this relation comparatively shape-preserving or form-receiving here? | yielding posterior muscle; shape-preserving anterior pressure boundary | fixed tissue class, virtue, or sign |
> | Proposed sign or traditional relation | Which Yin/Yang or later coordinate tendency is proposed? | a future assignment under axial, opening/rotational, or expansive mode | established anatomy or measured mechanics |
>
> **Caption.** Region, relative domain, mechanical role, and proposed sign describe different objects. Dashed correspondences among them remain later hypotheses; none is built into the definitions.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four columns separate anatomical region, inside–outside relation, changing hard/soft role, and future Yin/Yang or coordinate assignment. The final column in each row states what that category cannot be treated as identical to.

Keeping the columns separate protects rather than weakens the broader hypothesis. If a future model predicts that certain relations recur together, the prediction can be tested against counterexamples. A correspondence that is true by definition cannot fail and therefore cannot explain why one body, task, or phase differs from another.

Consider one structure across a single movement. It may begin in a comparatively shape-preserving role, accept deformation while controlling motion, transmit tension as another joint changes relation, and then become mechanically quiet after an external support receives the object. Its anatomical region has not changed. Its role has. A neighboring structure may make the opposite transition, while a pressure boundary helps preserve the organization of the trunk across both phases. The whole-body account is therefore not a contest in which hard defeats soft. It is an account of where shape is preserved, where form is received, and how those roles exchange without losing the task.

The same discipline applies to the word *exterior*. Skin is exterior relative to the tissues beneath it, yet a deep cavity wall can be exterior relative to its contents. A posterior layer can lie inside another posterior layer. A later Yin/Yang correspondence may assign importance to such nested relations, but posterior location cannot settle the assignment. By preserving these distinctions now, Book I can supply examples and counterexamples to later formal work instead of quietly deciding its result.

## Development and training create specific options

Support is acquired and reorganized. Early movement does not consist of a weak version of one completed adult pattern. Body proportions, contact possibilities, muscle and tendon properties, sensory calibration, confidence, environmental opportunity, and learned coordination change together. The history is not contained in anatomy alone.

A longitudinal study followed eighteen infants at two or three time points between birth and walking onset. Trial-to-trial organization of leg-muscle activity changed across development: early variability could be represented through relatively few modeled locomotor primitives, while later activity became more regular as the identified primitive structure changed.[^09-04] The small electromyography and modeling study does not supply a universal developmental law. It does show why development should not be described as one fixed coordination merely becoming stronger.

Naturalistic observation provides another scale. Recordings of twelve- to nineteen-month-old infants showed large numbers of short, variable locomotor bouts, with steps and falls distributed through ordinary exploration rather than confined to periodic straight walking.[^09-05] The sample averages are not milestones or instructions. They show that variability, repetition, contact, failure to complete a step, and renewed attempts can all be part of acquiring a task.

Childhood and adolescence continue the history without following a single mechanical script. Growth changes segment lengths, mass distribution, leverage, contact geometry, and the relation between a familiar task and present capacity. New environments and activities add skills and exposures. A strategy can be viable during one period and reorganized as proportions, goals, or opportunities change. The relevant continuity is not visual preservation of one pattern. It is the repeated construction of workable relations among the current body, task, support, and surroundings.

Adult mechanics remain historical as well. Occupation, sport, caregiving, travel, inactivity, injury, chosen practice, and ordinary repetition can make some demands familiar and others novel. Two people with similar gross anatomy may reach the same external result through different timing, contacts, confidence, or effort because they arrive with different histories. Those differences need not be errors. They become mechanically important when the question concerns exposure, transfer, fatigue, recovery, or available alternatives.

Posterior structures participate throughout this history, but “posterior engagement” is too coarse to describe what changes. Growth alters geometry and mass distribution. Experience alters prediction and contact choices. A task that is difficult under one set of proportions may become ordinary under another. Different developmental routes can arrive at viable ways of standing, moving, reaching, or using assistance. The useful question at each stage is what anatomy, task, environment, support, and strategy are available now—not how closely the person resembles one adult template.

Training is also specific. It can alter force, power, endurance, tissue dimensions, stiffness, timing, skill, confidence, perception, or task strategy, and those changes do not transfer evenly. In a six-week randomized comparison of thirty older adults, conventional high-intensity resistance training produced larger changes in the trained strength tests, while loaded functional practice produced larger changes in gait speed and timed-up-and-go; some isometric and muscle-size measures changed in both groups.[^09-06] The study was small and short. Its value here is that it separates “improvement” into trained exposure, measured outcome, and transfer to another task.

A posterior muscle group can become stronger without becoming more important in every activity. A task can improve because timing, confidence, contact, or another system changed. A measured gain can persist, fade, or transfer selectively. Training can therefore expand one option without restoring an assumed natural route. This chapter makes no program recommendation. It establishes that current participation and capacity are historical, acquired, and measure-specific.

> **Figure 9.4 — Lifespan as changing options, not one peak and decline [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> development:  changing geometry + exploration + control + opportunity
> training:     exposure A -> outcome A; transfer to outcome B remains a separate question
> pregnancy:    changing anthropometry + tissue and pressure relations + fatigue + support
> injury/pain:  changed starting state + sensation + confidence + available strategies
> illness:      condition-specific changes in energy, recovery, control, sensation, or goals
> disability:   body + device/help + environment + participation goal form one viable system
> aging:        multiple trajectories in capability, experience, recovery, support, and reserve
>
> At every line: posterior significance persists; its form and share can change.
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Life contexts change several parts of the mechanical system at once. The lines are parallel questions rather than stages on a single ideal trajectory, and no line receives a correction rule.
>
> **Text alternative.** Seven parallel lines describe development, training, pregnancy, injury or pain, illness, disability, and aging as changes in geometry, state, support, experience, or goals. A shared note states that posterior importance can persist while its expression changes.

## Pregnancy changes the model, not the person's status

Pregnancy changes the person–environment system through time. Mass and its distribution change. Anthropometric assumptions used to estimate segment centers can become less accurate. Tissue and pressure relations, fatigue, recovery, comfort, available support, and chosen strategies may change. None of those changes supplies one pregnancy posture or one posterior deficit.

In a three-dimensional gait comparison involving fifteen women late in pregnancy and again one year postpartum, overall kinematic changes were smaller than a stereotyped “waddling” account would suggest even though body mass and trunk mass distribution changed. Hip and ankle kinetic measures increased, and pelvic-tilt changes varied among individuals.[^09-07] The external task could remain recognizable while internal demands and individual trajectories differed.

A separate repeated-measures treadmill study of fifteen pregnant participants found gestation-related changes in center-of-mass-based walking-balance measures. The estimated result also changed materially with the anthropometric method used to locate the trunk center of mass.[^09-08] The model has to change when the body being modeled changes. A familiar silhouette or a calculation based on nonpregnant segment assumptions cannot establish the actual internal distribution.

Posterior structures may contribute differently as geometry, pressure relations, support, and fatigue change, but anterior, lateral, deep, sensory, and environmental partners remain part of the account. A handrail, changed pace, footwear, rest, or another chosen support can be an effective part of the system rather than evidence that an unassisted pattern has failed. The cited studies do not establish symptoms, fall mechanism, treatment, or a correction. They establish variable mechanics within a changing and still viable task.

Pregnancy also makes timescale explicit. A comparison between late pregnancy and a later postpartum measurement does not describe every transition between them, and a group mean does not describe every participant. The same person may use different solutions as the task, day, comfort, or available support changes. A useful mechanical model follows those changing conditions rather than treating pregnancy as a fixed category appended to an otherwise complete adult model.

## Pain, injury, illness, and connective-tissue variation require separate accounts

Pain can change movement without identifying its own origin. In a crossover experiment with thirty healthy adults, electrical stimulation was coupled to lumbar flexion or extension during repeated box lifting. Participants reduced movement in the pain-provoking direction, and some changes persisted after stimulation ended.[^09-09] Because the pain was experimentally imposed and direction-linked, the study supports adaptation to that protocol. It does not show that a similar movement in chronic pain reveals the initiating tissue, earlier load path, or needed correction.

Injury changes the starting state. Material properties, sensation, confidence, active control, external support, and the task itself may be different after injury. The mechanical question is not automatically “Which posterior route failed?” It is: given the present tissue state, goal, contacts, and alternatives, what does the current organization preserve and what demand does it redistribute? Any specific injury would require its own evidence before the direction or magnitude of that reorganization could be asserted.

Illness is not one mechanical category. A particular condition or its treatment may alter energy availability, recovery, circulation, sensation, control, range, attention, or the value of assistance. Another condition may affect none of those variables in the task being studied. A useful account must name the condition, relevant variable, task, time, treatment context, and comparison. The only general claim needed here is that illness can change the system being modeled and cannot be represented as a generic departure from a canonical healthy body.

Connective-tissue variation shows why a label does not dictate a strategy. In a cross-sectional comparison of twenty-nine people classified with joint hypermobility syndrome and thirty controls, investigators reported group differences in walking speed, stance and double-support duration, joint moments, and power. The observed gait was described as relatively stiff rather than visibly hypermobile.[^09-10] Selection, symptoms, and cross-sectional design prevent a causal conclusion. The result demonstrates that passive-range classification does not uniquely determine how a person organizes an active task.

These contexts also clarify *compensation*. A compensation is first a change that preserves something valuable: task completion, comfort, protection of a current tissue state, balance, participation, or energy. It may later prove efficient or costly, temporary or stable, optional or necessary. Those are separate questions. Calling it compensation does not diagnose hidden damage, predict future failure, or tell the person to remove it.

Preservation and consequence must be evaluated on their own timescales. A strategy can solve the immediate problem and increase demand somewhere else. It can also look unusual while remaining comfortable, durable, and well suited to the person's priorities. Either possibility needs evidence. The existence of redistributed demand does not establish that the redistribution exceeds capacity, and the absence of an immediate symptom does not establish that every exposure is inconsequential. Part III will supply the language for dose, concentration, continuity, and recovery that those questions require.

The chronology matters. A changed strategy can follow pain, injury, illness, or altered support; it can also precede a symptom or be unrelated to it. A later observation does not reconstruct the unobserved transition by itself. Part III will ask when a useful substitution persists, concentrates demand, or narrows available options. Chapter 9 supplies the positive baseline: reorganization can be coherent and successful under the conditions in which it occurs.

## Disability and assistance belong inside the system boundary

Disability cannot be represented mechanically by subtracting abilities from an unmarked reference body. The World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health treats functioning and disability as interactions among health conditions and contextual factors, including environment, activity, and participation.[^09-11] The classification is not a constitutive model of tissue. Its relevant discipline is that the body, task, environment, and desired participation belong in the same description.

An assistive device adds contacts, constraints, geometry, mass, sensory information, and control requirements. It can create a route that does not exist in the unassisted model. In a within-subject study, twenty healthy participants walked while unloading one ankle and foot with forearm crutches, a knee crutch, or an unloading orthosis. Kinematic, force, metabolic, comfort, and stability measures differed among devices.[^09-12] The study does not represent disabled users, long-term use, clinical effectiveness, or every device. It demonstrates that the chosen support changes the mechanical solution and its tradeoffs.

A complete assisted system is therefore:

```text
person + device or helper + fit and contact + ground + task + environment + control history
```

Removing a wheelchair, cane, prosthesis, orthosis, rail, chair, helper, or environmental support from that boundary may remove what makes the task viable. It does not reveal the true person beneath an artificial compensation. Assistance can be ordinary architecture.

The interface matters as much as the device name. Contact location, fit, friction, stiffness, timing, user control, and the ground or furniture against which the device acts can change the resulting forces and possibilities. A device can reduce demand at one region while adding work, pressure, attention, or coordination elsewhere. Those changes are neither automatically beneficial nor automatically harmful; they identify the actual system that should be measured.

Assistance also changes what counts as capacity. If a person can reliably complete a valued task with a chosen device or another person's help, that capability belongs to the assisted system. An unassisted laboratory result may answer a narrower research question, but it cannot replace the participation outcome by definition. The boundary should be selected to match the question, not selected in advance to privilege independence from support.

This view also prevents symmetry from becoming an undeclared goal. An asymmetric strategy can be stable, economical, comfortable, skilled, or required by the available contacts. Its value depends on the person's goals and alternatives, not on visual resemblance to a bilaterally symmetric diagram. Laboratory mechanics can compare contacts, forces, moments, energy, and performance. It cannot determine a person's priorities or preferred participation without lived-experience and accessibility input.

Posterior structures remain significant within assisted and disabled systems. Their contribution may be increased, reduced, redistributed in time, or joined through a different external carrier. No single direction follows from the category. The posterior question remains empirical and task-specific rather than disappearing or becoming a deficit score.

## Aging changes reserve along more than one trajectory

Aging is not one posterior-chain decline. Muscle mass, force, power, tendon behavior, bone, cartilage, balance, sensation, recovery, confidence, medication, health conditions, task familiarity, and environment can change at different rates and in different directions. Population averages describe populations; they do not assign an individual trajectory.

An eight-year study followed 2,364 adults who were seventy to seventy-nine and initially well functioning. The analysis identified three gait-speed trajectories with meaningfully different rates of change.[^09-13] The categories were statistical descriptions, not destinies. They show that even one familiar mobility measure does not follow a single aging curve.

Different measurements also answer different questions. In longitudinal data from 934 adults aged at least sixty-five, baseline lower-extremity strength and power related to later mobility outcomes, but baseline level and change over time were not interchangeable predictors.[^09-14] A later analysis from the same cohort found that leg power discriminated later loss of activities of daily living better than knee strength in men, while neither measure showed the same advantage in women.[^09-15] Strength, power, walking speed, and daily activity are related, not substitutable.

This chapter uses *reserve* provisionally as a conditional margin. For a defined task, time window, and current state, reserve is the margin between the demand being met and the capability available through the whole person–environment system. It is not one scalar already measured by age, gait speed, posterior strength, or a laboratory maximum.

Nor is reserve necessarily one hidden quantity waiting to be found. A person may have ample force for a task but little endurance for its repetition, or sufficient steady-state capability but a narrow margin under an unexpected perturbation. Recovery may become limiting even when the first attempt is easy. A supportive environment may enlarge practical margin without changing tissue capacity. For now, reserve is best treated as a family of task-specific margins whose dimensions must be declared rather than collapsed into one score.

The margin can change from either side. Training may expand one capability. Illness, sleep loss, or recent exertion may narrow it temporarily. A rail can reduce effective demand during a transition. Familiarity, pacing, or task redesign can make the same goal occupy less of the available margin. A device may reduce demand at one region while adding another requirement. Recovery time can matter even when peak capability is unchanged.

Experience and assistance are therefore part of reserve, not contaminants in its measurement. A slower pace may preserve a useful margin. A familiar route may require less attention. A chair at the right height can make a transition available. None of these proves superior health or optimal mechanics. Each shows why reserve belongs to a declared task and boundary rather than to a person as a permanent score.

Posterior capacity can be an important component of reserve. It may matter greatly for a particular gait phase, transition, carry, or perturbation. But posterior strength alone cannot represent sensory confidence, balance, endurance, recovery, environment, and alternative support. The positive claim survives intact: posterior capability is consequential. Its consequence belongs to the whole system.

## Candidate observations are questions, not tests

The larger project needs observable consequences if it is to become testable. The correct response is not to suppress recognizable signs; it is to state what question each sign might answer.

**Participation** asks whether a named structure or system contributed during a task. Candidate observations include electromyography, tendon strain, pressure, contact force, device load, joint-moment sensitivity, or modeled muscle force. Each needs a task, phase, signal model, and alternative account.

**Capacity** asks what a selected system can meet under stated conditions. Candidate observations include maximal or repeated task output, force, power, endurance, range under demand, and recovery of performance. Repeatability, safety, task specificity, strategy, and population matter. A capacity result is not a tissue-health score.

**Compensation** asks what changed to preserve a valued outcome. Timing, contact, asymmetry, bracing, pace, support, assistance, or route may change. Chronology, the preserved goal, available alternatives, and any cost must be established before the change is called adverse.

**Reserve** asks what margin remained as demand was graded, support was removed or added, a perturbation occurred, fatigue developed, or recovery proceeded. The question needs a stopping rule, timescale, whole-system boundary, and a definition of the capability being compared.

A sit-to-stand transition illustrates the separation. Observing trunk inclination or foot placement describes movement. Measuring seat and ground reaction forces adds external load information. Estimating joint moments adds a calculation whose assumptions must be stated. Surface electromyography may indicate selected muscle activation without determining total force. Repeating the task under a graded demand may inform one capacity or fatigue question. Adding arm support may reveal how an external contact reorganizes the solution. None of these observations alone establishes compensation, reserve, tissue condition, or the reason one strategy was chosen.

The same marker can therefore serve different questions only through different study designs. Slower movement might reflect deliberate pacing, limited power, pain avoidance, unfamiliarity, a precision goal, or the requirements of a device. Greater asymmetry might preserve contact, reduce discomfort, accommodate anatomy, or simply fall within ordinary variation. A useful marker does not carry its interpretation in its appearance. Comparison, chronology, task definition, and alternatives give it meaning.

> **Figure 9.5 — Observations sorted by the question they may answer [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Question | Candidate observation | Possible provenance | Validation still empty |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Participation | activation, tendon strain, pressure, contact, modeled contribution, device load | observed, measured, calculated, modeled | reliability, construct validity, carrier alternatives |
> | Capacity | force, power, endurance, repeated output, task range, recovery | measured or calculated under a protocol | repeatability, task transfer, population, safety |
> | Compensation | changed timing, contact, asymmetry, pace, bracing, route, or assistance | observed, measured, inferred, or embodied | chronology, preserved goal, alternatives, cost |
> | Reserve | response to graded demand, perturbation, fatigue, recovery, or changed support | measured, modeled, or inferred | margin definition, stopping rule, timescale, meaning |
>
> **Caption.** A visible or measurable change becomes a candidate research object only after its question and provenance are named. The empty validation column prevents any observation from becoming a diagnosis, personal score, or correction rule.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows sort observations into participation, capacity, compensation, and reserve. Each row includes possible evidence states and an explicitly unfinished validation column.

Observation states must remain explicit. An observed movement is not a force measurement. A calculated joint moment is not an individual-muscle force. A modeled contribution is not direct observation. An inference about compensation requires chronology. An embodied continuity can motivate measurement without becoming an instrument reading. A change after assistance shows that the boundary mattered; it does not diagnose why.

This measurement discipline leaves room for null results. An asymmetry may be reliable but add no useful prediction. A posterior marker may not distinguish the selected outcome. A visible brace may be purposeful. Reported fatigue may occur without a decline in measured output, and output may decline without identifying a tissue. The project advances when an observation narrows, revises, or fails to support a proposed relation—not only when it confirms one.

## Three independently gated posterior propositions

The posterior argument now has three levels. They are related by the research program, but each has its own evidence and publication job.

**Level 1 — anatomical and mechanical existence.** Posterior structures form a major, layered anatomical and mechanical system. Chapter 7 established the anatomy: large-by-measure muscles, substantial tendons, long and short axial layers, broad aponeuroses and fasciae, branching skeletal junctions, and bounded regional continuities. Chapter 8 established task-specific mechanics: posterior structures can make substantial contributions to moments, work, braking, propulsion, elastic behavior, balance, and ordinary function. This level is a Book I conclusion. *Major* does not mean exclusive, sufficient, or dominant in every task.

**Level 2 — a conditional whole-body lens.** Anterior–posterior distribution is a useful way to investigate whole-body load sharing when that comparison changes a prediction, measurement, or interpretation. It can ask whether a task is resolved differently as posterior and anterior contributions, contacts, or exposures change. It remains one lens alongside lateral, deep, pressure, temporal, sensory, and environmental relations. This level is also Book I. The lens may add little for a particular task or outcome, and that null result is allowed.

**Level 3 — the preferred-organization hypothesis.** We expect posterior participation to be necessary but insufficient within the preferred organization investigated in Book II. The later model proposes an all-Yang organization involving downward axial resolution, external or opening rotation, and outward expansion. Posterior participation alone is not sufficient: ordinary extension, visible backward movement, or large posterior work can occur without the proposed organization. The expectation is direct, but it is not derived by Chapters 1–9 and does no load-bearing work in Book I.

*Necessary* at Level 3 still needs a scale and definition. The proposal may concern a whole-person organization while a selected posterior structure is quiet, lengthening, internally loaded, or mechanically secondary during one phase. Book II must define participation, the preferred state, the relevant efficiency or comparison criterion, and observations that would disfavor necessity. Tasks or scales with absent or optional posterior contribution are countercases to explain, not exceptions to absorb after the fact.

> **Figure 9.6 — Three posterior propositions with independent gates [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> LEVEL 1  Posterior anatomical and mechanical system exists
>          evidence: documented anatomy + bounded task contribution
>          posture: Book I conclusion
>
> LEVEL 2  Anterior–posterior distribution is a conditional whole-body lens
>          evidence: comparisons that change prediction, measurement, or interpretation
>          posture: Book I organizing synthesis
>
> LEVEL 3  Posterior participation is expected necessary but insufficient
>          within the later preferred organization
>          evidence still required: Book II definitions, derivation, efficiency criterion,
>          countercases, scale choice, and discriminating measurements
>          posture: direct authorial hypothesis; nonderived and non-load-bearing here
>
> PROHIBITED: Level 1 or 2 -> proof of Level 3
> PROHIBITED: Level 3 -> validation of Level 1 or 2
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The three propositions are not rungs on an automatic ladder. Levels 1 and 2 carry Book I independently. Level 3 preserves the series hypothesis without borrowing evidence from the first two or lending authority back to them.
>
> **Text alternative.** Three separate blocks state the Book I existence claim, the conditional anterior–posterior lens, and the later necessary-but-insufficient preferred-organization hypothesis. Blocked arrows prevent evidence from leaking upward or downward among them.

A reader can therefore accept Level 1, use or test Level 2, and remain unconvinced by Level 3 without contradiction. The project can also revise Level 2's usefulness in a particular domain without erasing posterior anatomy. Keeping the gates independent gives the stronger hypothesis somewhere honest to stand while its formal work remains ahead.

## From viable support to load management

Posterior support is substantial, variable, and inseparable from the whole person–environment system. Its anatomy and ordinary function justify focused attention. Its available contribution changes with development, training, pregnancy, pain, injury, illness, connective-tissue variation, disability, assistance, aging, and reserve. Those changes do not arrange bodies along one scale from normal to defective.

Hard and soft remain changing roles rather than posterior and anterior territories. Compensation begins as preservation of something valuable. Assistance can be architecture. Reserve is a conditional margin rather than a youth or health score. Candidate observations become useful only when their question, provenance, validation, and alternatives are specified.

This closes the positive architecture of Part II. Level 1 establishes the posterior system; Level 2 authorizes a conditional anterior–posterior lens; Level 3 states the preferred-organization hypothesis directly without making it carry Book I.

Part III begins from this viable baseline. It asks what happens as demand approaches available capacity, continuity or handoff changes, exposure concentrates, a form-receiving structure is maintained under deformation, control becomes unstable, or a compensation alters what happens next. Those are questions about changing load management, not a catalogue of defective bodies.
