## Part II synthesis — Cooperation before priority

The architecture of support is plural. Skeletal geometry, joint contact, active force, tensile transfer, restraint, glide, containment, pressure, and control solve different parts of a task. Their contributions overlap and change through time. No tissue label supplies its role in advance.

This cooperative account strengthens rather than weakens the posterior case. The posterior body contains a large, layered set of muscles, tendons, fasciae, joints, skeletal relations, and control demands. Posterior structures participate materially in stance, locomotion, propulsion, lifting, deceleration, balance, transfer, and reaching. The exact contribution depends on speed, phase, environment, strategy, state, and the quantity being studied. Morphological continuity does not establish one cable, and task contribution does not establish universal dominance.

Three statements therefore remain separate. The posterior chain exists as a useful scope-declared anatomical system. Posterior structures are mechanically important in many tasks. Posterior participation may also prove necessary within the preferred organization investigated later in the series. Part II supports the first two at their proper scale. It does not use them to smuggle in the third.

The same boundary applies to hard and soft roles. A posterior structure can receive form; an anterior or pressure-mediated relation can preserve shape. A visible extension can use an internal distribution that differs from another visually similar movement. Good support is not the same as rigid support, maximum posterior activity, or one ideal alignment.

Part II has described successful and variable cooperation. That makes the next problem possible to state. What happens when demand exceeds current capacity, a carrier fails to engage, a compliant structure must preserve geometry it cannot readily release, or a strategy that protects function alters later exposure? Part III develops a vocabulary for those adverse organizations without turning them into diagnoses.

# Part III — Load management, failure, and compensation

The same movement can be useful training, ordinary work, temporary protection, or an exposure a tissue cannot presently recover from. The difference is not contained in posture or force alone. It depends on direction, rate, repetition, duration, variability, sequence, material state, capacity, recovery, environment, and what the system is trying to preserve.

Part III studies what changes when mechanical demand loses a viable distribution. It does not begin with a list of conditions. It begins with six families of organization that can be described and challenged before a medical conclusion is drawn.

Chapter 10 establishes the baseline: mechanical homeostasis as viable changing ranges rather than one fixed pose, and capacity as a present relation between a system and a defined exposure. Chapter 11 asks whether a demand crossed an interface, was handed off, leaked, was interrupted, or was carried by a substitute. Chapter 12 separates global geometry from the local concentrations it may or may not produce. Chapter 13 examines deformation or lost excursion maintained by an ongoing constraint. Chapter 14 distinguishes instability, discoordination, bracing, and repeated demand. Chapter 15 follows compensation and rerouting through time. Chapter 16 asks what evidence would be required for a local change to matter at a larger scale.

The families overlap, but they are not synonyms. A narrowing is not the same thing as the load that maintains it. Instability is not simply excess movement. Bracing can be successful protection. A substitute route can preserve the task without being costly, or incur a cost that appears only after repetition. A global shift can coexist with no meaningful local change. A plausible regional chain can stop when its intermediate quantities remain unmeasured.

The reader's task is to keep capability and consequence together. A changed strategy deserves to be understood for what it preserved before it is judged for what it may have cost. Every adverse account also needs a null: a condition under which the proposed carrier, exposure, or downstream effect is absent. Part III supplies that grammar so that the medical chapters do not inherit a foregone mechanical cause.

# Chapter 10 — Mechanical homeostasis, capacity, dose, time, and environment

A person moves the same manageable object to the same shelf four times. The first transfer follows an ordinary period of rest. The second comes late in a long sequence of similar transfers. The third follows an interval too short to assume that every relevant variable has recovered. Before the fourth, familiarity, a changed hand contact, a cart, or another person's assistance has changed how the task is shared.

This is a hypothetical comparison, not a test of lifting technique. Object, destination, and approximate external route remain similar. The four trials might also look similar. Yet the mechanical problem is not fully specified by appearance, object mass, or task completion. Contact forces, speed, joint moments, muscle activity, internal sharing, perceived effort, and subsequent recovery can differ. A person may finish all four transfers while the state in which each transfer ends is not the same.

The point is not that repetition hides damage. Repetition may improve coordination, leave the measured state materially unchanged, produce transient fatigue, alter symptoms, contribute to longer-term adaptation, or meet a limit. Assistance may lower one exposure while adding another or may simply make participation possible. Before any of those interpretations is chosen, the system, exposure, capacity, environment, response, and timescale have to be named.

This chapter calls that time-dependent problem *mechanical homeostasis*. The term does not identify one pose or one whole-body set point. It names a proposed ability to maintain and recover specified mechanical relations within viable, changing ranges. Capacity is the corresponding present ability of a defined system to meet and recover from a defined exposure. Neither term is useful as a hidden score. Together they provide the neutral baseline needed before later chapters ask how demand can become poorly distributed, concentrated, constrained, unstable, or compensatory.

> **Figure 10.1 — One task, four histories [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Trial | What remains approximately similar | What changes before or during the trial | Outcome left open |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | After ordinary rest | object, destination, broad task | recent exposure and recovery state | unchanged response, ordinary variation, or another branch |
> | Late in a sequence | object, destination, broad task | repetition, sequence, current fatigue or skill state | stable output with unchanged or changed internal state |
> | After a short interval | object, destination, broad task | recovery interval and starting state | recovered, partly recovered, or differently organized |
> | With familiarity or assistance | object and destination | control, contact, support, or system boundary | reduced, redistributed, added, or newly manageable exposure |
>
> **Caption.** A nominally similar task can enter a different mechanical history. The comparison is hypothetical and does not rank the trials or establish that any trial is beneficial, harmful, adapted, or injurious.
>
> **Text alternative.** A four-row table compares the same object-transfer task after rest, late in repetition, after a short interval, and with familiarity or assistance. Each row separates what remains similar, what changes, and several outcomes that remain unresolved.

## A viable range is not a pose

Homeostasis is often pictured as constancy: a variable departs from a target and is returned to it. Mechanical systems complicate that picture because useful function involves movement, changing contact, changing force, and temporary deformation. A hand must conform to an object. A joint must traverse a range. Muscle force changes from approach to acceptance and release. Cartilage, tendon, and other tissues deform as part of ordinary support. A viable mechanical state therefore cannot mean that all relevant quantities remain fixed.

Research on mechanical homeostasis commonly examines bounded systems such as cells, engineered tissue equivalents, vessels, or selected tissues. Within those systems, investigators ask how a preferred mechanical state is established, maintained, or restored. Even there, the sensed variable, the target, and the mechanism can remain unsettled, and the relevant range may itself change.[^10-01] Current biomechanical reviews treat mechanical homeostasis as important to tissue and organ modeling while emphasizing that neither the biology nor its mathematical representation is complete.[^10-02]

Book I extends that bounded idea as a project-level synthesis. The question becomes: can a declared task system maintain or recover task-relevant mechanical relations within a viable range as demand, state, and support change? The extension is useful only if each use identifies:

- the system and scale;
- the task and environmental conditions;
- the measured or proposed variable;
- the comparison, target, or viable range;
- the time window and recovery criterion; and
- an observation that would count against the account.

A range satisfying those conditions may include asymmetry, variation, temporary strain, fatigue, assistance, and more than one successful strategy. It may also move with development, training, injury, illness, recent work, or changing resources. Calling the range viable does not mean comfortable, symmetrical, average, optimal, or healthy. It means only that a stated function or mechanical relation remains available under the stated conditions and criterion.

The variables need not be identical at every scale. A cell-seeded construct might be studied through tension or deformation. A joint-level model might track contact, excursion, or response to perturbation. A task model might track whether output, precision, and recovery stay inside declared bounds. Moving from one scale to another requires an explicit bridge. A tissue measure cannot become whole-person homeostasis merely because both are described as mechanical, and successful performance cannot establish that every local variable remained inside a preferred range.

Nor does viability require return to one initial value. Some systems return toward a prior state; others establish a changed but workable range after practice, development, or altered support. The relevant comparison might be within one person across time, between two task conditions, or against a validated material or performance criterion. Each comparison answers a different question. The project term remains useful only when that question is visible.

The object transfer makes this distinction concrete. The system does not return to its initial geometry after every phase. It passes from support by the first surface, through hand contact and object acceptance, into carrying, placement, and release. Contacts, muscle force, pressure, and joint relations change throughout. A cart or handrail can become part of the viable system by changing its boundary. Nothing has to be “corrected” for the system to have changed successfully.

This use of mechanical homeostasis can fail. If its variables cannot be operationalized, if it adds nothing to established concepts such as stability, tolerance, or control, or if it can redescribe every result after the fact, it should be narrowed or replaced. The term earns its place by organizing comparisons that can be observed, modeled, and contradicted—not by supplying a biological preference that has not been measured.

## Capacity belongs to a system and an outcome

Capacity is often spoken of as if each tissue or person carries a fixed amount. That shorthand breaks down as soon as the endpoint changes. The capacity to complete one transfer is not the capacity to repeat it for an hour. A muscle's maximal voluntary force is not a tendon specimen's fatigue life. A joint's usable excursion is not a person's tolerance of symptoms. The ability to preserve task output is not the time required for a selected variable to recover afterward.

Here, *capacity* means the present ability of a defined system to meet and recover from a defined exposure under defined conditions. At minimum, a capacity claim needs five qualifiers:

1. **System:** tissue, interface, region, task assembly, or whole-person performance.
2. **Exposure:** the mechanical quantity, direction, magnitude, rate, configuration, and history being considered.
3. **Outcome:** completion, precision, stability, material integrity, symptom tolerance, recovery, or another declared endpoint.
4. **State:** recent loading, development, training, injury, illness, pain, sleep, medication, assistance, and other modifiers relevant to the question.
5. **Time:** one event, a sequence, a day, a training interval, or a longer trajectory.

These qualifiers do not form a generic causal checklist. Some state variables alter the mechanical system directly. A handrail adds a contact; a joint position changes geometry; active force changes internal sharing. Other variables alter tissue response, perception, behavior, or the goal of the task. Some may be incidental in a particular comparison. A useful account names the modifier and the link it is proposed to change instead of pouring every circumstance into an undefined reserve.

Scale matching prevents several common substitutions. If the outcome is tendon integrity, task completion is at most indirect evidence. If the outcome is balance during a transfer, an isolated maximum-force test does not by itself specify the available strategy. If the outcome is recovery of a measured disc variable, comfort and visible posture answer different questions. A capacity claim becomes informative when its endpoint could, in principle, be observed and when a competing endpoint could change without being mistaken for it.

The same discipline applies to thresholds. A material test can define failure through a stated force, stress, strain, or cycle criterion. A task threshold can be the point at which precision or completion is no longer maintained. A symptom-tolerance threshold concerns reported experience under stated conditions. These thresholds can coexist and need not be crossed together. “The load exceeded capacity” is therefore incomplete until both sides of the comparison have the same system, quantity or outcome, and time window.

Capacity also changes with the chosen boundary. At the boundary around a tendon specimen, failure under a specified test can be a meaningful endpoint. At a joint, the question may concern a resultant moment, local contact, or usable motion. At the person-plus-object boundary, success may mean that the object reaches the shelf. At a wider boundary, a cart, orthosis, mobility aid, or second person is not an afterthought: it is part of the system that makes the task possible.

This matters because a demand–capacity account can otherwise become a disguised judgment about the person. If an environment supplies a poor grip, an inaccessible height, forced timing, or no opportunity for support, the mismatch does not reside only inside the body. Conversely, assistance does not prove deficiency. It changes contacts, available routes, timing, and exposure. Capacity is relational by definition.

The distinction also protects the book's hard/soft model from misuse. A shape-preserving route can be capable for one direction and task while a form-receiving structure remains free to yield, glide, contain, or recover. In another phase, their roles can change. “Capacity” does not mean that soft roles should carry no demand or that hard roles never deform. It asks whether the particular division of mechanical labor preserves the declared function and the relevant freedoms over the chosen time.

## Exposure has a history

Task-level demand and internal exposure are not synonyms. *Demand* names what the task and surroundings require at a chosen boundary: support an object, oppose gravity, accelerate a segment, remain within a workspace, or tolerate a contact. *Exposure* names the resulting mechanical history at the selected tissue, interface, segment, or modeled subsystem.

The distinction is a sequence:

```text
task and environment
    -> body state, configuration, and external contacts through time
    -> measured external forces, motion, and timing
    -> calculated segment forces and moments
    -> modeled sharing among active, passive, pressure-mediated,
       skeletal, and external carriers
    -> estimated local force, stress, strain, pressure,
       deformation, or excursion history
    -> separately evidenced response and outcome
```

The same object mass can create a different moment when its distance, acceleration, support, or orientation changes. The same net joint moment can be shared differently among muscle, tendon, contact, pressure, and passive restraint. A visible activity labeled “light,” “sedentary,” “repetitive,” or “high impact” therefore does not locate a tissue dose.

The exposure descriptor introduced earlier is best treated as a structured record:

> **Figure 10.2 — Exposure is a record, not a dose score [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> selected quantity and system
>     + magnitude and direction
>     + rate and duration
>     + repetition and variability
>     + sequence and task phase
>     + rest and recovery interval
>     + starting state and material history
>     + measurement and model uncertainty
> ```
>
> **Caption.** A mechanical exposure record keeps dimensions and chronology available for a selected system. Its entries are not assumed to share units, carry equal importance, or add into a universal score.
>
> **Text alternative.** A vertical list begins with a selected quantity and system and adds magnitude, direction, rate, duration, repetition, variability, sequence, task phase, rest, recovery, starting state, and uncertainty. The caption states that these fields form a record rather than an additive dose number.

Two histories can share a peak and differ in duration. They can share nominal work and differ in rate, direction, or recovery interval. The same events can occur in another sequence, so the state at the start of each event changes. Which fields matter is an empirical question for the selected tissue and outcome, not a reason to call every descriptor equally predictive.

The word *cumulative* needs the same care. It can refer to cycle count, elapsed time, impulse, mechanical work, time above a chosen level, a fatigue-damage estimate, or simply an ordered record of prior events. Those objects have different units and assumptions. Summing repetitions ignores their direction and rate; summing work does not necessarily describe peak stress; a fatigue model calibrated for one material and loading mode cannot be transferred to another tissue by changing the label. In this chapter, cumulative exposure means that chronology remains available for analysis. It does not mean that all prior demand has been converted into one conserved quantity stored in the body.

A history can also contain recovery, variation, and learning rather than only accumulation. A later event may begin from a more capable state, a less capable state, or a state that is different along several dimensions. That is why the exposure record includes starting state and uncertainty. The record preserves possible explanatory variables; it does not prejudge their sign.

A small handgrip experiment illustrates the sequence problem. Participants completed ascending and descending submaximal force plateaus. The preceding force history affected measured fatigue accumulation, and some voluntary-force recovery appeared during a later lower-intensity plateau.[^10-03] The protocol does not yield a whole-body dose law or a recovery rule for other tissues. It shows that a list of peaks omits information that can distinguish two histories.

Occupational guidance makes a related point at a different scale. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health treats intensity, frequency, and duration, together with combinations of force, posture, repetition, contact stress, vibration, and work organization, as distinct exposure features.[^10-04] Guidance for identifying workplace factors is not a local tissue model, but it supports a disciplined refusal to turn “more load” into one undifferentiated quantity.

History also separates performance from state. Muscle fatigue is task-specific: a measured reduction in maximal force or power does not necessarily stop a submaximal task.[^10-05] In a small repetitive-lifting study, participants maintained essentially constant movement performance and modeled lumbosacral torque while fatigue-related muscle input–output characteristics changed.[^10-06] Continued performance did not prove unchanged internal sharing. The measured fatigue response did not prove damage.

For the object transfer, at least three observations should therefore remain in separate columns. *Task output* records whether the object reached the shelf. *Mechanical state* records changes in contact, speed, moment, activation, motion, or a local exposure estimate. *Response* records a declared endpoint such as maximal-force change, perceived effort, soreness, recovery time, or a tissue measure. No one column can silently stand in for the others.

Suppose the shelf is reached at the same time in two trials. In the later trial, a hand remains on a support for longer, speed falls, and the modeled joint moment changes. Those observations establish a changed solution, not its value. The change might preserve output efficiently, reflect fatigue, exploit learning, respond to discomfort, or be ordinary variation. Additional measurements and a declared outcome are what turn the changed solution into an interpretation.

## Recovery is a process, not empty time

Rest means that a declared exposure has stopped or changed. It does not mean that every variable has returned to baseline. To claim recovery, the account must name what changed, the comparison state, the measurement, and the time at which the criterion was met.

A bounded material example makes the point. In cadaveric human lumbar discs exposed to axial creep loading and then unloaded, loading and recovery followed different time courses. Under that protocol, recovery was several times slower than loading, and measured height and stiffness approached their initial values only after long unloading intervals.[^10-07] This is evidence about cadaveric discs under a specified experiment, not a prescription for sleep, work breaks, or whole-person recovery.

Living measurement adds another caution. In a study of seventeen sedentary workers, selected quantitative magnetic-resonance indices of intervertebral-disc composition differed between morning and evening measurements.[^10-08] The study supports attention to measurement time. It does not isolate the mechanical exposure responsible for the difference, show that ordinary daytime loading is damaging, or establish a relationship to symptoms.

The broader inference is modest and useful. A snapshot need not be independent of its history. The relevant history, however, depends on the system. Maximal muscle force, tendon stiffness, disc height, perceived effort, task skill, pain, and material damage are not interchangeable recovery variables. One can return while another remains changed. A kinematic return to the starting pose is especially weak evidence: it shows geometry at one moment, not restoration of material state, capacity, physiology, comfort, or future function.

The comparison state also matters. Recovery can mean return toward a pre-exposure value, movement into a task-acceptable range, restoration of a performance criterion, or establishment of a changed baseline after adaptation. These meanings should not be mixed. If the proposed variable naturally fluctuates across a day, a single earlier measurement may not be an adequate target. If a task has been learned, exact return to the initial performance pattern may be neither expected nor desirable. The criterion must follow the scientific or functional question rather than an assumption that the earliest state was ideal.

Recovery can also occur during changed activity rather than complete inactivity. The handgrip example showed partial recovery of one voluntary-force measure during a lower-intensity phase. That observation remains task- and measure-specific. It does not establish that reducing intensity always restores capacity, that recovery is complete, or that continued task performance is harmless.

This is why universal rest intervals do not follow from the chapter's model. The model asks for a recovery window because chronology matters. The answer must still be supplied by a selected system, exposure, variable, criterion, and evidence.

## Environment changes the mechanical boundary

The environment enters mechanics through contact, constraint, support, available movement, timing, and repetition. Floor compliance changes the ground relation. A handle changes where and how an object can be contacted. A seat and backrest redistribute support. A shelf height changes geometry. A tool, visual target, vehicle vibration, sport rule, or work pace changes the task that must be solved. These features may reduce one demand, add another, or alter how demand is distributed.

They do not acquire one fixed sign. Prolonged sitting, screen use, repetitive work, specialized sport, and constrained visual attention are contexts, not diagnoses. The same chair may support one task and obstruct another. A rigid surface may improve precision while increasing local contact pressure. Variability can distribute exposure in one setting and introduce control demand in another. Consistency can preserve accuracy or maintain the same exposure. The direction of effect depends on the stated system and outcome.

Assistance belongs in this account without becoming evidence of a defective body. A cane, orthosis, exoskeleton, cart, handrail, chair, or second person supplies contact or support, changes the system boundary, and can alter the route by which demand is resolved. The result may be lower exposure at one selected structure, greater exposure elsewhere, slower task performance, improved stability, or access to a task that was otherwise unavailable. Those possibilities require measurement; none is licensed by the device label alone.

Work organization is mechanical in the same conditional sense. Timing, sequence, recovery opportunity, task switching, and control over pace can change an exposure history even when the workstation geometry does not change. Social and institutional conditions can therefore enter a mechanical account through concrete boundary variables without being reduced to mechanics. Conversely, a mechanical change does not account for every way an environment affects participation, stress, expectation, or health.

The complete relation can be drawn without pretending that it is an equation:

> **Figure 10.3 — Demand becomes exposure before it meets capacity [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> TASK-LEVEL DEMAND
> objective + external conditions + time
>                 |
>                 v
> CONFIGURATION AND BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
> body state + contacts + constraints + support + environment
>                 |
>                 v
> SELECTED-SYSTEM EXPOSURE
> named quantity + direction + rate + history + uncertainty
>                 |
>                 v
> EXPOSURE RELATIVE TO PRESENT CAPACITY
> same system + declared outcome + recovery window
>                 |
>                 v
> OBSERVED RESPONSE OR OUTCOME
> kept distinct from the exposure that preceded it
> ```
>
> **Caption.** External demand is translated through configuration and boundary conditions into a measured or modeled exposure at a selected system. Capacity is evaluated relative to that exposure and a declared outcome. The diagram is a reasoning sequence, not a validated scalar function.
>
> **Text alternative.** Five boxes descend from task-level demand to configuration and boundary conditions, selected-system exposure, exposure relative to present capacity, and an observed response or outcome. Each box lists required descriptors. The caption says the sequence is not an equation or universal score.

The order matters. Comparing object mass directly with “whole-body capacity” skips configuration, contacts, routing, and local exposure. Comparing a local tendon strain with a general performance score mixes boundaries and outcomes. A bounded model can relate commensurate measurements, but the model has to show that relation rather than letting a smooth diagram imply it.

Environment is therefore neither background nor culprit. It is part of the defined mechanical system. This framing preserves both responsibility and possibility: task design, social support, resources, accessibility, and available assistance can change exposure without turning every difficulty into an individual deficit or every environmental change into a cure.

## One exposure can lead to several trajectories

Mechanical exposure is not yet biological or clinical meaning. Living tissues can respond differently according to tissue, state, dose, chronology, and the outcome being measured. Even the words used for those responses refer to different observations.

Human tendon training studies provide evidence for one branch. Across healthy lower-limb interventions, a systematic review and meta-analysis found changes in tendon stiffness, modulus, and cross-sectional area, with results depending in part on the loading program and local strain. The evidence was concentrated in Achilles and patellar tendons and did not identify one universal optimum.[^10-09] Repeated exposure can therefore participate in a demonstrated longer-term change without proving that every repeated load is adaptive or that the same program transfers to another tissue.

Experimental tendon-fatigue models establish a different branch. Repeated loading can produce progressive mechanical and microstructural change in selected specimens and protocols, while translation from those models to living tendinopathy remains complex.[^10-10] Controlled animal bone-loading studies likewise distinguish adaptive lamellar responses from injury-associated responses, with magnitude, frequency, inserted rest, age, model, and endpoint affecting the result.[^10-11] Articular-cartilage mechanobiology varies with amplitude, rate, frequency, loading history, and tissue state.[^10-12] These literatures establish that outcome cannot be read from repetition alone. They do not supply a whole-body injury threshold.

The framework therefore needs a fork rather than a single arrow:

> **Figure 10.4 — A defined exposure does not choose one outcome [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
>                         +-> no material observed change
>                         +-> successful short-term accommodation
>                         +-> practice or altered coordination
> DEFINED EXPOSURE ------+-> longer-term adaptation or remodeling
>                         +-> transient fatigue with recovery
>                         +-> sensitization or symptom change
>                         +-> accumulated material change or injury
>                         +-> immediate task or material failure
>
> Each branch requires its own system, measure, chronology, and evidence.
> Branches may overlap or occur at different scales.
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The same exposure description can be followed by several observed trajectories. The diagram authorizes questions, not a mandatory sequence or a direct exposure-to-disease claim.
>
> **Text alternative.** One defined exposure branches into no observed change, accommodation, practice, adaptation or remodeling, fatigue and recovery, symptom change, accumulated material change or injury, and immediate failure. Two notes state that every branch needs separate evidence and that branches can overlap.

The branch labels should not be collapsed. *Accommodation* can mean that the task is completed under current conditions without establishing a lasting change. *Practice* concerns altered performance or coordination. *Adaptation* and *remodeling* require a specified change over time and are not automatically beneficial. *Fatigue* requires a task- and measure-specific decline; it is not material damage by definition. *Injury* requires its own biological or structural evidence. Symptoms are observations with their own mechanisms and context. *Failure* can refer to material failure or inability to meet a declared task criterion, and those are different endpoints.

Chronology alone does not select a branch. A symptom appearing after repeated work establishes temporal order, not the local exposure, biological response, or causal contribution. A material change observed after training does not reveal which element of the program produced it without an appropriate comparison. An absence of symptoms does not measure tissue state. The chapter's sequence is deliberately slower: first describe demand and exposure, then observe the response, then test the bridge to function, findings, symptoms, or a clinical interpretation.

A useful model must retain ordinary nulls. Two people can complete the same task with visibly different strategies and no measured adverse change in the observed period. The same person can repeat a task while skill improves and local exposure stays similar, rises, or falls. A support can change exposure without changing symptoms. Symptoms can change while the selected mechanical measure changes little. These comparisons prevent every difference from being renamed hidden overload.

The adverse branches remain important. The questions that motivated this framework include how modest but repeated or poorly resolved demands might accumulate, shift among carriers, precede symptoms, or contribute to later consequences. Those questions are preserved, not answered by assertion. The next chapters separate interrupted handoff, concentration, maintained constraint, instability, and compensation so each proposed failure family receives its own mechanics and alternatives. Tissue-specific biology and condition-specific meaning require later bridges.

## A changing margin is not a score

The relation among task demand, selected-system exposure, and present capacity changes through time. That observation invites the language of a margin or reserve. It does not yet justify a number.

For a tested specimen under a stated loading mode, exposure and failure criteria may be expressed in commensurate quantities and a threshold may be relatively sharp. For repeated performance, the criterion may be gradual or multidimensional. For a whole person, “capacity” may include several noncommensurate endpoints, supports, and choices. Subtracting an estimated local strain from a task score, or a body-wide capacity number from object weight, would produce arithmetic without a coherent mechanical object.

*Reserve* can still name a conditional systems concept: the currently available margin to preserve a declared function while accommodating a perturbation or additional demand. The word must carry the same qualifiers as capacity. Reserve for what system, exposure, outcome, state, and time? It cannot become an invisible substance inferred whenever a posture, strategy, or environment is disliked.

A useful graphic may therefore show several bands rather than one subtraction. One band can represent a measured or modeled exposure with uncertainty. Another can represent the observed range in which a declared outcome remained available. Environmental changes can appear as alterations to the demand-to-exposure relation rather than as unexplained jumps in bodily capacity. Recovery can change the later capacity estimate. The bands may overlap without a precise crossing point, and the uncertainty may be too large to identify a margin at all. That honest result is more informative than a precise but dimensionally incoherent score.

A changing margin also does not dictate temporal order. Measured capacity can fall before task output changes. Performance can remain stable through altered sharing. Symptoms can appear before, after, or without the selected mechanical threshold. Training can increase one capacity while leaving another unchanged. Assistance can restore task availability without changing the person's tissue state. A model that permits these possibilities is more useful than a single falling line because it tells us what must be measured to distinguish them.

The opening transfers can now be interpreted without ranking them. Each begins with a task-level demand. Configuration and boundary conditions—including any cart, handrail, altered grip, or assistance—translate that demand into an exposure at the selected system. The system meets that exposure with a present, outcome-specific capacity shaped by its history. Task output, mechanical state, response, and recovery are then observed separately. Only after those records exist can the trial be called unchanged, accommodated, training, fatiguing, compensatory, injurious, or failing.

The durable conclusion is simple: a mechanical snapshot cannot carry a longitudinal judgment. Mechanical homeostasis is the proposed maintenance and recovery of declared relations within viable dynamic ranges, not return to one pose. Capacity is exposure-specific and current, not a permanent trait. Dose is a structured history, not a universal sum. Environment and assistance belong to the system boundary. Repetition can precede benefit, no material change, tradeoff, or harm, and each branch needs its own evidence.

The wider series will ask whether some whole-body organizations manage demand more efficiently than others. That hypothesis is not needed here and receives no support merely from the existence of a viable range. Book I first needs the more basic account developed in this chapter: what the task required, how the system was configured and supported, what exposure reached the selected structure, what capacity and recovery criterion were relevant, and what actually changed.

That baseline gives the next chapter its question. If demand can be distributed among several active, tensile, skeletal, pressure-mediated, and external routes, what counts as a successful handoff among them—and what observations would show that a handoff was interrupted, bypassed, or reassigned?

# Chapter 11 — Continuity, handoff, leakage, interruption, and substitution

The object has reached the second support. In one version of this familiar hypothetical transfer, the person places it down without another external contact. In a second version, a forearm briefly contacts the support while the object is lowered. The object reaches the same place in both versions. Its weight is transferred to the same final surface. Yet the contacts available to the person, and therefore the possible internal allocation of demand, are not the same.

What can we conclude from the successful endpoint? We can observe the object, the support, the added forearm contact, and the timing of release. With suitable instruments, we could measure external forces and motion. From those measurements and a declared model, we could calculate net segment or joint moments. We still would not know, from the endpoint alone, how muscle force, tendon tension, joint contact, pressure-mediated support, passive restraint, and external assistance shared the task.

Chapter 10 established that task demand, local exposure, present capacity, and outcome must be kept separate. This chapter adds another separation. *Balance* describes the net force-and-moment account required at a selected boundary. *Allocation* describes how candidate structures, contacts, and mechanical roles participate inside that account. Balance constrains allocation, but it rarely selects one unique internal solution.

That distinction is the starting point for a vocabulary of transfer. A task can remain mechanically continuous while its dominant carriers change. One relation can hand a mechanical job to another. A route can be interrupted, bypassed, overloaded, supplemented, or replaced while the visible endpoint remains intact. The words become useful only when they identify what changed and what observation could show that the proposed change did—or did not—occur.

> **Figure 11.1 — Balance constrains; allocation branches [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> DECLARED PERSON–OBJECT BOUNDARY DURING FINAL PLACEMENT
>
> observed or measured external contacts
>     ground + object + optional forearm support
>                     |
>                     v
> calculated net force and moment requirements
>                     |
>          +----------+-----------+------------+
>          |                      |            |
>          v                      v            v
>   modeled active and       modeled joint   modeled pressure,
>   tensile sharing          contact and     passive, and other
>                            skeletal route  contributing routes
>          \_____________________|____________/
>                               |
>                     internal allocation
>                    remains nonunique unless
>                       separately resolved
>
> solid description = observed or measured
> double description = calculated from declared inputs
> branching description = modeled or hypothesized
> ```
>
> **Caption.** External force and moment balance constrain the selected system, but several internal allocations can satisfy the same net account. The branches are candidate carriers, not a measured preferred route.
>
> **Text alternative.** Observed or measured ground, object, and optional forearm contacts feed a calculated net force-and-moment account. That account branches into active and tensile sharing, joint contact and skeletal transfer, and pressure, passive, and other contributors. The branches reunite at a note stating that internal allocation remains nonunique unless separately resolved. Line descriptions distinguish observation or measurement, calculation, and model or hypothesis.

## Continuity means that the needed relations remain available

In ordinary speech, continuity suggests one thing running without a break. That image is too narrow for a living movement. The body does not need one material cable extending from the object to the floor. It needs a workable succession or cooperation of contacts, structures, and controls through which a defined demand can be received, transformed, transferred, opposed, and ultimately resolved.

We use *mechanical continuity* for that task- and phase-specific availability. The definition begins with the job rather than with a named tissue. During the placement phase, the object must decelerate, contact the support, and transfer its weight away from the hands. The person must manage the changing object contact while remaining supported. Several relations can operate in parallel, and their contributions can rise or fall over the phase. Continuity is present when the selected system retains enough of those relations to complete the declared mechanical job without requiring an unacknowledged substitute.

Availability does not mean participation. A forearm support may be within reach and remain unused. A muscle may be anatomically capable of contributing but produce little force in the selected phase. Participation does not mean dominance, and dominance does not establish that the route is preferable. These are different questions.

The relevant scale must also be stated. A visually smooth whole-body movement does not prove uninterrupted transfer at a selected interface. An abrupt-looking movement does not prove that internal continuity was lost. At the level of a muscle–tendon unit, continuity may concern active force transmitted through a deforming tendon to its attachment. At a joint, it may concern changing active moments, contact, and passive restraint. At the person–environment boundary, it may include a handrail, device, furniture, or another person. A path can be represented as a sequence, a branching network, a distributed field, or a time-varying combination. The representation should match the question rather than forcing the body to resemble a drawn line.

A complete route account also needs somewhere for the selected demand to be resolved. An arrow that begins at the object and disappears at the pelvis is not a continuous mechanical explanation. Depending on the boundary, the terminal relation may be ground contact, another external support, opposition by another segment, a change in momentum, or internal stress and pressure fields that satisfy the stated balance. During placement, the receiving surface progressively accepts the object. During walking, alternating ground contacts and changes in momentum enter. In a smaller tissue system, tractions and constraints at the region's boundary must be declared. The terminal account prevents continuity from becoming a pleasing anatomical trace with no mechanical closure.

Nor must continuity be binary. One candidate relation may have limited excursion yet still participate. Several weak contributors may cooperate. A path may be available for one direction and unavailable for another, or for one interval but not the next. At that point, a continuous numerical description of participation may be more informative than a yes-or-no label. The word remains useful as long as it identifies the relations required by the proposed account and permits partial, shared, and uncertain states.

Bounded measurements make the point concrete. During stimulated contractions of the tibialis anterior in five men, increasing contraction was accompanied by increasing estimated tendon force, stress, displacement, and strain.[^11-01] During one-legged hopping in ten men, the Achilles tendon deformed substantially and returned elastic energy to the task.[^11-02] These are direct series connections at a limited anatomical scale. They show that transmission can include deformation, storage, and return. They do not establish one continuous route through the whole body.

Continuity can also be distributed across regional contributors. In twenty-five adults walking at a self-selected speed, net hip, knee, and ankle moment contributions to a support-moment description changed across stance and covaried with one another.[^11-03] The measurements and calculations do not reveal unique muscle forces or rank the joint strategies. They demonstrate the more basic point: a whole-task support relation can continue while the dominant regional contribution changes.

This definition also leaves room for uncertainty. If the external account closes but the internal distribution has not been measured or defensibly modeled, continuity at the task boundary may be observed while continuity along a proposed internal route remains unresolved. “Unresolved” is not a failure of the task. It is the correct state of the route claim.

## A handoff changes the mechanical job

A *handoff* is a change in carrier, role, direction, scale, contact, or phase through which a task remains mechanically resolved. The term does not imply that force is a packet passed between isolated parts. It is bookkeeping for a change in how a selected quantity or relation is managed.

A muscle can generate active tension that reaches bone through tendon. A joint can redirect resultants as contact geometry changes. A tendon can store energy during one interval and return it during another. A ligament can become more engaged as configuration changes. Cartilage can deform and distribute contact. Adjacent tissues can move together and relative to one another. A pressure-supported assembly can contribute to shape preservation. An external support can accept part of a demand previously carried within the person. Several of these events may occur simultaneously.

The quantity does not have to keep the same descriptive form across the handoff. Muscle activation is not force. Tendon tension is not joint contact pressure. A segment moment is not a tissue stress. Stored strain energy is not a line of action. The relations among them require geometry, material behavior, contact, time, and an explicit model. What remains continuous is the mechanically closed task account, not one scalar label that travels unchanged through every scale.

This matters at biological interfaces. At an idealized bonded boundary, traction compatibility helps close the local mechanical account. A real attachment may grade material properties over a region, change fiber direction, deform, slide elsewhere, and distribute contact. Calling that region a handoff does not replace those mechanics. It directs attention to the interface and asks which quantity entered, which relation emerged, what changed form, and what uncertainty was introduced. If those questions cannot be answered, *handoff* is still a useful observation prompt but not yet a detailed model.

The book's compact formulation gives this changing division of labor a positive center:

> Load wants to travel through the hard body so that the soft body can remain soft.

“Wants” is a heuristic about geometry, relative stiffness, contact, active control, pressure, and available paths—not an intention possessed by force and not a new law of motion. In technical use, *load* must become the particular force, moment, pressure, contact, deformation, or exposure being discussed.

The hard/soft distinction is motivated by traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts, but the traditional and mechanical categories are not definitionally identical. Book I uses the motivation to ask a mechanical question: which relations are comparatively shape-preserving, path-establishing, constraining, or structurally resolving while transmitting demand, and which must remain comparatively form-receiving and able to conform, glide, contain, expand, change pressure, or recover for the task? Force transmission alone does not answer that question.

Hard and soft are roles, not materials. They belong to a relation at a stated direction, phase, state, scale, and time. Bone often performs a hard role, but active muscle, tendon, ligament, fascia, cartilage, pressure, coordinated assemblies, and external supports can also help preserve a relation. A tissue performing a soft role is not weak, passive, unloaded, or unimportant. The same structure can transmit substantial force along one direction while receiving form, bending, or sliding in another. A handoff succeeds not by eliminating deformation but by preserving the particular freedoms each participant requires.

Pressure prevents the distinction from becoming a bone-only model. In a coupled finite-element and musculoskeletal model of static lifting, estimated effects of intra-abdominal pressure on spinal loading and stability changed with posture, coactivation, and the modeled pressure level.[^11-04] The result depends on the model and does not establish breathing as a whole-body routing driver. It does show that a deformable, pressure-mediated assembly can contribute to a relatively shape-preserving support job.

Normal deformation supplies the necessary null. Healthy knee cartilage imaged under cyclic compressive loading showed sliding displacement and regionally complex intratissue strain.[^11-05] The hopping study likewise showed tendon deformation and elastic recoil. In both examples, substantial loading and shape change are part of the studied mechanical role. Deformation is not evidence that demand escaped from a proper route. A form-receiving structure can be heavily loaded and still remain available for its work.

> **Figure 11.2 — Roles can change across one handoff [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Relation and phase | Comparatively shape-preserving or resolving job | Comparatively form-receiving job | What the example establishes |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Muscle–tendon–bone during rising tension | Active force, tensile transmission, attachment, and skeletal geometry cooperate | Tendon can elongate, change course, and store energy | A bounded multistructure handoff that includes deformation |
> | Joint contact as configuration changes | Contact geometry and active/passive contributors maintain a usable relation | Cartilage conforms and distributes contact while carrying demand | Shape change can be ordinary rather than leakage |
> | Pressure-supported trunk assembly | Pressure, wall tension, activation, and geometry may increase assembly support | The assembly remains deformable and phase dependent | A hard role need not be performed by bone alone |
> | Forearm support during object placement | External contact supplies another path to the environment | Local contact tissues conform while the person–support relation carries force | Roles and system boundary can change without ranking the strategy |
>
> **Caption.** Hard and soft name relative jobs in a declared relation, not permanent tissue classes. The vocabulary is motivated by TCM hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts but is mechanically defined here; the examples do not establish exact traditional correspondence or one preferred route.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows compare a muscle–tendon–bone relation, changing joint contact, a pressure-supported trunk assembly, and added forearm support. Each row names a comparatively shape-preserving or resolving job, a form-receiving job, and the limited conclusion supported. Tendon and cartilage deformation are shown as normal mechanical participation, and no tissue is assigned one permanent role.

## Leakage must name a receiver and a mismatch

The positive hard/soft formulation implies a possible negative case. A relation needed to preserve gross organization may become unavailable or poorly allocated, while a structure that needs to receive form assumes more of a path-establishing, restraining, or load-bearing job. The project's word for this possibility is *leakage*.

Leakage is not literal fluid escape. It is not every force carried by a soft tissue, every deformation, every anterior or lateral exposure, or every departure from a visually preferred line. It is a routing hypothesis: altered allocation produces a named exposure in a named receiver that is poorly matched to the receiver's required freedom, present capacity, task, direction, dose, or recovery context.

That hypothesis must be unpacked. A leakage account needs at least:

1. the receiving structure or relation;
2. the mechanical quantity and direction at issue;
3. its magnitude, duration, repetition, phase, and other relevant history;
4. the freedom or function the receiver must retain;
5. the proposed available route and the proposed change in allocation;
6. a reason the exposure is considered poorly matched rather than merely present;
7. an alternative explanation; and
8. an observation that would disfavor the account.

Possible translations include greater or more sustained deformation, changed pressure, increased active tension, restricted excursion or glide, altered contact, a changed moment, or an exposure that exceeds a declared present capacity. Each translation names a different mechanical object. None becomes adverse merely because it is measurable.

Consider two candidate leakage stories about the added forearm support. In the first, local skin and subcutaneous tissue conform under the contact while the broader person–support relation transmits force. The tissues deform, the endpoint is preserved, and no loss of their required freedom is demonstrated. Nothing in that description qualifies as leakage. In the second story, an interface is proposed to remain deformed after the phase, to lose relative excursion needed in a later movement, and to receive a repeated exposure poorly matched to its present capacity. That account contains a leakage candidate, but only the first two statements are not enough. The maintained state, required excursion, exposure history, capacity comparison, and later result must each be observed or supported separately.

The distinction is especially important when the receiver is active. Increased muscle activation may represent an effective contribution, a chosen stabilization strategy, a response to perturbation, or a substitute carrying more of a task. To call it leakage, the account must identify the intended or required freedom that is lost, show a poorly matched exposure or cost, and compare another plausible allocation. More activation alone does not establish that demand has entered the wrong place.

Location is equally insufficient. An exposure does not become adverse because it is anterior, posterior, medial, lateral, superficial, or deep. Spatial language can identify the receiver. It cannot supply the mismatch. The same anatomical region may be well suited to one direction, phase, and dose and poorly suited to another. Leakage is therefore a receiver-and-relation claim, not a moral map of the body.

Suppose a compliant interface deforms during object placement and returns while its required excursion, task output, and later state remain within the declared comparison range. That is a normal-deformation null, not hidden leakage. Suppose a pressure-supported assembly assumes more of a support job while reducing active demand elsewhere. That may be an effective handoff rather than an improper one. The hard/soft model is not protected by renaming every successful alternative as concealed cost.

*Misrouting* adds an evaluative comparison. It proposes that one allocation is less suitable than another for the stated task, dose, capacity, and required freedoms. The criterion might concern local exposure, reserve, energetic cost, precision, stability, recovery, or another declared outcome. Without such a criterion and a comparison, misrouting means only that the observer expected something else.

Leakage and misrouting therefore remain hypotheses even when the geometry looks compelling. A felt discontinuity can motivate the same hypothesis, but embodied experience is evidence of an experience in a task and phase. It is not, by itself, measurement of the carrier or quantity. The route becomes a mechanical claim only when the proposed receiver, exposure, and alternative path can be inspected.

## Interruption, bypass, overload, substitution, and rerouting differ

A single change in posture, activity, or support is sometimes narrated as if it simultaneously proved a broken chain, excessive demand, compensation, and harm. The terms describe different states and require different comparisons.

An *interruption* means that a relation required by the proposed route is unavailable or insufficient during the stated phase. The missing requirement might be contact, excursion, geometry, force capacity, control, or another declared variable. Interruption does not identify why the relation is unavailable, show that it was necessary to every viable route, or imply total task failure.

A *bypass* means that an alternative route participates while another route that remains plausibly available is used less or not at all. Added hand support can create a bypass. A person may choose it for comfort, access, precision, speed, habit, or no measured reason. A bypass can be beneficial, neutral, costly, or simply different.

An *overload* means that an engaged relation receives an exposure exceeding a specified present capacity criterion. Chapter 10's qualifiers still apply: system, quantity, direction, history, outcome, state, and time. High force is not automatically overload. Fatigue, discomfort, or altered motion may prompt an overload question, but they do not define the required exposure–capacity comparison.

A *substitution* occurs when another structure, contact, carrier, or strategy performs enough of a role to preserve a declared endpoint. The original route may be interrupted, bypassed, reduced, or merely not chosen. Substitution is neutral until its benefit, cost, or consequence is measured. It may make a task newly possible or better suited to a person's anatomy, disability, current symptoms, available device, or environment.

*Rerouting* is the broadest temporal term. It describes a changed distribution among candidate relations over a stated interval or phase. Rerouting can include a changed load share without a categorical interruption or substitution. It should not be used as a permanent whole-body label when only one task comparison has been observed.

These states can coexist. A relation can remain partly available, continue to participate, and receive an exposure that exceeds the selected capacity criterion. An external support can bypass one route and substitute for one part of its job. A strategy can reroute demand before any failure occurs. When measurements cannot distinguish the states, the allocation is unresolved rather than secretly interrupted.

A matched comparison shows why the names matter. Imagine that the same object placement is repeated with a support positioned within comfortable reach. In one trial the support is untouched. In another it accepts forearm force for part of the lowering phase. If the original internal route was still available and the person simply chose the new contact, *bypass* may describe part of the change. If a required relation could not perform its proposed job and the contact made the endpoint possible, *interruption with substitution* is a candidate. If the original relation stayed engaged but a defined exposure exceeded a matched capacity criterion, *overload* is the relevant claim. If force sharing changed continuously without a categorical loss, *rerouting* may be enough.

The visible support contact establishes none of those internal states by itself. A matched study would need to hold the endpoint and other task features sufficiently stable, measure the external contact, estimate or measure the internal quantities that distinguish the candidates, and state the capacity criterion if overload is claimed. Even then, mixed results may be the most accurate answer. The value of the vocabulary is that each term asks for different evidence instead of letting one visible difference carry the entire narrative.

> **Figure 11.3 — One endpoint, distinct transfer states [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Candidate state | Route availability | Participation and endpoint | Exposure–capacity status | Discriminating comparison and null |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Continuous shared routing | Required relations remain available | Several carriers may share the task | Open unless measured | Change one contact or carrier; distribution may remain effectively unchanged |
> | Interruption | A proposed requirement is unavailable or insufficient in the phase | Endpoint may fail or another relation may preserve it | Open | Restore the named requirement; null if the route was never necessary |
> | Bypass | Original route remains plausibly available | Alternate participation rises while the original falls | Either may remain within capacity | Vary the alternate support; null if the difference is ordinary variability |
> | Overload | Route is available and engaged | Participation remains present | Declared exposure exceeds a matched current capacity criterion | Change dose or recovery; high force or fatigue alone is insufficient |
> | Substitution | Original route may be interrupted, bypassed, reduced, or unchosen | Another carrier preserves the declared endpoint | Benefit and cost remain open | Compare internal measures at equivalent endpoint; substitute may be equally or better suited |
> | Mixed or unresolved | Availability or distribution is partial or unknown | Endpoint may be preserved | Unknown or multivariable | Improve measurement or narrow the claim; uncertainty is a valid result |
>
> **Caption.** Transfer states are analytical distinctions, not labels or ranks. The same endpoint can occur in several states, and more than one state can apply to the same phase.
>
> **Text alternative.** Six rows compare continuous shared routing, interruption, bypass, overload, substitution, and mixed or unresolved allocation. Columns distinguish route availability, participation and endpoint, exposure relative to capacity, and an informative comparison with a null. No row ends in harm or a preferred technique.

## The same endpoint can conceal different allocations

The endpoint-equivalence null is fundamental: two versions of a task can reach the same visible result through different internal organizations, and the difference can have no demonstrated adverse consequence. The reverse is also true. Similar appearance does not guarantee similar allocation.

Biomechanical redundancy makes the first possibility precise. In detailed model instances matched to the postures of three cats, broad ranges of muscle activation could produce prescribed hindlimb endpoint forces; relatively few modeled muscles had nonzero lower bounds across the tested conditions.[^11-06] The result is a model-based existence proof, not a direct measurement of human whole-body routing and not evidence that every feasible solution has the same cost.

Human reaching provides a complementary observation. Participants stabilized a pointer's endpoint position and orientation while joint configurations varied across trials and target conditions.[^11-07] The experiment does not identify tissue forces. It shows that endpoint stability and internal configuration are separate variables.

External assistance makes the redistribution more visible. In a study of fifteen healthy younger adults, moving robotic handles during standing and sitting increased vertical handle force while reducing peak hip and knee extension moments compared with static handles.[^11-08] The person–device system preserved the chair-transition endpoint while selected demand shifted toward the upper-body contact and away from selected lower-limb moments. This is measured evidence of changed allocation. It does not establish long-term benefit, universal superiority, or what another population would experience.

The inference can also stop in the other direction. In one person with an instrumented knee implant performing four gait patterns, changes in external knee loading and electromyography were generally weak indicators of changes in measured total, medial, and lateral knee contact force.[^11-09] One participant cannot settle every gait model. The study demonstrates why an external moment, muscle-activity signal, or visible strategy cannot automatically stand in for an internal contact-force change.

Local anatomical relations beyond a direct muscle–tendon series can be investigated with the same restraint. In a lower-limb experiment, changing hip and knee positions while holding the ankle apparatus constant changed ankle resting position and passive torque; the authors interpreted the findings as consistent with myofascial force transmission.[^11-10] The result supports a bounded positional interaction and an indirect mechanical effect. It does not establish a clinically dominant force line from foot to skull.

Endpoint equivalence therefore creates a question, not a verdict. A changed allocation might reduce one local exposure, increase another, alter energetic cost, preserve reserve, accommodate anatomy, or make no consequential difference under the observed conditions. Each outcome requires its own measure and time window. Task success cannot prove unchanged routing, and routing change cannot prove hidden harm.

## A route account must be inspectable and vulnerable

A route narrative earns explanatory value by allowing another reader to reconstruct it and by risking a result that narrows or rejects it. Four records help keep its principal objects separate. For candidate relation (e) at phase or time (t):

```text
A_e(t): availability — can this relation perform the stated job now?
U_e(t): use — to what extent does it participate in the selected transfer?
E_e(t): exposure — what defined mechanical history reaches it or a named receiver?
C_e(t): capacity — what present, outcome-specific capacity meets that exposure?
```

These symbols are labels for records. They are not components of a validated score, not a vector whose entries can be added, and not a law for a force packet moving along an edge. Availability can be partial or uncertain. Use can be distributed. Exposure and capacity must refer to the same receiver, quantity, direction, outcome, and time window before they can be compared. The records prevent several shortcuts: available is not used; used is not dominant; dominant is not preferred; loaded is not overloaded; and deformed is not harmed.

Applied to the object-placement comparison, a candidate forearm-support edge might be recorded as available because the surface is reachable, used because contact force is measured during a declared interval, exposed through a time-varying contact-force or pressure history, and capable relative to a selected comfort, skin, task, or recovery endpoint. A candidate lower-limb relation might remain anatomically available while its modeled moment contribution falls. Neither record says that one route is better. The entries make clear which conclusions rest on observation, which on calculation, and which remain hypotheses about local exposure or capacity.

The records can also reveal that the proposed graph is the wrong representation. If participation is diffuse, highly state dependent, or inseparable from a field of contact and pressure, a single edge may conceal more than it clarifies. The account should then use a network, field, or lower-resolution relation. Formalism is serving the chapter only when it makes the hypothesis easier to challenge.

The account then needs enough context to make the records meaningful: the task and endpoint, phase, system boundary, incoming demand, candidate carriers and contacts, proposed route, observed allocation change, proposed substitute, local exposure, alternatives, and disfavoring observations. It must also preserve how each entry is known. Direct observation, instrument measurement, calculation, model output, inference, hypothesis, and embodied report are different kinds of support.

> **Figure 11.4 — An inspectable route account [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Record | Required question | Permitted evidence states | Unknown is allowed |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Task, endpoint, phase, and boundary | What event and system are being explained, and when? | Observation, measurement, or declaration | No—the claim must be bounded |
> | Incoming demand and external balance | Which force, moment, pressure, contact, acceleration, or constraint enters? | Measurement or calculation from stated inputs | Yes, if the account narrows accordingly |
> | Candidate carriers and availability | Which skeletal, active, tensile, pressure, compliant, or external relations could perform the job? | Anatomy, model, inference, or hypothesis | Yes |
> | Participation or allocation change | Which relation is proposed to carry more, less, or another role? | Measurement, calculation, model, or inference | Yes |
> | Receiver, exposure, and capacity | What quantity and history reach what receiver, and relative to which current outcome criterion? | Measurement, model, inference, or hypothesis | Yes |
> | Alternative and disfavoring result | What else could explain the observations, and what result would weaken the account? | Prespecified comparison | No for a serious routing hypothesis |
> | Embodied force line | What continuity was felt, in which task, side, and phase, and what correlate is proposed? | Embodied report first; mechanical relation remains hypothesis | Yes |
>
> **Caption.** A route account separates observations, measurements, calculations, models, inferences, hypotheses, and embodied reports. Blank or unknown internal-allocation cells are preferable to completing a route through narrative confidence.
>
> **Text alternative.** Seven rows record the task and boundary, incoming demand, candidate carriers, allocation change, receiver and exposure, alternatives and disfavoring results, and any embodied force-line report. Each row lists appropriate evidence states and whether an unknown value is allowed. The final row keeps felt continuity separate from a measured mechanical route.

Several observations could count against a proposed routing account. The candidate carrier may not be anatomically or mechanically available in the stated phase. The external balance may not close under the proposed arrows. Changing the visible configuration may leave the relevant internal exposure materially unchanged. A proposed substitute may not change when the presumed interruption is removed. The receiver may deform and recover normally without the predicted loss of excursion or function. Another model may predict the measurements with fewer assumptions. Repeated measurement may fail to distinguish the proposed states. The hard/soft description itself may add no prediction beyond ordinary geometry, contact, pressure, activation, and capacity.

These are constructive outcomes. A failed local leakage account does not decide every larger question about preferred organization. It does require that this account be narrowed, rebuilt, or left unresolved. A route model is strongest when it can lose.

## From transfer to concentration

Return once more to the two object placements. Both succeed. The added forearm contact plainly changes the system boundary and creates another available path. It does not, by itself, tell us whether an internal route was interrupted, whether a bypass was chosen, whether a local exposure rose or fell, or whether either version was preferable. Those claims require the allocation record.

The chapter's positive conclusion is stronger than mere uncertainty. Living movement depends on workable relations through which demand can be received, transformed, transmitted, redirected, stored, returned, opposed, and resolved. Those relations can change carriers and roles without losing continuity. The hard/soft formulation asks whether gross structural demand is being resolved through capable shape-preserving relations while form-receiving structures retain the freedoms their functions require.

Its critical conclusion is equally specific. Continuity is not one hidden cable. Deformation is not leakage. Interruption, bypass, overload, substitution, and rerouting are not synonyms. Similar endpoints can conceal different allocations, and different allocations can be neutral or beneficial. A serious route account names the system, phase, quantity, carriers, receiver, exposure, capacity, alternatives, and a result that could count against it.

The next question is what happens after redistribution has been established or credibly proposed. A modest whole-task demand can become a larger local stress, strain, pressure, or contact exposure near a smaller area, changing geometry, or material transition. Chapter 12 takes up that problem of concentration. Only after concentration is distinguished can Chapter 13 ask what relation might maintain a deformation or loss of excursion through time.
