# Chapter 16 — Scale transition and possible regulatory consequences

One way to follow a compensation is to ask where its mechanical effects appear next. Consider a laboratory manipulation of walking. Investigators restricted extension of one knee in seventeen healthy adult men, recorded motion and ground reaction forces, and entered those measurements into a musculoskeletal model of the lumbar region. Under the restricted conditions, the participants walked more slowly and changed their trunk alignment. In the condition with the greater nominal restriction, the model estimated a larger lumbar extension moment during defined phases of gait; selected modeled paraspinal forces and components of the L4–L5 joint reaction force also increased across comparisons.[^16-01]

The experiment provides a clear transition, but not a simple chain. A condition imposed at the knee was followed by changes in the gait task and by modeled changes at the lumbar region. The brace did not transmit one identifiable force directly from knee to spine. Speed, segment motion, ground contact, active control, and the assumptions of the lumbar model all participated. Nor did the estimated increase establish overload, damage, or a naturally occurring history. The result belongs to the changed walking solution.

A second restriction experiment prevents that result from becoming a rule. Eight adults without reported gait impairment walked with unilateral and bilateral restrictions at the ankle, knee, or both. Some conditions changed measured ground reaction force peaks and loading rates. Yet participant-scaled models estimated relatively similar lower-limb joint reaction forces across many comparisons because modeled muscle forces changed during loading response.[^16-02] A visible redistribution and a changed external measure did not dictate the proposed internal exposure.

These experiments are not contradictory. They used different restrictions, models, regions, and outputs. Together they establish the chapter's central proposition: a mechanical change can cross from one region or level of description to another, but its destination, magnitude, and meaning cannot be read from the initiating change alone. Sometimes another region participates differently. Sometimes active redistribution keeps a selected internal result similar. Sometimes the important change occurs in a quantity that was not measured.

The previous chapter followed compensatory solutions through time. A successful strategy could persist, resolve, transfer, or become the starting condition for another task. This chapter follows such organization across scale. It asks how a local relation can recruit a region, how several regional strategies can form a repeatable whole-task organization, and how that organization can focus demand back onto a local receiver. It then stops the mechanical argument before sensation, flow, tissue response, or energetic demand are allowed to merge into one systemic conclusion.

## Scale is not a zoom control

The word *scale* can suggest that the same object merely becomes larger or smaller. That is not what happens here. A local field, a regional distribution, and a task-level result require different information.

At a local scale, the object might be strain within a declared tissue volume, pressure at an interface, excursion of a nerve relative to its bed, or contact stress over a surface. At a regional scale, the record might contain segment motion, ground contact, net joint moments, muscle activation, or modeled force sharing. At the task scale, it might contain walking speed, object control, support geometry, external work, or whole-body angular momentum. A whole-person record adds goals, fatigue, pain, attention, assistance, environment, and other circumstances that can alter the task without being reducible to one mechanical variable.

Moving between these levels requires a bridge. A task-level result does not contain a local stress field waiting to be magnified. A local measurement does not contain the organization of the whole task waiting to be enlarged. Geometry, contacts, forces, moments, activation, pressure, material behavior, and time connect the levels, and the necessary set depends on the question.

This point changes the familiar phrase *kinetic chain*. The phrase can be a useful prompt to look beyond one joint. It is not an explanation until the intermediate relations are named. If a knee condition is proposed to change a lumbar exposure, the account must identify the altered task, regional motion and forces, modeled or measured lumbar quantity, relevant phase, and plausible alternatives. If the selected lumbar quantity remains unchanged, the chain has not merely found a different hidden route; that null is part of the result.

Direction also remains open. A local pain state, restriction, or contact can precede a regional response. A common task change can alter both regions. A global support condition can change what is demanded locally. A later symptom can change movement and make the observed mechanical pattern a consequence rather than a cause. The scale map is therefore bidirectional from the start.

A useful transition record contains four entries:

1. the object and quantity at the starting level;
2. the intermediate contacts, motions, forces, moments, activations, or pressures;
3. the object and quantity at the receiving level; and
4. the task, chronology, alternatives, and null result that bound the relation.

Without those entries, connection is anatomical or visual. With them, a proposed transition can be measured, modeled, compared, or disfavored.

## Regional participation can become whole-task organization

Walking makes multiregion organization unusually visible. Arms, trunk, legs, ground contacts, speed, and external support can be manipulated separately, while task-level results can be calculated from their combined motion.

In one experiment, sixteen healthy young adults walked on a treadmill while following unilateral and bilateral arm-swing instructions. The manipulations changed the amplitude of the opposite arm and altered a phase-coordination measure of the lower limbs.[^16-03] This is evidence of interlimb coupling under the tested instructions. It does not reveal a unique carrier. Spinal mechanics, active control, balance, attention, and the novelty of the instruction remain possible participants.

A split-belt experiment makes the task level more explicit. Twenty-four healthy young adults walked with the treadmill belts moving at different speeds, either while holding a handrail or with their arms free. The initial asymmetry changed whole-body angular momentum through both the momenta of individual segments and the degree to which those segmental contributions canceled. Handrail contact reduced the early perturbation, changed the relation between whole-body angular momentum and step-length asymmetry, and produced a smaller early aftereffect.[^16-04]

The handrail did not simply add an abstract quantity called stability. It changed the boundary of the working system. The person, rail, belts, and contacts together produced a different task. Segmental behavior, aggregate momentum, and adaptation all changed, but none can stand in for the others.

Whole-body angular momentum is especially instructive because it is an aggregate. It can show that segmental contributions combine into a task-level quantity. It cannot uniquely recover the organization that produced that quantity. Different combinations can yield similar totals, and a similar-looking movement can conceal different internal contributions.

Arm-swing experiments also separate mechanical aggregation from energetic outcome. Twelve healthy adults walked under in-phase, restricted, ordinary, and several exaggerated arm-swing conditions. Increasing arm-swing amplitude generally reduced vertical angular momentum and ground reaction moment until the most exaggerated condition. Metabolic cost did not follow those mechanical measures indefinitely; the greatest swing raised rather than further reduced cost of transport.[^16-05] The task-level mechanical result and the metabolic result were related, but they were not one variable.

For this book, *whole-task organization* means a repeatable relation among declared regions, contacts, forces, timing, and task outcomes over a stated interval. It does not mean that every tissue shares one state. It does not require bilateral symmetry, visual straightness, low movement, unsupported performance, or one origin. A repeatable organization can be learned, assisted, protective, trained, disability-specific, culturally practiced, comfortable, temporary, or imposed by the environment.

The word *repeatable* also needs a boundary. A relation observed for ten laboratory trials is not a permanent bodily baseline. A pattern that transfers across speeds may not transfer across terrain. A strategy used during pain may resolve when pain changes. A durable account requires repeated measurement across the times, tasks, and environments for which durability is claimed.

## The arrow also runs back toward the local

Once several regions participate in a whole task, their organization can alter a local exposure in return. That statement is mechanical, but it is not automatic. The task-level description must pass through the same bridge developed earlier in this Part:

```text
task and environment
    -> body configuration, contacts, and active state
    -> regional forces, moments, pressure, and support relations
    -> interface sharing and local boundary conditions
    -> local stress, strain, pressure, activation, contact, or excursion
```

Suppose a repeated task changes support from two contacts to one, adds a handrail, redistributes mass, or alters the timing of a trunk segment. Any of those changes can modify regional resultants and interface conditions. A selected local receiver may then experience a different moment, pressure, strain, or excursion. But the visible configuration is not itself that exposure. Active force, a device, pressure-mediated support, or another contact can redistribute demand before it reaches the proposed receiver.

The knee-restriction experiment contains both directions in one sequence. A local experimental condition altered the gait organization; the resulting gait organization altered modeled lumbar quantities. The split-belt experiment likewise began with an environmental asymmetry, recruited several segments into a task-level response, and then expressed adaptation through individual steps. Local-to-global and global-to-local are not rival doctrines. They can be consecutive portions of one feedback history.

The null remains equally important. A visible whole-body change may leave the selected local exposure materially similar. It may change a different receiver. Or one common instruction, speed, pain state, or environment may produce both the global pattern and the local measurement without one causing the other. These possibilities belong beside the proposed arrow, not in a disclaimer at the end.

> **Figure 16.1 — A bidirectional multiscale map [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> local relation or receiver
>     measured or modeled: pressure, strain, contact, excursion, activation
>            <------------------------------->
> neighboring and regional participation
>     measured or modeled: motion, force, moment, timing, work, support
>            <------------------------------->
> repeatable whole-task organization
>     measured or calculated: contacts, endpoint, momentum, speed, external work
>
> At every transition:
>     common task or environment -> both observations
>     reverse direction          <- remains possible
>     active or external support -> redistributes demand
>     null                       -> selected receiving quantity does not change
>
> Whole-person state and goals modify the task; they are not a fourth
> mechanical quantity inferred from the three levels above.
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Local, regional, and task-level records contain different information. The arrows indicate relations that must be measured or modeled; they do not establish one origin, one preferred organization, or a physiological consequence.
>
> **Text alternative.** Three levels—local receiver, regional participation, and repeatable whole-task organization—are connected in both directions. Each level lists different measurable or model-dependent quantities. At each arrow, common task, reverse direction, active or external redistribution, and no change in the selected receiver remain explicit alternatives. Whole-person state modifies the task but is not inferred from a mechanical aggregate.

## A whole-body transition remains a research question

The multiscale map preserves a stronger possibility. Some bodily histories may involve more than an isolated change superimposed on an otherwise unchanged task. Repeated relations among contacts, timing, active support, and regional distribution may reorganize together, so that the next task begins from a meaningfully different multiregion state.

That possibility should be stated directly. It should not be settled by appearance. A lateral displacement, rotation, asymmetry, straight spine, or coherent silhouette does not reveal a force, moment, pressure, stress, or strain field. Nor does a smooth anatomical continuum prove that one mechanical relation propagated through the whole body.

A research program on *configuration transition* would first have to define the representation. Is the proposed object a set of regional resultants, a distribution of local strains, a network of contacts and active tensions, or a combination? It would then need criteria that distinguish ordinary movement within a capable repertoire from reorganization of that repertoire. Candidates might include a persistent change in cross-region coupling, loss or gain of available routes, a sharp gradient or reversal in a declared field, altered response to perturbation, or transfer of the new organization across tasks. Each candidate requires an observation, reference state, timescale, and failure condition.

A hypothetical longitudinal experiment shows what those requirements would add. Investigators could select one stepping task, vary its support conditions, and record contacts, ground forces, segment motion, activation, and a declared local receiver before, during, and after repeated exposure. The transition proposal would have to predict more than a retained pose. It might predict that a particular cross-region relation persists after the added support is removed, appears under a second task, and changes the measured or modeled exposure at the selected receiver. Ordinary variation within the existing repertoire would predict a return toward the earlier relations, no transfer, or no corresponding change at the receiver. A result would count against the proposal if the visible pattern remained but the declared coupling did not, if the coupling changed without the proposed local effect, or if both followed a common change in speed or instruction. Even a positive result would establish only a bounded transition in the tested participants and tasks. It would not identify a universal preferred state or establish a health consequence.

Longitudinal measurement is essential because a single image cannot show transition. The investigation would need to observe the earlier organization, the changing interval, retention or resolution, and competing causes such as development, training, injury, pain, disease, assistance, environment, and preference. A transition could be beneficial, neutral, costly, mixed, or irrelevant to the outcome being studied.

Book I does not need this stronger hypothesis in order for the multiscale result to stand. Regional mechanics can couple into task organization, and task organization can return demand toward local receivers, even if no general class of configuration transitions is ever established. Keeping the question non-load-bearing is what allows it to remain ambitious and testable.

## Sensation and control form one branch

Mechanical reorganization does not become sensory reorganization merely because both involve the same person. The sensory and control branch begins with defined objects: muscle activation, perceived effort, movement detection, position sense, interoceptive report, peripheral nerve behavior, or anticipatory and corrective action. These measures are not interchangeable.

Small contacts can affect control without carrying much structural support. In ten healthy adults standing with eyes closed, a haptic robot supplied approximately 1 N of velocity-dependent touch at the upper back. The contact reduced selected center-of-pressure sway measures, while added position-dependent vibration affected some outcomes differently.[^16-06] The result supports a task-specific response to a small information-bearing contact. It does not isolate a purely sensory carrier, because the contact force and the robot's mechanical behavior remained part of the condition.

Experimental pain supplies both a positive and a null. In thumb experiments completed by ten to twelve participants per condition, local muscle or skin pain impaired passive-movement detection at some anatomically relevant sites, while several control comparisons remained unchanged.[^16-07] In a separate experiment, twenty-eight healthy participants developed sustained forearm pain and hyperalgesia after nerve growth factor injections, yet the measured wrist joint-position error did not change over the observed days.[^16-08]

The correct conclusion is not that pain does or does not disrupt proprioception. It is that a local state can alter one selected sensory measure while another measure remains unchanged. Movement detection, position matching, effort, and protective action are different outputs. Pain may precede the sensory change. Attention or expectation may change control. Inflammation, medication, instruction, learning, or measurement error may affect both.

The project therefore retains a possible sequence in which a local mechanical state changes sensory information, altered information changes control, and control changes later mechanics. Every arrow remains open to a null or reverse result. No source here establishes a progression from strain to sensory uncertainty, chronic bracing, autonomic change, or illness. The branch is worth testing precisely because it has been divided into observations that can fail independently.

## Pressure, flow, and excursion divide into different objects

The next branch splits before it begins. Arteries, veins, lymphatic vessels, peripheral nerves, sliding interfaces, and pressure-bearing cavities do not share one outcome called flow. Their walls, contents, constraints, active behaviors, valves, pressure relations, and required motions differ.

Positional vascular findings demonstrate the problem. In nineteen healthy participants assessed bilaterally across seven arm positions, Doppler waveforms met the study's criterion for significant arterial compression in at least one position in 28.9 percent of participants. Peak systolic velocity and systolic rise time varied and did not correlate with that classification. Used as an isolated diagnostic result, the positional test would have produced many false-positive inferences about arterial thoracic outlet syndrome.[^16-09]

In forty-nine other healthy volunteers, a specified abducted, flexed, and externally rotated arm position increased the average measured cross-sectional area of the subclavian vein rather than narrowing it.[^16-10] That study addressed ultrasound visualization. It did not measure a complete venous-outflow result, symptoms, or benefit. The two vascular studies cannot be pooled into the claim that arm position either opens or closes the thoracic outlet. They measured different vessels, conditions, and outputs.

Peripheral nerve mechanics is different again. Ultrasound in healthy participants measured median nerve excursion during wrist, elbow, shoulder, and neck movements. Reported excursions ranged from 0.3 mm during contralateral neck side flexion at one observed location to 10.4 mm during elbow extension, with maneuver-specific estimates of additional forearm strain. The investigators judged the tested extended-limb strain likely below levels expected to impair nerve blood flow or conduction.[^16-11] Excursion is an ordinary function of the nerve in its moving bed; its presence is not evidence of entrapment, and its loss cannot be inferred from a symptom alone.

The causal order matters. A compliant tube that remains deformed may be held by external contact, surrounding geometry, wall tension, pressure difference, active tissue, or a combination. The deformation may alter lumen geometry; lumen and gradient may alter flow; flow may or may not alter a tissue outcome. The maintained stress and strain relation is not interchangeable with the narrower space it produces. At the same time, a hose analogy cannot supply vessel biology, active regulation, valves, branching geometry, or clinical meaning.

> **Figure 16.2 — Separate downstream branches [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Branch | Candidate mechanical input | Intermediate quantity that must be measured | Candidate output | Required null or alternative |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Sensory and control | contact, motion, pain state, expectation, support | named sensory measure, activation, or timed response | changed control, effort, or protective action | another measure is unchanged; control changed first |
> | Arterial or venous | geometry, contact, pressure, active state | vessel-specific lumen, gradient, waveform, velocity, or volume | perfusion or return in the stated system | ordinary positional change; no functional consequence |
> | Lymphatic | deformation, intrinsic contraction, valves, external pressure | segment-specific pressure or flow | drainage or volume change | compensation or no meaningful flow change |
> | Peripheral nerve | bed length, contact, tether, joint motion | excursion, strain, shear, or conduction | selected sensory or motor finding | ordinary excursion; no conduction or symptom change |
> | Sliding interface or cavity | motion, pressure, geometry, phase | relative glide, shear, expansion, or support pattern | task-specific function | adequate alternate motion or no relevant consequence |
> | Tissue response | named local exposure history | material, cellular, signaling, repair, or remodeling measure | response through a stated time | no response, useful response, or biology-first change |
> | Energetic or regulatory | defined strategy and task | work, activation, metabolism, effort, recovery, or named physiology | cost, benefit, reserve, or no change | assistance helps; higher effort does not predict outcome |
>
> **Caption.** The branches share a mechanical starting question but not an evidentiary shortcut. Support for one intermediate quantity cannot validate another branch, and a measured intermediate does not establish a symptom, diagnosis, or benefit.
>
> **Text alternative.** Seven rows separate sensory and control, arterial or venous, lymphatic, peripheral nerve, sliding interface or cavity, tissue response, and energetic or regulatory questions. Each row names a possible mechanical input, a branch-specific intermediate measurement, a candidate output, and a null or alternative. No row connects automatically to another.

The lymphatic, sliding-interface, and cavity rows in the figure are research obligations, not conclusions drawn from the arterial, venous, or nerve studies. Evidence about one conduit cannot be lent to another. Evidence about a nerve cannot establish vessel flow. A pressure change does not by itself establish improved circulation, and altered excursion does not by itself establish a symptom.

Separating these branches does not claim that they are biologically isolated. It prevents evidence from one branch from doing unearned work for another. A sensory response could change muscle activity; muscle activity could affect a local pressure relation; that relation could coincide with a vessel-specific measurement. Demonstrating such an interaction would require the proposed quantities to be measured on compatible timescales, their order to be established, and alternatives such as a shared task change to be compared. The interaction is a larger claim than either observation alone.

The separation also preserves informative disagreement. A task may change perceived effort while leaving a selected vascular measure similar. A positional change may alter a waveform without changing symptoms or control. A local tissue response may occur without a detectable change in whole-task cost. Such combinations do not make the map fail. They identify which branches participated and which did not. Integration becomes stronger after the branches have earned their own measurements, chronology, and null results.

## Response and cost need their own denominators

Tissue response begins only after a receiver and exposure history have been identified. Sensitization, inflammatory signaling, remodeling, repair, fatigue, wear, degeneration, and injury are different possible responses. They occur over different times and depend on material state, biology, capacity, and recovery. A mechanical change can occur without any of them. A biological change can also precede and alter motion, activation, material behavior, and local exposure.

The responsible handoff is therefore explicit:

```text
named receiver and exposure through time
    -> measured material, cellular, or signaling intermediate
    -> time-resolved tissue response
    -> functional or clinical outcome, if supported

coequal branches:
    no measurable response / useful response / recovery /
    biology changes mechanics first / exposure was misestimated
```

This chapter does not fill those arrows with a general inflammation story. Their evidence depends on tissue, dose, state, and time. The later mechanobiology discussion will have to earn each transition independently.

Energetic demand is a separate and more directly measured branch in the experiments available here. Even so, *cost* is incomplete without a numerator, denominator, task, and interval. It may mean muscle activation over several strides, positive mechanical work by a segment, net metabolic power at a stated speed, oxygen cost per distance, perceived effort, recovery time, attentional demand, or loss of task options. A strategy can improve one and worsen another.

The arm-swing experiment already showed that reducing selected angular-momentum measures did not guarantee a lower metabolic cost at the greatest tested amplitude.[^16-05] External assistance supplies a beneficial branch. Seven participants walked at 1.5 m/s with a 6.8 kg rucksack while a multi-joint soft exosuit used person-specific control parameters. Powered individualized assistance reduced measured metabolic cost relative to both no-device walking and the unpowered device condition.[^16-12] The experiment was small, and it did not isolate individualized tuning from powered assistance. It nevertheless demonstrates that an altered route including technology can lower a defined cost.

Assistance can also reverse from helpful to costly within tested conditions. Twelve healthy adult men walked with an energy-removing exoskeleton under several assistance magnitudes. Moderate assistance reduced metabolic cost by 3.4 percent relative to ordinary walking and reduced measured hamstring activity. Under the higher tested magnitude, metabolic cost exceeded ordinary walking and selected muscle activity rose relative to lower-assistance comparisons.[^16-13] This is a task-, device-, timing-, magnitude-, and sample-specific reversal, not a universal threshold.

These findings block two shortcuts. A mechanically altered organization is not inherently inefficient, and a greater amount of assistance is not inherently better. *Reserve* likewise cannot be a hidden energy store. It can describe remaining ability to repeat, vary, recover, or respond to perturbation for a declared task, provided those abilities are actually measured. Fatigue, low resilience, and diffuse symptoms may motivate such measurement; they do not establish a mechanical cause.

The term *regulatory* should be treated with the same discipline. A candidate regulatory claim must name the variable—heart rate variability, blood pressure, ventilatory work, endocrine response, temperature control, attention, or another measure—and then establish its own mechanical and physiological bridge. Activation, effort, or posture does not become autonomic dysfunction through vocabulary.

## One map, not one cascade

Part III began by asking how living structure manages demand within changing capacity. It developed continuity and handoff, geometric concentration, maintained constraint, instability and discoordination, and compensatory rerouting. The final addition is scale: local, regional, and whole-task organization can interact in both directions.

That conclusion is affirmative. A selected change can recruit another region. Several regions can combine into a measurable task-level organization. Environmental support can become part of that organization. The resulting distribution can alter a named local exposure. None of those statements requires one lesion, one visible pattern, or one universal route.

The larger configuration-transition question also survives. A body may reorganize in a way that deserves multiregion and longitudinal description rather than a list of isolated local changes. Whether such transitions form a general class, how they should be represented, and whether any one is beneficial or adverse remain open. The present chapter does not hide that program, and it does not use the program to prove itself.

Beyond mechanics, there is no single next arrow. Sensation and control, pressure and flow, nerve or interface excursion, tissue response, and energetic or regulatory demand each require their own system, intermediate measure, chronology, alternative, and null. One branch may be important while another is unchanged. A mechanical pattern may be coherent and have no meaningful physiological or medical consequence.

That is where Part III should end: not with a verdict about health, but with a map of questions that can now be asked precisely. Part IV begins by examining situations in which medicine already measures or changes mechanical conditions. The immediate question is not whether mechanics belongs in medicine. It is what established endpoint reasoning can tell us—and what, if anything, a longitudinal account of routing adds.

## Part III synthesis — A taxonomy of questions, not defects

Part III has replaced the vague idea of bad loading with a set of more exact possibilities.

A system can remain within a viable range or exceed a current capacity. A demand can pass through a selected carrier, branch, fail to cross an interface, or recruit a substitute. Global geometry can change the available paths while the clinically relevant question remains a local contact, pressure, stress, strain, or excursion. A deformation can persist because an external, intrinsic, repeated, active, or mixed relation continues to maintain it. Stability can depend on timing, feedback, support, and recovery rather than stillness. A strategy can preserve immediate function while changing later exposure. A regional change can remain regional or enter a wider relation only through identifiable intermediate links.

None of these families is automatically pathological. Concentration can be ordinary. Constraint can be temporary. Variability can be useful or inadequate. Bracing can protect. Compensation can be successful. A visible difference can be irrelevant to the outcome under study. The language earns its place by making those distinctions possible.

The Part also establishes a temporal order. Present state and capacity shape routing. Routing and handoff shape local exposure. A response can alter the next configuration. Compensation feeds back into later distribution. What looks like an upstream cause in one time window can be a downstream consequence in another. A later observation cannot reconstruct the whole sequence by itself.

This is the limit of a purely mechanical taxonomy. Medicine requires more: tissue biology, symptoms, function, diagnosis, prognosis, care context, and the whole person. Part IV begins from mechanics already embedded in medicine and asks what longitudinal load routing adds. It must preserve every intermediate link developed here while remaining prepared to find that mechanics is secondary, mixed, or uninformative in a particular problem.

# Part IV — From mechanical organization to medical meaning

Mechanical reasoning is already medical reasoning. Pressure must be generated, regulated, relieved, or maintained. Fractures require continuity and stability. Ventilation depends on pressure and deformable boundaries. Nerves, vessels, and tendons need adequate course, excursion, and interface behavior. Prostheses, orthoses, implants, beds, tools, and assistive devices redistribute demand through living tissues.

Part IV therefore does not introduce mechanics into a supposedly mechanics-free field. It begins with established uses and asks what a more longitudinal routing history could add.

Chapter 17 maps the common ground. Chapter 18 defines the proposed addition: follow a declared demand across regions and time rather than stopping at the present local endpoint. Chapter 19 supplies the biological bridge from mechanical exposure to tissue response. Chapter 20 compares that bridge across conduits, nerves, sliding interfaces, and pressure-bearing systems without pretending they share one material law. Chapter 21 makes the causal boundary explicit and restores biological, psychological, behavioral, environmental, and social alternatives at every stage. Chapter 22 asks how this lens could enter clinical workflow and interdisciplinary care without becoming a diagnosis, profession, or protocol of its own.

The sequence is intentionally demanding. A mechanical history is not established because a narrative sounds continuous. An exposure must be defined. The receiving structure must be named. The response must be appropriate to that structure and time. A finding, symptom, functional change, diagnosis, and outcome remain different objects. Reverse causation and feedback remain active: pain, inflammation, fear, fatigue, and illness can change movement and distribution.

The proposed lens succeeds at this stage if it improves the next question. It can identify a missing history, a candidate mediator, a comparison, or a measurement without claiming causal priority. It can also succeed by showing where a mechanical account stops. The worked narratives in Part V will test whether that discipline survives when the examples become concrete.

# Chapter 17 — Established mechanical reasoning in medicine

A pressure trace moves across a monitor. A ventilator supports a pressure-and-volume cycle. A plate holds the fragments of a broken bone in a selected relation. A surgeon releases a local constraint. A prosthetic socket transfers forces and moments between a device and living tissue.

None of these scenes is outside medicine. Each depends on physical quantities, geometry, material behavior, and time. Each also depends on biology, judgment, and the person receiving care. The mechanical account matters because it describes part of what the intervention is intended to change—not because it replaces the rest of medicine.

This gives a skeptical reader a strong objection to the premise of this book: *Isn't this already medicine?*

The honest answer is yes. Mechanics is not a neglected foreign language waiting to be introduced into medical care. Biomechanics, rehabilitation, surgery, cardiopulmonary medicine, orthotics and prosthetics, ergonomics, and many other fields already measure and alter pressure, flow, stability, contact, motion, support, and force distribution. Book I inherits that work.

A narrower question remains. A present mechanical endpoint does not always contain the history that produced it. The pressure measured now does not record every earlier task and tissue state. A stable fracture construct does not disclose the entire injury and healing history. A changed interface distribution does not reveal one unique way demand arrived there. Local endpoint reasoning and longitudinal routing reasoning are related, but they are not the same record.

This chapter establishes the common ground. It asks what medicine already does mechanically, what those endpoints can legitimately establish, and what they leave open. The next chapter will have to show whether following demand, substitution, compensation, and exposure across time creates an additional object worth keeping.

## A mechanical endpoint can be a medical endpoint

Medicine regularly makes distinctions that are mechanical before they are diagnostic. Pressure is not flow. Flow is not perfusion. Volume is not tissue strain. Stability is not healing. Component strength is not interface tolerance. A treatment can influence several of these at once, but their coexistence does not make them one variable.

During cardiac arrest, for example, external chest compression supplies part of a pump action that the circulation is not providing. Current American Heart Association guidance relates compression, recoil, interruption, ventilation, forward flow, and coronary perfusion pressure while keeping return of spontaneous circulation and survival as later outcomes.[^17-01] The relationships are physical and medically consequential. They are also incomplete. Compression depth is an input that can be controlled; perfusion pressure is an intermediate; survival depends on additional events and states.

This example matters because it is difficult to caricature as posture coaching. External contact with the body is intentionally used to support circulation. Yet no one needs to reconstruct a person's complete mechanical history before beginning that support. The cause of the arrest, its duration, rhythm, oxygenation, medication, injuries, and system of care remain separately important. Immediate endpoint reasoning is not inferior because it is local and urgent.

Assisted ventilation supplies another example. A device can help generate pressure differences and volume change when a person cannot sustain adequate ventilation alone. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, authoritative guidelines distinguish tidal volume, plateau pressure, positive end-expiratory pressure, oxygenation, recruitment, extracorporeal support, medication, and the state of the lung and circulation.[^17-02][^17-03] These are not interchangeable settings on one scalar called respiratory mechanics. They are coupled quantities and decisions within a living cardiopulmonary system.

Mechanical support can therefore have two truths at once. It can be necessary, and it can create a new exposure. A ventilator supports gas exchange while pressure, volume, timing, regional heterogeneity, and tissue state affect what the lung experiences. This is not a contradiction. It is ordinary medical reasoning about a physical intervention in a biological receiver.

> **Figure 17.1 — Mechanics already inside medicine [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Domain | Selected mechanical object | Intended endpoint | Biology and context retained | What the endpoint does not reveal |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Circulatory or ventilatory support | pressure, flow, volume, timing, external contact | temporary support of pump or ventilation function | cause, rhythm, lung state, circulation, injury, medication, time | one complete history of failure |
> | Fracture fixation | alignment, continuity, restraint, relative motion, construct sharing | a selected mechanical environment for healing | fracture pattern, blood supply, soft tissue, infection, repair, behavior | one outcome from stability alone |
> | Local decompression | contact, pressure, deformation, available excursion | change in a declared local condition | nerve state, anatomy, systemic contributors, recovery | one initiating cause or severity axis |
> | Living device interface | distributed pressure and shear across time | capable transfer between person and device | tissue state, fit, comfort, goals, adaptation, environment | tolerance or value from one peak |
>
> **Caption.** Established medical domains intentionally measure or alter different mechanical objects. Their endpoints are legitimate without becoming complete causal histories or sharing one constitutive law.
>
> **Text alternative.** Four rows compare circulatory or ventilatory support, fracture fixation, decompression, and a living device interface. Each row separates its mechanical object and intended endpoint from biological context and the upstream history that remains unresolved.

The point of the table is not that all medicine can be placed inside a mechanical grid. It is that some medical questions already have a mechanical object precise enough to measure or change. The biological and personal context does not weaken that precision. It tells us what the mechanical endpoint means and what it cannot mean by itself.

An endpoint record becomes useful by declaring its boundary. In resuscitation, the boundary may include the chest, circulation, external contact, ventilation, and a short interval of urgent care. In fracture fixation, it may include the fragments, construct, surrounding tissue, applied load, and a phase of healing. At a prosthetic interface, it may include the person, device, ground, selected task, and the surface across which contact is measured. Redrawing the boundary changes the question. It does not expose one finally correct system hidden beneath the others.

The record also needs a verb. A pressure was *measured*. A flow was *supported*. A relative motion was *limited*. A local constraint was *released*. A force was *calculated* from measured inputs. A tissue exposure was *modeled* under stated assumptions. These verbs preserve the difference between what instruments recorded and what an analysis inferred. “Mechanical improvement” is too broad if the text cannot say which of those events occurred.

Time is part of the boundary as well. An immediate change can establish that an intervention affected a selected condition. It does not determine whether the change persisted, whether a living receiver accommodated it, or whether the person's function changed. A longitudinal follow-up can add those observations without reconstructing every event before the intervention. Present state, intervention, short-term endpoint, biological response, and longer outcome remain connected but distinct entries.

This discipline prevents an odd reversal. The endpoint is sometimes dismissed as superficial because it does not explain origin. Yet a well-defined endpoint may be measured more reliably than the history proposed to explain it. The proper comparison is not local simplicity against whole-body sophistication. It is one bounded record against another, each judged by the question it can answer.

## Substitution supports a function without reproducing its cause

The resuscitation and ventilation examples share a useful structure: an external action or device temporarily performs part of a physical job. We can call this *mechanical substitution* as long as we name the substituted function.

The word does not imply that a machine becomes the organ, that normal physiology has been recreated, or that the initiating problem has been repaired. Chest compression supports a circulation-related function. Assisted ventilation supports movement of gas through pressure and volume change. An orthosis can limit a selected motion or change contact. A prosthesis can make a valued task possible through a new person–device assembly. Each substitution has a declared boundary and an incomplete resemblance to the function it supports.

Substitution is often discussed as if it were a temporary compromise on the way back to an unaided original state. That assumption is unnecessary. Some supports are used briefly. Others become capable and valued parts of a person's continuing mechanical system. The medical question is whether the assembly serves the person's selected function under its actual conditions—not whether it resembles an unsupported body.

This view also clarifies why support deserves its own exposure analysis. An added route can reduce one demand while increasing another. A brace can constrain motion while changing contact. A prosthetic socket can transmit an external resultant while creating spatially and temporally varied pressure and shear at the residual limb. A ventilator can sustain gas exchange while its pressure-and-volume cycle enters the tissue's mechanical history. The substitution cannot be judged from the supported endpoint alone.

None of this requires the claim that substitution is generally beneficial or harmful. It creates a comparison. What function became available? What physical intermediate changed? What new demands entered the assembly? What biological receiver encountered them? What did the person value? Those questions are already familiar in clinical engineering and rehabilitation. They will later constrain any claim that a body has compensated or rerouted demand.

## Fixation creates a condition for healing

Fracture fixation makes the cooperation between mechanics and biology unusually visible. A construct can restore length and alignment, provide restraint, alter interfragmentary motion, and transfer force across a disrupted region. Those are intentional mechanical changes. They do not heal the fracture by themselves.

AO fracture-fixation principles distinguish compression plating intended to create absolute stability from bridge plating intended to create relative stability while preserving length and rotational and transverse alignment.[^17-04] In a bridge construct, force can pass through the plate and screws while the fracture zone remains comparatively undisturbed. As continuity develops and a gap closes, sharing between construct and bone can change.

The word *stability* therefore needs a specific comparison. It can refer to the motion permitted between fragments under a declared load and construct, not to a universal absence of movement. The chosen condition depends on the fracture and healing strategy. Blood supply, soft-tissue state, infection, repair biology, time, and the person's activity remain part of the result.

Experimental work can separate some of these variables without turning them into a universal rule. In a ten-sheep tibial-osteotomy model, active fixators generated a spatial gradient from 2.5 to 25 percent interfragmentary strain. Five animals were loaded from the first postoperative day and five from day 22. Computed-tomography measures at five weeks found that the distribution of repair tissue varied with strain magnitude and loading time: lower tested strains favored more tissue within the gap, while higher strains shifted calcified repair tissue toward external callus.[^17-05] The study does not establish a numerical treatment threshold for people. It demonstrates that a construct-defined mechanical field, its timing, and a biological repair distribution can be studied as different objects.

Fixation supports three modest conclusions. Medicine intentionally creates mechanical paths. The relative motion and distribution within those paths can matter to healing. And the mechanical environment remains one participant in a biological history.

Those conclusions are stronger than the generic claim that “structure matters.” They are weaker than the claim that a restored path determines recovery. Their strength comes from stating the boundary clearly.

They also reveal several meanings hidden inside the word *success*. A construct can achieve its selected alignment and restraint. Repair tissue can develop over time. The person can regain a valued function. Complications can remain absent or occur despite the earlier mechanical result. These outcomes can support one another, but no one of them substitutes for the others.

Suppose a radiograph shows maintained alignment while healing is delayed. The mechanical endpoint should not be retroactively declared unreal simply because the biological outcome was unfavorable. The account should ask whether the measured stability was adequate for the intended strategy, whether local motion or distribution differed from what the image could show, and which biological or contextual conditions participated. The reverse also holds: healing after a particular construct does not prove that only that mechanical environment could have succeeded.

This is why fixation is a useful foundation for the book rather than proof of a universal routing doctrine. It shows that the path through an assembly can be intentionally changed and that the change can matter. It also shows that mechanics becomes medically meaningful through receiver state, time, and outcome rather than by displacing them.

## Decompression changes a local relation

The term *decompression* can sound as though a procedure proves a complete mechanical explanation. It does not. It names an intended change in contact, pressure, deformation, or available space within a particular system. Whether that change identifies cause, predicts recovery, or explains symptoms is an additional question.

Carpal-tunnel pressure studies provide a measured example. In a prospective study of 103 women aged twenty to fifty with unilateral idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome and 25 controls, canal pressure varied with wrist position and was higher in the clinical group before surgery. It fell markedly immediately after open release, rose somewhat by two months, and remained within the control range during one year of follow-up.[^17-06] The operation changed a local pressure condition. That is a meaningful mechanical result.

Another operative study measured 48 wrists in 39 people before and after endoscopic release. Maximum static pressure with the wrist neutral fell from 56.7 to 7.4 mm Hg. Preoperative maximum pressure did not correlate with electrodiagnostic severity or median-nerve cross-sectional area, although the latter two measures correlated with each other.[^17-07] A large pressure change, an anatomical measure, and an electrophysiological measure did not collapse into one severity scale.

This example preserves the distinction developed in Chapter 13. In an extrinsic account, a maintaining relation precedes the geometry and pressure it produces. In an intrinsic account, tissue state may persist within the receiver. In a mixed account, both participate. Release can demonstrate that changing one boundary changes a selected local quantity. It cannot retrospectively observe which combination initiated the condition or how every tissue responded through time.

Treatment response must be held to the same rule. Symptom improvement after a mechanical intervention can support the relevance of the targeted relation to that outcome. It does not prove that the relation was the sole cause, that a body-wide route produced it, or that the same intervention would have the same meaning elsewhere. Conversely, imperfect symptom recovery does not erase a measured pressure change. Endpoint, tissue state, symptom, and history are different records.

Decompression is thus not a metaphysical restoration of “space.” It is an intervention with an anatomical boundary and one or more measurable mechanical consequences. The precision of that local account is exactly what prevents it from becoming proof of a larger story.

## Living interfaces make distribution visible

A device can survive while the tissue receiving its load does poorly. This fact makes distribution a medical-engineering concern rather than a refinement added after component strength.

Consider a prosthetic socket. Ground contact and inertia produce forces and moments that must cross an interface of finite area. Socket geometry, suspension, alignment, material, residual-limb volume, active control, and the chosen task all affect how that transfer occurs. Pressure and shear vary by site and phase. Comfort, skin state, participation, and long-term tolerance are later, non-equivalent outcomes.

In one study, ten men with unilateral transfemoral amputation used three socket designs during level walking, ramp ascent and descent, and stair ascent and descent. Sensors recorded pressure in anterior, lateral, posterior, and medial regions. Patterns and extrema varied with location and task; small design groups and sensor failures limited the comparison.[^17-08] The result establishes local and task-dependent distribution, not a universal socket ranking or tissue threshold.

A single-person transtibial study changed sock layers to simulate looser and tighter fit while measuring both pressure and shear at three sites during standing and level walking. Small fit changes produced site- and phase-specific differences, and pressure and shear did not rise or fall as one uniform quantity.[^17-09] The observation is illustrative rather than population-level evidence. Its value here is conceptual: a map of pressure alone does not contain the complete interface traction state.

Time adds another dimension. In a single-participant alignment study, peak pressure, duration above 90 percent of that peak, and time–pressure integral changed differently across sagittal alignment conditions.[^17-10] A peak, a duration, and an integrated exposure answer different questions. None independently determines comfort, tissue perfusion, injury, or person-valued use.

The interface example connects established practice to this book's language of routing. Care already asks where externally applied demand goes at a local boundary. It measures parts of the distribution, changes geometry or fit, and checks consequences. But a local pressure map is not a whole-body route. The person's gait, assistance, environment, tissue state, and prior history can all influence it without being recoverable from it.

A complete-looking color map can hide that incompleteness. Sensors sample selected locations and frequencies. A measurement made during level walking does not automatically represent stairs, slopes, prolonged standing, heat, fatigue, or a change in residual-limb volume. Pressure at the surface does not directly measure strain inside every tissue layer, and pressure alone omits tangential traction. The map can still be valuable. Its resolution and task define what it can resolve.

The person supplies information the map cannot replace. Comfort, confidence, security, participation, effort, and the value of a device are not errors added to an otherwise objective mechanical result. They are separate outcomes of the person–device system. A low pressure peak is not a sufficient definition of a good interface, just as a strong component is not a sufficient definition of a usable prosthesis.

The same logic applies beyond prosthetics. A surgical plate transfers demand through screw–bone and plate–bone relations. A support surface distributes contact over skin and deeper tissue. An orthosis changes motion and pressure at several boundaries. Established practice therefore already contains a local routing question: how does an external or reconstructed assembly share demand with living material? The proposed longitudinal framework must add something beyond that mature question rather than merely renaming it.

## An endpoint does not contain its route

The examples now permit a general distinction. An *endpoint record* asks what the present mechanical condition is, which quantity can be changed, and whether the selected change occurred. A *history record* asks how the condition developed: which demands entered, which paths were available, what substituted or compensated, what exposure reached a receiver, and what changed next.

The endpoint record can be rich. It may include repeated measurements, tissue state, symptoms, function, and response to intervention. Calling it local does not make it simplistic. The history record can be poor. It may be assembled from memory, current appearance, and a model whose assumptions were never tested. Calling it whole-body does not make it comprehensive or true.

Several histories can converge on a similar endpoint. Elevated interface pressure can reflect anatomy, swelling, device fit, alignment, task, active strategy, or combinations. A fracture construct can face similar mechanical demands after different injuries and within different biological states. Canal pressure can vary with position and local tissue conditions without uniquely encoding the events that produced them.

Several endpoints can also follow one history. The same injury can lead to different repair environments, compensations, symptoms, and functional results. The same period of ventilatory support can expose heterogeneous regions differently. The same device alignment can interact with different tissue states, strategies, and goals. A history therefore does not behave like a code that deterministically generates one endpoint, any more than an endpoint behaves like a recording of its past.

This many-to-many relation is the real reason to distinguish the records. It is not an argument that causation is unknowable. It is a warning that causal resolution must come from chronology, discriminating measurements, intervention, comparison, and explicit assumptions—not from the smoothness of a narrative. In favorable cases, those sources can strongly narrow the history. In others, a plural account is the most accurate result.

The inverse is also possible: a well-documented event can make part of the history unusually clear. A recorded trauma, a known experimental manipulation, or repeated prospective measurements may identify the earlier state better than a later reconstruction. Even then, the route from event to tissue response and outcome can contain uncertain intermediate steps.

This is why an elaborate story is not automatically an advance. A history earns relevance only if it changes a defined result. It might improve explanation, prediction, recurrence analysis, measurement, communication, or research design. It might reveal that two apparently similar endpoints arose under different exposures. It might also add nothing, create false confidence, or duplicate work already performed by biomechanics, rehabilitation, ergonomics, or occupational medicine.

> **Figure 17.3 — Endpoint and routing questions [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Endpoint record | Routing-history record |
> |---|---|
> | What condition is present now? | What task and environment supplied demand through time? |
> | Which mechanical quantity is measured? | Which contacts, structures, supports, and active states participated? |
> | What local or system-level change is intended? | What was observed, calculated, modeled, recalled, or left unknown? |
> | Did the selected endpoint change? | Did the added history improve a declared explanation or test? |
> | Can this record answer the immediate question alone? | Does this record add value beyond established accounts? |
>
> **Caption.** Endpoint and routing records answer different questions. Either can be sufficient for a declared purpose; integration is useful only when the combined record produces a defined improvement.
>
> **Text alternative.** Two columns compare five endpoint questions with five routing-history questions. Both culminate in a sufficiency test rather than assuming that one record is superior.

The boundary is productive. It lets us value established endpoint reasoning without requiring it to do historical work. It also prevents the proposed routing framework from claiming importance merely because it contains more arrows.

## The proposal belongs inside the existing landscape

The project can now state its proposed addition without accusing medicine of forgetting the body. Mechanical reasoning is already distributed across specialties. Biomechanics measures and models motion, force, moments, contact, and internal distribution. Rehabilitation studies function, capacity, learning, support, response, and adaptation. Ergonomics and occupational health study tasks, environments, and exposure. Surgery and device fields intentionally alter local geometry, stability, contact, and transfer. Medical specialties define tissue states, diagnoses, immediate risks, and endpoints.

The proposed question is whether a more explicit relationship among those observations is sometimes useful. What demand entered the person–environment system? Which paths and supports were available? What changed across phase, region, and time? What strategy preserved function? Which local exposure is observed or modeled? What biological response is separately supported? Which alternative history fits the same endpoint?

At this stage, that is an integration proposal, not an established new framework. Its components have substantial precedent. Its added value has to be shown relative to those precedents. A valid result may be that an existing discipline already contains the needed record. It may be that the history cannot be reconstructed reliably. It may be that the local endpoint is already explained and managed well enough for the purpose at hand.

Those outcomes do not make mechanics less medical. They determine where the longitudinal proposal earns a role.

## Common ground, then a harder test

Medicine already reasons in pressure, flow, volume, stability, contact, geometry, support, and distribution. It substitutes for physical functions, constructs mechanical environments for healing, changes local constraints, and designs interfaces that must transmit demand through living tissue. These are not metaphors. They are established forms of care and research.

Their limits are equally clear. A pressure change is not a complete nerve history. A stable construct is not healing by itself. A device-interface map is not tissue tolerance or person-valued function. A successful endpoint does not uniquely identify its cause. And a complete upstream reconstruction is not always required for effective action.

Book I therefore does not propose to add mechanics to medicine. It proposes to ask whether mechanical observations already held in different places can be related across time without losing their provenance, system boundary, or alternatives. That relationship must do more than sound coherent.

Chapter 18 takes up the harder test. It will define a longitudinal routing record, compare it with existing biomechanics, exposure science, rehabilitation, and clinical frameworks, and identify results that would support, narrow, duplicate, or disfavor it. Only then can the book claim an addition rather than a restatement.

# Chapter 18 — The proposed addition: longitudinal load routing

Imagine a research visit at which a local interface shows less excursion during a particular task than it did in an earlier record. The change is measured now. The task is also harder now. Those two observations may matter, but they do not contain their own history.

Perhaps a documented local event altered the interface, after which movement and support changed. Perhaps a repeated task changed first, a successful compensation became habitual, and the interface encountered a different exposure over time. Perhaps illness, inflammation, medication, sleep, stress, development, or another change in capacity came first and mechanics changed in response. Perhaps several of these occurred, or the decisive interval was never observed.

This is a hypothetical comparison, not a patient history or diagnostic exercise. Its purpose is to make a missing object visible. The endpoint can be measured precisely while more than one prior sequence remains compatible with it. A longer sequence may help distinguish those possibilities. It may also remain too incomplete to do so.

We use *longitudinal load routing* for a structured record of how a defined task and environment, available mechanical paths, demand distribution, local exposure, compensation, and changing state relate across time. The record can combine direct observations, measurements, calculations, models, reports, and explicit unknowns. It is ordered forward in time even when some of it is assembled retrospectively.

The proposed value is not a recovered hidden cause. It is an inspectable account in which observations held at different scales and by different disciplines can be placed in temporal relation without losing how each became known. Such an account can generate a better exposure question, distinguish competing histories, reveal a missing measurement, or organize prospective research. It can also add nothing.

That last possibility is not a ceremonial disclaimer. It is the standard the proposal must survive. Mechanics, ergonomics, occupational exposure science, rehabilitation, and medicine already study important parts of mechanical history. A routing record earns a place only when it adds a defined result beyond those existing accounts.

## A present endpoint underdetermines its history

Chapter 17 distinguished an endpoint record from a history record. The endpoint record asks what condition is present, what quantity was measured, and whether a selected intervention changed it. The history record asks what demands preceded that condition, what paths and supports were available, what changed, what exposure reached a receiver, and what happened next.

Neither record is automatically more rigorous. A current pressure, excursion, alignment, motion, or interface distribution may be measured well. A proposed whole-body history may be assembled from memory and an untested model. Conversely, repeated measurements may document much of a history while a present endpoint remains ambiguous. The relevant comparison is between the questions the records can answer, not between local simplicity and systemic sophistication.

The inverse problem is many-to-many. Similar endpoints can follow different events, tasks, tissue states, compensations, and recovery conditions. One documented event can also lead to different later distributions, responses, findings, and functions. A current endpoint constrains the candidate histories; it does not usually select one by itself. Causal reasoning therefore requires a defined contrast, chronology, assumptions, and observations capable of distinguishing alternatives. A coherent sequence is not an identified effect merely because every arrow can be narrated.[^18-01]
