## Part V synthesis — What a complete narrative changes

The four narratives have not produced one mechanical diagnosis. They have produced a more demanding form of explanation.

The geometry narrative showed that orientation and line of action can alter moments, contacts, and modeled fields while leaving internal allocation and clinical consequence open. The thoracic-outlet narrative distinguished a changed lumen or excursion from the relation that maintains deformation and from the condition-specific evidence needed for medical interpretation. The instability narrative separated motion, control, repeated demand, capacity, response, and symptom rather than treating instability as a visible defect. The mixed chronic narrative preserved several live accounts at once and showed why a strategy must be understood for what it protects before compensation is blamed for cost.

Across all four, the same result appeared in different forms: a coherent chain is not the same as an established chain. Boundaries, carriers, quantities, chronology, receiver state, biological response, and alternatives each require their own support. A negative or nonunique result is not a failure of the method. It prevents the framework from becoming a story generator that confirms itself.

The cases also clarify the current practical limit. Observation can motivate a comparison. A valid measurement can characterize one relation. Neither automatically creates a diagnostic threshold, a treatment target, or an individualized correction. Those applications require their own evidence, purpose, reliability, benefit, harm, and decision-value work.

Part VI gathers what can responsibly follow now. It begins with a portable set of questions, then separates education, environmental design, prevention, measurement, intervention development, implementation, and health-system change. The final task is equally important: distinguish the mechanical foundation completed in this volume from the stronger body-wide hypothesis that gives the series its title.

# Part VI — Reasoning, prevention, development, and the wider hypothesis

A framework can change inquiry before it changes care. That is the governing distinction of Part VI.

The lowest-risk use of the book is a better question: What demand entered the system? What configuration and paths were available? How were shape-preserving and form-receiving roles divided? Where, if anywhere, might a local exposure have accumulated? What, if anything, did a changed strategy preserve? What changes with task, support, time, or state? What can actually be measured, and where should the inference stop?

Chapter 27 develops those questions as a reasoning scaffold rather than a score, screen, or protocol. Chapter 28 asks what this book's narrower mechanical literacy can contribute to the broader domain of movement literacy, education, environmental design, and outcome-specific prevention research. It keeps comprehension, behavior, exposure, injury, symptom, participation, and system outcomes separate. Chapter 29 then distinguishes six development functions—research, measurement, education, therapeutic development, implementation, and health-system work—from those application domains. The tracks can inform one another and can operate across more than one domain, but none advances merely because another produced an encouraging result.

This staging preserves the project's ambition. A present additive role for a routing lens is not a permanent claim that medicine can never be reorganized around better mechanical knowledge. It is the evidence posture appropriate before constructs, measurements, benefits, harms, professional roles, equity effects, burdens, and opportunity costs have been established.

Chapter 30 then closes the volume on three levels. The durable Book I foundation stands first. Posterior anatomy supplies a bounded organizing lens. The wider preferred-configuration program is stated directly as a hypothesis, with its current signed modes and posterior expectation, its destination in later books, and a rejection test that leaves the foundation intact.

The Part therefore moves from what can be asked now to what must be built next. It offers no corrective routine. Its endpoint is a researchable horizon: definitions clear enough to fail, measurements matched to their purposes, applications that do not borrow evidence from one another, and a series title whose strongest meaning is disclosed rather than assumed.

# Chapter 27 — Mechanical questions and observations in clinical reasoning

## Questions do not become a test by being ordered

Return once more to the ordinary transfer used throughout this book. A person lifts a familiar object from one support, carries it several steps, and places it on another support. The task is simple enough to recognize and rich enough to expose a recurring error: a visible action does not reveal one internal mechanical story.

The first difference is the system boundary. For the combined person-and-object system, the hand–object interaction is internal. For the person alone, the object acts across the boundary. For the object alone, the hands act across the boundary in the other direction. A boundary around a forearm, joint, or tissue changes the accounting again. Moving inward is not merely zooming in on the same force diagram. It creates a different system with different boundary actions.[^27-01]

The second difference is the level of the claim. A nearly steady carry can have little acceleration while substantial forces remain present. A calculated net joint force or moment can be compatible with several combinations of muscle, ligament, contact, and pressure. An observed trunk shape can coexist with different active strategies, supports, histories, and receiver states. Each description may be useful, but none licenses the next description automatically.

This chapter condenses the method of Book I into seven questions. Their order matters because it makes missing links visible. Their answers do not produce a score, a mechanical diagnosis, or a treatment choice. An answer can support one proposed link, weaken it, redirect attention to another chronology, leave several accounts unresolved, or stop the route entirely. The sequence is therefore a reasoning scaffold: a way to ask what is known, what follows under stated assumptions, and what has not yet been established.

> **Figure 27.1 — One transfer, several system boundaries [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Boundary | Interaction crossing the boundary | A quantity that may be available | What remains unresolved |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Person + object | Ground and external supports | Total external force and moment balance | Distribution within the person and object |
> | Person | Object, ground, and other supports | External actions on the person; segment estimates under assumptions | Individual muscle, joint-contact, or tissue forces |
> | Object | Hands and destination support | Object motion and contact forces where measured | How the person produced those actions |
> | Segment or joint | Neighboring segments and crossing structures | Net force and moment resultants | Unique muscle, ligament, contact, and pressure sharing |
> | Tissue or interface | Surrounding contact, attachment, pressure, and material boundary conditions | Local stress, strain, pressure, or deformation only if measured or modeled appropriately | Biological response, symptom, or clinical meaning |
>
> **Caption.** Changing the system boundary changes which interactions are external and which quantities can be balanced. The table is not a movement assessment and does not identify a preferred way to transfer the object.
>
> **Text alternative.** A five-row table moves from a combined person-and-object system to the person, object, joint, and tissue. Each smaller boundary introduces new interactions and new unresolved internal distributions; no row automatically determines the next.

> **Figure 27.2 — Seven questions with equal-weight stopping branches [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> 1  demand and boundary
>          |
> 2  configuration and available paths
>          |
> 3  shape-preserving and form-receiving roles
>          |
> 4  candidate local exposure
>          |
> 5  preserved function or outcome, if any
>          |
> 6  change across task, support, time, or state
>          |
> 7  measurement, uncertainty, and legitimate use
>
> At every arrow:
> support | weaken | redirect | remain unresolved | STOP
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The sequence moves inward only as far as the evidence permits. A stop is a valid result for the present question, not proof that mechanics is irrelevant in every other question.
>
> **Text alternative.** Seven numbered steps descend from demand to measurement and intended use. Beside every transition are five equally weighted outcomes: support, weaken, redirect, unresolved, and stop.

Confidence belongs to propositions, not to the narrative as a whole. A task history can be well documented while its internal distribution remains unknown. A local exposure can be measured while its role in symptoms remains weak. A symptom can change reproducibly with support while the initiating history remains unresolved. The account should therefore say which arrow changed and why. It should not award points for the number of mechanically interesting observations or average unlike evidence into one confidence rating.

The questions are also recursive. A proposed path may require a smaller boundary, which creates a new demand question at that scale. A changed strategy may lead back to the history to ask when it appeared. A measurement limit may require a coarser conclusion rather than another inference. Recursion is useful only while each pass names a more precise object or a consequential uncertainty. When it merely adds anatomical detail without discriminating among accounts, the scaffold has reached a stop.

## 1. What demand entered the system?

Begin with the event rather than the presumed fault. What task occurred? What was supported, accelerated, resisted, contacted, carried, or stabilized? Over what phase and interval? Which boundary is under study? What environment, assistance, equipment, pace, repetition, and recovery opportunity belonged to the event?

These questions do not require a complete force record. They require the description to remain at its actual resolution. *Lifted a box from the floor* names an event but not the object's mass, acceleration, hand forces, foot contacts, or segment resultants. *Worked at a computer for six hours* names a broad context but not an uninterrupted exposure, a particular configuration, or a local tissue dose. *Pain began after work* orders two reports coarsely but does not establish what demand preceded the change.

The boundary must be stated before forces and paths are named. During the object transfer, the external demand on the person includes the object's action, ground contact, and any other support. Within the person, force and moment resultants depend on how the body is divided for analysis. A stationary or slowly moving phase does not mean zero mechanical demand; it means that the net force and moment balances have a particular relation to acceleration. Conversely, visible motion does not tell us which internal structure bore the demand.

History belongs here because one event can meet a receiver changed by previous events. Task frequency, duration, variation, prior injury or illness, activity, sleep, care, equipment, and time to recover can change the boundary conditions or the state that receives the next demand. They should not be compressed into a generic *mechanical history*. Each item enters at a named link: task opportunity, present capacity, response, behavior, or another condition that may shape both the task and the outcome.

The first question can stop the inquiry. If the task cannot be identified, if the relevant interval is unknown, or if the proposed exposure is inferred only from a symptom or later finding, the account may remain a plausible research question but cannot advance as an observed demand history. A more detailed story is not necessarily a more accurate one.

## 2. What configuration and paths were available?

Configuration describes the relation among structures, contacts, supports, and active states during a declared part of the task. It is more specific than a posture label and less specific than an internal stress field. The useful question is not merely *what shape was visible?* It is *what mechanical options did that relation make available under these boundary conditions?*

Joint geometry can change moment arms and contact. Foot placement can change the external line of action. A handrail can add a support path. Active stiffness can preserve one relation while permitting motion elsewhere. Posterior structures may participate substantially in one task and minimally in another, but their visible prominence or presumed absence is not itself a finding of deficient routing. Anterior, posterior, lateral, rotational, pressure-mediated, and externally supported contributions remain possible until the task and quantities distinguish them.

Ordinary observation can describe configuration, but it must name the object observed. Agreement for video-based posture observations varies with the parameter and the categorization scheme; broadening a category may improve agreement while reducing resolution.[^27-02] Thus *rounded*, *shifted*, or *asymmetric* is not yet an operational observation. A description needs a segment, reference, direction or plane, task phase, observer or instrument, and uncertainty.

Touch does not bypass this requirement. A systematic review of low-back palpation found poor reliability for bony and joint-mobility palpation, inconsistent reliability for soft-tissue procedures, and limited validity evidence across the included methods.[^27-03] That evidence is region- and procedure-specific, not a ban on touch. It does block a stronger shortcut: palpation cannot be treated as direct access to an otherwise hidden whole-body force path without a validated method for that use.

Several internal paths can produce a similar external action, and one path can serve several external actions. Configuration narrows a possibility space; it rarely selects a unique solution. The route should stop here when the proposed path is only drawn onto anatomy, when no carrier or physical quantity is named, or when the visible relation does not distinguish the proposed route from ordinary alternatives.

## 3. How were hard and soft roles divided?

The hard-and-soft distinction asks how mechanical labor was divided within the declared interaction. A relatively hard role is shape-preserving or structurally resolving at the selected scale, direction, and time. A relatively soft role is form-receiving: yielding, conforming, accommodating, containing, or permitting glide while remaining mechanically active and consequential.

These are roles, not tissue bins. Bone deforms. Muscle can create a shape-preserving path through active tension. A ligament can preserve a relation while elongating. Cartilage can receive form while distributing pressure. A pressurized vessel can receive surrounding shape while its wall sustains stress and its contents affect its behavior. External support can take part of a shape-preserving role that would otherwise be distributed within the person.

The project's compact intuition—load wants to travel through the hard body so that the soft body can remain soft—becomes useful only after it is translated into a local question. Which demand? Which relatively shape-preserving assembly? Which form-receiving structure? Which direction, quantity, phase, and duration? *Remain soft* does not mean unloaded. It means retaining the deformation, glide, containment, or pressure-bearing behavior required for that structure's function without presuming a harmful retained state.

The division can change during one task. During the object transfer, the ground, skeleton, active muscle, joint geometry, connective tissue, and object can share shape-preserving work in different phases. Muscle, tendon, cartilage, vessel, skin, abdominal contents, and other interfaces can receive and redistribute form. The vocabulary does not determine that one division is ideal, that posterior participation is always required, or that a form-receiving role is a failure.

This question earns its place when it identifies a relation that can be examined. It loses force when *hard* simply means good and *soft* means burdened, or when a tissue name substitutes for a measured quantity. If the proposed role cannot be tied to the task and receiver, the route should remain at the level of configuration rather than advance through an assumed role failure.

## 4. Where, if anywhere, might local exposure have accumulated?

External demand is not local exposure. Between them lie configuration, contact, active contribution, material properties, and internal sharing. A segment-level force or moment is a resultant: it balances the declared free body without revealing the unique forces that produced it. Estimating individual muscle forces, for example, requires assumptions about recruitment, anatomy, optimization, and model validity because several internal solutions can satisfy the same net demand.[^27-04]

The receiver and quantity therefore have to be named. A joint surface may receive contact pressure and shear. A tendon may receive tensile stress and strain. A vessel wall may deform under pressure-derived and surrounding actions while lumen geometry and flow remain separate objects. A nerve may experience deformation, excursion, pressure, or altered interface behavior. *Load* can remain useful in general prose, but a consequential local claim must say whether it means force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, contact, work, or another quantity.

Accumulation adds time. A large brief exposure, a smaller sustained exposure, repeated cycles, variable loading with recovery, and a retained material state are not interchangeable. The relevant dose may include magnitude, direction, rate, repetition, duration, sequence, and recovery, while capacity may change through adaptation, illness, injury, fatigue, learning, care, or ordinary variation. No scalar *load burden* should be invented merely because the full vector or history is difficult to measure.

The phrase *if anywhere* is load-bearing. A changed configuration can redistribute demand without creating an adverse concentration. A local field can be heterogeneous and ordinary. A tissue can deform and recover. A proposed exposure can be too small, too transient, poorly measured, or unrelated to the selected outcome. Another biological or contextual process can dominate the receiver's response even when a mechanical exposure is real.

This question may support a bounded mechanical proposition while stopping before medical consequence. It may establish that geometry plausibly changed an internal distribution, yet leave tissue response unknown. It may reveal that a calculated surrogate failed to track a measured internal quantity. It may also find no receiver-specific exposure at all. None of these endings licenses a diagnosis or correction.

## 5. What, if anything, did the changed strategy preserve?

A difference becomes a compensation only when there is something it helped preserve under a changed condition. The preserved object might be task completion, balance, comfort, tissue tolerance, vision, breathing room, confidence, participation, or another valued function. Without a prior state, a perturbation or constraint, and an outcome that remained possible, *compensation* can become a retrospective label for any difference.

Protection comes before cost. A person who uses a handrail, reduces excursion, changes pace, recruits another region, or avoids one task may be preserving safety, capacity, participation, or comfort. That strategy may be temporary or durable. It may consume more effort, narrow options, redistribute exposure, or have no demonstrated cost. Successful preservation and adverse redistribution are separate propositions.

Chronology matters. If pain, illness, fatigue, fear, medication, or environmental constraint preceded the changed strategy, the strategy may be a response rather than the origin of the selected outcome. If a change preceded symptoms, it still does not become causal unless a relevant carrier, exposure, response, and time relation are supported. A shared change in work, sleep, resources, or activity may produce both the strategy and the outcome. The mechanically coherent story must compete with these orders rather than absorb them as minor modifiers.

This is where confirmation pressure is most dangerous. In one bounded experiment, confirmatory information search was associated with persistence in an incorrect preliminary diagnosis among psychiatrists and medical students.[^27-05] In another vignette experiment, family physicians' evaluation of incoming evidence could be distorted toward a leading hypothesis.[^27-06] Neither study estimates bias in biomechanical reasoning. Together they justify a simple discipline: record what changed and what remained possible before naming the change compensation, and state an observation that would favor a reverse, adaptive, shared-cause, or incidental account.

The question can end affirmatively with *useful adaptation*, *no demonstrated cost*, or *preserved function with unresolved tradeoffs*. It can also end with *nothing has yet established that this difference preserved anything*. Compensation is earned by the relation among state, task, change, and preserved outcome; it is not presumed from asymmetry, muscle activity, stiffness, or continued task performance alone.

## 6. What changes with task, support, time, or state?

Variation can help distinguish a relation, but modulation is not origin. If a symptom, movement, pressure, or task tolerance changes when support changes, the result may show that the present system is mechanically modifiable. It does not by itself establish why the problem began, which internal variable changed, or whether repeating the condition would be beneficial.

Compare only what the question can support. A change across tasks may identify task specificity. A change with an external support may show that boundary conditions matter. Repeated observations may estimate within-person variability. A time series may place a change before or after another event. Recovery after rest may reveal state dependence. None of those comparisons becomes a tissue mechanism without the intermediate measurements.

The relevant state is wider than local anatomy. Pain, attention, expectation, confidence, sleep, illness, medication, training, previous care, work control, assistance, and opportunity for exposure can change movement, force, participation, report, or recovery. They can be causes, consequences, shared determinants, or modifiers at different links. Calling the account whole-person does not mean adding them as a checklist; it means locating each one where it can change the proposed sequence.

Negative and noncorresponding results refine the next question. If a configuration changes while the selected internal measure does not, the path from configuration to that quantity weakens. If a report changes while a selected kinematic record does not, the two observations should remain distinct. If a local mechanical state changes without the predicted function or symptom, the later arrow may stop. If the same outcome occurs across materially different histories, a proposed unique chronology loses priority.

Task modulation can also reveal capable variation. More than one strategy may meet the same demand. A stable strategy may be effective under one support and costly under another; a variable strategy may be adaptable or simply noisy. The book's vocabulary does not assign value from variability, symmetry, stiffness, posterior participation, or range alone. The declared task, receiver, outcome, and timescale decide what the variation means.

## 7. What can actually be measured, and what remains uncertain?

The final question applies to every preceding one. An ordinary observation, an embodied report, a research instrument, a validated clinical measure, a calculation, a model output, an inference, a reconstruction, and a hypothesis are different evidence objects. They can inform one another without becoming interchangeable.

Measurement begins by defining the measurand or construct, method, conditions, result, and uncertainty. Metrology distinguishes measurement from its result and separates repeatability from reproducibility; many clinical and embodied constructs are not physical quantities, but they still require an operational definition appropriate to their use.[^27-07] The FDA–NIH BEST resource likewise separates biomarkers from clinical outcome assessments and distinguishes patient-, clinician-, observer-, and performance-based outcomes while making validation dependent on context of use.[^27-08] A sensor output, image, report, and performance therefore belong in separate columns unless evidence justifies a relation among them.

Measurement properties answer different questions. Reliability concerns discrimination relative to variation. Agreement and measurement error concern how close repeated results are in their units. Validity concerns whether the interpretation represents the intended construct or quantity. Responsiveness concerns detection of change. Interpretability concerns what a value means. A consensus taxonomy separates these domains rather than allowing one favorable coefficient to validate an instrument wholesale.[^27-09] Agreement and reliability can even lead to different impressions because reliability depends partly on heterogeneity in the sampled population.[^27-10]

A detectable change is not automatically important. A small difference may exceed technical error yet add no meaningful information; a large reported change may remain nonspecific for mechanism. Foundational work on minimally important difference made the person's perspective and consequences of change central, but it did not create one universal threshold for individual decisions.[^27-11]

The distance from observation to clinical use is longer still. Screening is an organized population activity with a target condition, follow-up, quality, benefit, burden, and harm obligations; seven conceptual questions do not meet that definition.[^27-12] Diagnosis is an iterative, collaborative process embedded in a health-care work system, not the output of one mechanical measure or narrative.[^27-13] Even statistical discrimination or accuracy does not encode the consequences of acting on a result.[^27-14]

> **Figure 27.3 — From an observation to a legitimate use [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Development object | Question it must answer | What success does not establish |
> |---|---|---|
> | Ordinary observation or report | What was noticed, by whom, under what task and ambiguity? | Internal exposure, cause, or diagnosis |
> | Operational measure | Is the construct or quantity defined and produced reproducibly enough for its purpose? | Validity, meaning, or utility |
> | Validated assessment for a declared context | Does the interpretation hold in the intended population, setting, and use? | Screening, diagnosis, or improved decisions |
> | Screening or diagnostic study | Are target condition, comparator, threshold, flow, bias, and applicability handled? | Net benefit or safe implementation |
> | Decision-relevant application | Does acting on the information improve a named outcome relative to alternatives, burden, and harm? | Transfer to another population, setting, or purpose |
>
> **Caption.** Each stage adds obligations rather than merely confidence. Chapter 27 supplies the first row and a development question; it does not claim the later rows.
>
> **Text alternative.** A five-row ladder moves from ordinary observation through operational measurement, validated assessment, screening or diagnostic study, and decision-relevant application. Each row lists a distinct requirement and a stronger conclusion it still cannot establish.

Uncertainty should be attached to the link it affects. Unknown task history limits the demand claim. Nonunique internal sharing limits the path claim. Measurement error limits change. Poor construct validity limits interpretation. Missing chronology limits origin. Nonspecific modulation limits mechanism. Lack of incremental value limits use even when the measurement itself is sound.

The scaffold should stop when the proposed observation is not operational, the internal distribution is nonunique and unmeasured, the receiver or quantity cannot be named, response chronology is missing, error is too large for the intended distinction, modulation is equally compatible with alternatives, or the result adds nothing consequential to an existing account. It should also yield when another concern has higher immediate priority, when the question lies outside the user's role, or when a validated domain-specific method should replace a generic mechanical scaffold.

## Four narratives, four different endings

The worked narratives in Part V did not demonstrate the same proposition four times. They tested different portions of the sequence and ended at different evidentiary boundaries.

Chapter 23 established a strong, bounded relation among task, geometry, internal distribution, and local fields in selected knee and lumbar contexts. It also showed that an external surrogate can fail to track a measured internal force and that an imposed interface change can have no detected effect on selected contact measures. The route became less complete when it approached living tissue history, symptoms, and clinical meaning.

Chapter 24 began with focal anatomy, current arterial findings, distal occlusion, collaterals, and a pressure difference observed together in a source-grounded teaching composite. It therefore carried a clinically consequential chain farther than a generic corridor example could. Yet repeated deformation, wall transition, and the full untreated chronology remained reconstructed, while healthy anatomy and waveform comparisons prevented anatomy or positional change from becoming sufficient.

Chapter 25 treated repeated demand as demand applied to a changing receiver. Passive restraint, task-level relation maintenance, and perceived instability could correspond or diverge. Prospective studies supplied selected temporal order without a complete mechanism, and proximal kinematic observations did not automatically become proximal tissue exposure. Useful adaptation, retained change, new event, mixed state, and unresolved history all remained available.

Chapter 26 used a transparent hypothetical rather than an empirical case or teaching composite. Its office-work and nonspecific-low-back-pain chronology was constructed to compare possible orders, not to establish that one route occurred in a person or population. The mechanical account could end as substantial, mixed, reverse-causal, adaptive, low priority, or unresolved, and no regional carrier was established merely because the story was mechanically coherent.

> **Figure 27.4 — Four narratives, four evidentiary outcomes [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Narrative | Strongest supported region of the chain | Load-bearing limit or null | Legitimate outcome |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Geometry and localized strain | Geometry can alter selected internal distributions and local fields | Surrogates can fail; later biological and clinical arrows remain separate | Strong bounded mechanical relation; downstream meaning open |
> | Thoracic outlet constraint | Focal anatomy and current arterial findings coexist with a consequential distal state | Repeated deformation and wall transition are reconstructed; anatomy is not sufficient | Substantive focal account with an unresolved historical interval |
> | Instability and changing capacity | Later demand meets a state altered by event, recovery, adaptation, and behavior | Passive, task, report, and proximal measures can diverge | Several measured state relations; transition mechanism incomplete |
> | Silent compensation and mixed chronic presentation | A hypothetical chronology can expose the records a real route would require | No empirical case and no established regional carrier | Substantial, mixed, reverse, adaptive, low-priority, or unresolved hypothesis |
>
> **Caption.** The same seven questions do not force the same conclusion. Each narrative advances only through the links its observations, measures, and sources support.
>
> **Text alternative.** A four-row table compares the Part V narratives. The first has a strong bounded geometry relation, the second a focal current arterial chain with a reconstructed history, the third several state domains that can diverge, and the fourth a transparent hypothetical with multiple possible endings.

## A scaffold that is allowed to stop

The seven questions improve reasoning only if they remain vulnerable to answers the project did not prefer. They ask for the task before the path, the configuration before the local exposure, the preserved outcome before the presumed cost, and the evidence state before the clinical interpretation. They make a mechanical account easier to examine because its arrows are exposed.

They do not establish that every clinical history needs a longer mechanical explanation. A concise existing account may already contain the relevant information. The proposed carrier may be unmeasurable at the required scale. A mechanical relation may be real but secondary for the selected outcome. Further inquiry may add burden, anxiety, inequity, opportunity cost, or false precision without improving understanding or consequence. Stopping under those conditions is not failure; it is part of the method.

If the sequence is ever developed beyond a conceptual scaffold, attractive wording will not be enough. Its constructs, intended users, contexts, comparators, measurement properties, alternatives, harms, access, incremental value, and consequences will need staged development and evaluation. Guidance for complex interventions emphasizes iterative work across context, theory, stakeholders, uncertainty, implementation, and evaluation; it does not validate this sequence or dictate that it become an intervention.[^27-15]

For now, the outcome is narrower and useful. A reader can describe a demand, declare a boundary, separate visible configuration from internal distribution, ask how shape-preserving and form-receiving roles were divided, name a possible receiver and quantity, test whether a changed strategy preserved anything, compare task and state, and stop at the strongest supported link. Chapter 28 carries that discipline into education, environments, and prevention claims, where clearer language can be valuable before individualized correction or medical effect has been established.

# Chapter 28 — Education, prevention, movement literacy, and environmental design

## Beyond “sit correctly”

Imagine a computer station shared by several people during a day. One person is tall and reads through bifocals. Another uses a wheelchair and needs open space below the work surface. A third is pregnant and finds sustained sitting uncomfortable. A fourth prefers forearm support because of fatigue. The task is nominally the same, but the available contacts, reaches, visual relations, assistance, schedules, and recovery opportunities are not.

The familiar response is a command: sit correctly. The command compresses a complicated system into a body shape and assigns the person the work of maintaining it. Even when kindly meant, it leaves essential questions unanswered. Correct for which task phase? Relative to which support? For how long? With what visual demand? Who can move the screen, change the schedule, obtain assistance, or leave the station? What outcome is the command expected to change?

A language of mechanical demand begins elsewhere. It describes what the task asks, which supports and alternatives exist, how long and how often the demand recurs, how the situation changes with fatigue, and what recovery is available. It keeps visible the difference between what can be observed and what remains unknown. A person may report pressure or fatigue; an observer may describe contact and configuration. Neither observation, by itself, reveals a unique internal load path, a tissue stress field, or the origin of a symptom.

That distinction matters because language changes how people interpret their bodies. In interviews about low-back pain, some clinical messages were remembered as reassurance, while others were understood as evidence of vulnerability and a need for protection; participants connected those interpretations with confidence, vigilance, worry, guilt, or frustration.[^28-01] The interviews do not prove that one phrase causes a particular outcome. They do show that education is not mechanically or psychologically neutral merely because it contains no exercise.

The purpose of *mechanical literacy* is therefore not to teach people to detect hidden faults. It is to make person–task–environment relations easier to describe while preserving uncertainty. In this book, mechanical literacy is a proposed contribution to the broader domain of *movement literacy*. Movement literacy names the wider educational field; mechanical literacy names this book's narrower vocabulary for demand, support, exposure, and uncertainty. The claims in this chapter concern that narrower construct. The same discipline can inform public education, professional communication, environmental design, and carefully specified prevention programs. It does not yet authorize screening, diagnosis, individualized assessment, treatment, or personal correction.

> **Figure 28.1 — One task, two kinds of language [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Command language | Mechanical-literacy language |
> |---|---|
> | Hold one presumed correct shape | Name the task and its changing phases |
> | Treat the body as the correction target | Name contacts, supports, assistance, tools, and environmental constraints |
> | Assume appearance reveals internal loading | Separate visible configuration, reported experience, measured exposure, and unknown internal distribution |
> | Assign a generic duration or break rule | Describe actual duration, pace, repetition, variability, and recovery opportunity |
> | Treat compliance as success | Prespecify comprehension, access, comfort, participation, exposure, symptom, injury, or another outcome |
> | Place responsibility on the individual | Ask who controls the equipment, schedule, space, staffing, cost, and alternatives |
>
> **Caption.** A richer description does not identify an ideal setup. It reveals more of the system and makes the intended outcome explicit.
>
> **Text alternative.** A two-column table contrasts a command to maintain one body shape with a description of task phases, supports, duration, variation, recovery, control, evidence state, and a named outcome. The literacy column does not claim to reveal internal loading or prescribe a correction.

## A public language for demand and options

Mechanical literacy uses a small set of ordinary questions. What does the task require? What carries or supports the person and the object? How long, how fast, and how often does the demand occur? What varies, and what remains constrained? What capacity and fatigue are relevant now? What recovery opportunities exist? Which alternatives are realistic in this setting?

These are not disguised measurements. *Demand* remains a broad task-level term when the internal force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, or deformation is unknown. *Support* includes the ground, furniture, tools, assistance, another person, or any other declared contact. *Option space* means the strategies a person can realistically use, not the maximum number of imaginable movements. Cost, safety, disability, pain, culture, schedule, work control, and competing duties can make a theoretical option unavailable.

Health literacy is not simply information deposited in an individual. The World Health Organization describes it as socially situated, shaped by communities, organizations, culture, and political conditions.[^28-02] The mechanical vocabulary proposed here should inherit that structural lesson, not the authority of the source. It has not yet been shown to improve comprehension, communication, agency, or health. It should be compared with simpler existing language and revised if people cannot use it without inventing hidden damage.

Education studies show why every step must be measured separately. A large, nonrandomized public back-pain campaign coincided with improved beliefs among members of the public and general practitioners, while descriptive changes in compensation claims could not be attributed securely to the campaign.[^28-03] A later cluster-randomized eHealth program did not improve back-pain beliefs, disability, or absenteeism relative to a digital information letter, despite a potentially favorable cost-utility estimate.[^28-04] Medium, audience, comparison, engagement, and outcome changed the result; neither study settles whether education in general “works.”

The same separation appears in a two-school-year program for children. Posture knowledge, observed handling behavior, and time in selected trunk and neck positions changed, while fear-avoidance beliefs did not and pain did not clearly improve.[^28-05] Knowledge, observed behavior, a posture-duration measure, belief, and symptom were five different outcomes. None inherited the result of another.

This chapter therefore distinguishes six destinations for the framework:

1. **Public education** asks whether an audience understands and can use a vocabulary without added fear, vigilance, stigma, or burden.
2. **Professional education** asks whether people in established disciplines communicate or reason more accurately within their scopes.
3. **Environmental design** asks whether changes to tasks and settings alter access, usability, exposure, performance, comfort, fatigue, or participation.
4. **Prevention** asks whether a named adverse endpoint changes in a named population over a stated time.
5. **Clinical use** would ask whether using the information in care improves a patient-facing decision or outcome relative to alternatives and harms.
6. **Research** asks whether constructs can be defined, measured, compared, and disfavored before wider use.

These are application domains: places where some part of the framework might eventually be used. They differ from Chapter 29's development tracks, which name the kind of work being done. Research, measurement, education, therapeutic development, implementation, and health-system development can operate across more than one domain. Public and professional education share an education track while retaining different audiences and outcomes; environmental design may require research, measurement, implementation, and system work. Chapter 29's research track has the narrower job of testing proposed physical and causal relations, even though research methods are required throughout the program.

The destinations can inform one another, but they do not share an automatic promotion path. Comprehension is not behavior. Behavior is not internal exposure. Exposure is not injury. A clinical application is not validated because the public language is understandable. A research measure is not useful merely because it is reproducible.

That separation changes how teaching should be built. A first lesson might ask learners to distinguish the task from the person performing it, name supports and constraints, and mark internal quantities as unknown. Its immediate test is whether they understood that distinction. A later exercise might ask whether the language transfers to a different task without becoming a fault-finding routine. A still later study might examine whether recognized options become usable options in a real setting. Each stage can fail independently. A lesson that is memorable but increases fear is not rescued by recall. A vocabulary that improves description but adds no useful information can remain educationally interesting without being promoted into professional or clinical use.

Mechanical literacy also needs a positive account of uncertainty. “Unknown” should not mean that a dangerous process is presumed but hidden. It can mean that no internal quantity was measured, that several distributions remain mechanically possible, or that the available detail is unnecessary for the question at hand. A learner who can stop at a good task description has succeeded; the lesson should not reward the invention of a deeper route merely because the framework contains one.

Different modes of explanation can serve different audiences. Diagrams may clarify contacts and boundaries. Ordinary metaphors may make duration or recovery easier to discuss. Tactile and embodied examples may help a person report experience. None should be presented as a direct measurement of internal force, stress, strain, pressure, or a force line. The representational form changes how an idea is encountered, not its evidence state.

## Professional education without a new jurisdiction

Physicians, nurses, therapists, movement professionals, occupational-health teams, ergonomists, engineers, coaches, designers, educators, and researchers encounter different portions of the same person–task–environment system. Their scopes, methods, and responsibilities remain distinct. A shared vocabulary might help them state what was observed, which quantity was measured, what outcome matters, and where a causal sequence remains incomplete. That is a coordination hypothesis, not a claim that every profession needs a larger dose of mechanics.

The World Health Organization treats interprofessional education and collaborative practice as strategies that must be adapted to local workforce and system needs.[^28-06] It does not endorse this book's grammar. A legitimate development question would compare the proposed vocabulary with existing documentation and handoff practices: Does it improve question quality or agreement about task and evidence state? Does it reduce unsupported inference or duplication? Does it instead add time, confusion, or scope crossing?

A pragmatic cluster-randomized low-back-pain program illustrates the distance between professional and patient outcomes. Clinicians' knowledge, attitudes, confidence, and guideline-concordant behavior improved, but the groups did not differ on the primary six-month disability measure or secondary patient outcomes.[^28-07] The program also changed management, so it is not a pure test of education. Its useful lesson is narrower: professional learning can succeed by its own measures without demonstrating superior patient recovery.

Clinical use is a separate destination for exactly this reason. Converting Chapter 27's questions into a form, score, examination sequence, or decision aid would require a declared clinical purpose, intended users, comparison, measurement properties, patient-facing consequences, burdens, and harms. This chapter offers none of those tools. Shared language should support existing responsibilities only after it shows added value within them.

## Modern exposure is a sequence, not a verdict

Screen work, manual work, caregiving, sport, transport, sitting, standing, and assistive-device use are activity categories. They are not doses and they are not diagnoses. Each can combine long duration, specialized repetition, constrained visual or hand demands, high pace, low control, limited variation, or insufficient recovery. Each can also support valued skill, participation, livelihood, comfort, training, or independence.

The mechanically relevant object is the sequence. A technology or setting shapes the task. The task and organization shape contacts, pace, repetition, variation, control, and available strategies. Those conditions create an exposure relative to a changing capacity and recovery context. The possible responses branch: useful adaptation, capable specialization, stable tolerance, fatigue, symptom modulation, injury, reduced participation, or no important effect. A later change in behavior, care, work, sleep, or environment feeds back into the next exposure.

Measured changes in an early node do not guarantee later changes. In a cluster-randomized office study, a multicomponent intervention reduced sitting at 12 months by about 22 minutes per day without a height-adjustable desk and about 64 minutes per day with one, relative to control. Most measured cardiometabolic, fatigue, musculoskeletal, and work outcomes showed no noticeable intervention effects, although selected wellbeing and pain measures changed modestly.[^28-08] The intervention changed sitting. That result neither makes sitting inherently pathological nor proves disease prevention.

Design can also redistribute demand. In a large participatory-ergonomics trial, selected decision-control measures improved modestly, reported exposure to awkward trunk postures increased, most physical and psychosocial exposure outcomes were null, and loss to follow-up was substantial.[^28-09] A companion analysis found no reduction in low-back- or neck-pain prevalence, intensity, or duration and no primary prevention effect; low-back-pain recovery improved while neck-pain recovery did not.[^28-10] The same program produced a small organizational benefit, an adverse exposure result, several nulls, and one favorable recovery result. Pooling them into a single verdict would erase what the study actually found.

The opening workstation makes the sequence concrete. During one short session, the available arrangement may be comfortable and effective. Across a longer shift, visual precision, task pace, forearm support, opportunities to change position, and accumulating fatigue may alter the demand. If the worker has control over timing and setup, the response options differ from those available under a fixed schedule. If a symptom appears, it may modify later behavior and exposure; it does not retrospectively identify the initial internal route. If no symptom appears, that absence does not prove that every measured exposure was negligible. The history has to be reconstructed at the resolution the claim requires.

This is also why repetition and variability are not simple opposites. Repetition can build skill and capacity, contribute to valued specialization, or concentrate exposure. Variability can distribute demand, disrupt precision, increase cognitive burden, or have no consequential effect. Recovery can occur during a task, between tasks, during sleep, after a schedule change, or through adaptation across longer periods. The useful question is not whether a category is good or bad. It is which demand, receiver, state, interval, and outcome are being compared.

> **Figure 28.2 — The branching modern-exposure sequence [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> work, care, transport, sport, technology, assistance, or environment
>     -> task duration, pace, repetition, support, variation, and control
>     -> external demand and available strategies
>     -> exposure relative to changing capacity and recovery
>     -> useful adaptation | capable specialization | stable tolerance
>        fatigue | symptom modulation | injury | participation change
>        no important effect
>     -> later behavior, care, environment, resources, and bodily state
>     -> next task and exposure
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Modern context changes boundary conditions, but its consequences branch. Every arrow requires its own observation, measure, or stated uncertainty.
>
> **Text alternative.** A feedback sequence begins with work, care, transport, sport, technology, assistance, or environment. It passes through task dose and control, external demand and strategies, and exposure relative to capacity and recovery. It then branches to adaptation, specialization, stable tolerance, fatigue, symptom modulation, injury, participation change, or no important effect before feeding later state back into the next exposure.

This sequence restores a serious concern about contemporary life without making modernity a disease. It asks better questions about prolonged tasks and constrained options. It also permits the answer that a specialized pattern is capable, an assistance strategy is enabling, a measured change has no health consequence, or a proposed mechanical contribution has low priority for the outcome under study.

## Design changes the available system

Human factors and ergonomics already treats performance and wellbeing as properties of interactions among people and other system elements, spanning physical, cognitive, and organizational domains.[^28-11] Work-system guidance places people, tasks, tools, technologies, organization, and environment inside one design problem and emphasizes worker participation, individual differences, continuing evaluation, and redesign.[^28-12] This broader boundary prevents “ergonomics” from collapsing into chair dimensions.

For this chapter, the design system contains five coupled elements:

```text
person and changing state
    <-> task and performance requirement
    <-> assistance, tools, and supports
    <-> organization, schedule, resources, and control
    <-> built, social, and information environment
```

No element is presumed to be the fault or the correction target. A change in support may reduce one demand and increase reach, pressure, visual effort, cognitive burden, cost, or dependence on unavailable assistance. A standard arrangement can fit the tall bifocal wearer at the opening station while blocking the wheelchair user's approach. Moving the screen may improve one person's visual relation and worsen another's. The lesson is not that standards are useless. It is that standardization, fit, reported comfort, measured exposure, access, and prevention are different objects.

Control should follow agency. A person cannot choose staffing, production pace, procurement, transport, classroom furniture, or whether a public counter is accessible. Occupational-health guidance therefore prioritizes eliminating, substituting, or redesigning harmful work conditions before relying only on education that asks individuals to manage them.[^28-13] Education can still help people name demands and participate in redesign. It should not become a low-cost substitute for equipment, assistance, schedule control, or source reduction.

The intervention evidence again resists a slogan. In a one-year randomized trial among call-center operators, forearm support was associated with less selected upper-body pain and a lower incidence of a physician-ascertained neck or shoulder disorder.[^28-14] This is a meaningful positive result for a specified support, workforce, disorder definition, and period. It does not identify universal equipment dimensions or a unique internal mechanism.

Other programs produced null or mixed results. A participatory intervention in 119 kitchens generated and implemented hundreds of changes but did not improve pain, local fatigue, musculoskeletal sick leave, or perceived physical workload during intervention or follow-up.[^28-15] In a childcare trial, physical exertion and several pain outcomes did not differ, sickness absence decreased, and self-efficacy worsened slightly.[^28-16] Activity, participation, and implementation are not themselves efficacy. Nor does a null trial establish that participation or design can never help.

External support deserves particular care in this model. Support changes the boundary conditions under which a task is performed; it does not automatically reduce total demand or signal incapacity. A handrail can enable participation. A backrest can make sustained attention possible. A lifting device can shift demand from one person while introducing coordination, time, or access requirements elsewhere. Removing support can be useful in a training setting and exclusionary in a public one. The value belongs to the declared task and outcome, not to an abstract ranking of supported and unsupported bodies.

The same applies to option count. More theoretical alternatives do not always improve a system. Too many adjustments can increase cognitive work, delay a time-sensitive task, or place the burden of solving a design problem on the user. One stable strategy may be highly capable. What matters is whether the available strategies are usable, compatible with the person's priorities, and revisable when state or task changes. Option space is a description of feasible relations, not a health score.

Accessibility changes the model rather than decorating it. The United Nations distinguishes universal design from reasonable accommodation in a particular case and explicitly preserves assistive devices for people who need them.[^28-17] The World Health Organization's classification of functioning places participation and environmental factors inside its account of functioning and disability.[^28-18] Its disability policy calls for consultation and inclusion across design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation, while joint WHO–UNICEF guidance treats assistive technology as support for functioning, participation, and inclusion amid large access gaps.[^28-19] None of these sources supplies a mechanical outcome. Together they prevent unsupported movement, symmetry, youth, or independence from becoming the hidden design standard.

> **Figure 28.3 — Environment and realistic option space [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | System element | Variables that can change | Result to examine separately |
> |---|---|---|
> | Person and changing state | fatigue, pain, pregnancy, disability, illness, skill, preference | report, effort, tolerance, agency |
> | Task | object, sequence, precision, duration, pace, repetition | performance, exposure, error, fatigue |
> | Assistance, tools, and supports | another person, device, contact, automation, information | access, usability, redistributed demand, dependence |
> | Organization | staffing, scheduling, rotation, authority, resources | control, recovery opportunity, participation, burden |
> | Built, social, and information environment | reach, clearance, visual relation, circulation, language, digital access | fit for different users, exclusion, tradeoffs |
>
> Standardized arrangement A -> fits user 1 and supports the task
>                            -> constrains user 2's approach or visual relation
>
> **Caption.** Option space is practical, not abstract. A design changes several relations at once and can expand access for one person while transferring demand or narrowing access for another.
>
> **Text alternative.** A five-row table couples the person, task, assistance, organization, and environment. Each row distinguishes design variables from outcomes. A final branch shows the same standardized arrangement fitting one user while constraining another.

## Prevention has six different objects

The word *prevention* is unfinished until its object is named. A defensible claim also names the population, baseline state, intervention, comparator, time at risk or follow-up, measurement, implementation, adverse outcomes, and relevant competing events. Lower-burden outcomes such as comprehension, recognized options, comfort, fatigue, or task tolerance can matter greatly. They should be called by their names rather than promoted into prevention of an unspecified harm.

The six prevention objects used here are exposure, symptom, injury or defined disorder, disability, recurrence, and participation. They are not steps in one guaranteed chain and they are not ordered by human value. Each has a positive or mixed example, a null, adverse, or boundary result, and a conclusion it cannot inherit.

The required record changes slightly with each object. Exposure needs a defined quantity or behavior and stated measurement conditions. A symptom needs its incidence, severity, duration, interference, or recovery identified. An injury or defined disorder needs a case definition, ascertainment method, exposure opportunity, and competing events. Disability needs a specified function and context. Recurrence needs a recovered baseline, exact event definition, surveillance interval, and censoring rules. Participation needs a person-valued life situation, access conditions, and some account of sustainability. Those differences are not clerical. They determine what event has occurred and which comparison is legitimate.

> **Figure 28.4 — Six outcome-specific prevention cells [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Prevention object | Positive or mixed result | Null, adverse, or boundary result | Result that does not transfer |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Exposure** | An office intervention reduced measured sitting | Most selected health and work outcomes did not change; another participatory program increased one awkward-posture exposure | symptom, injury, disability, disease, or mechanism |
> | **Symptom** | Forearm support reduced selected upper-body pain; one program improved low-back-pain recovery | Several participatory programs were null for multiple pain outcomes, and neck recovery did not improve | diagnosed injury, historical cause, tissue route, or general health |
> | **Injury or defined disorder** | Forearm support reduced one physician-ascertained neck or shoulder disorder in one workforce | Pain, posture, comfort, and exposure results are not injury results | transfer to another task, device, population, or disease |
> | **Disability** | Integrated care improved function and accelerated sustainable return to work | Professional education changed clinician outcomes without changing patient disability | pain reduction, isolated ergonomic efficacy, or mechanical cause |
> | **Recurrence** | An individualized walking-and-education program delayed a defined activity-limiting low-back-pain recurrence | Components could not be separated, and lower-extremity adverse events were more numerous | primary prevention, education alone, universal dose, or preferred configuration |
> | **Participation** | Integrated care improved sustainable return to work | A disability workplace intervention did not improve sustainable employment and slightly worsened mental health under low delivery | symptom or tissue improvement, unsupported independence, or universal system benefit |
>
> Every row additionally requires: population | comparator | timeframe | measure | implementation | harms.
>
> **Caption.** Favorable evidence in one cell does not fill another. Null and adverse results remain visible beside positive results rather than being averaged into a generic prevention claim.
>
> **Text alternative.** Exactly six rows separate exposure, symptom, injury or defined disorder, disability, recurrence, and participation. Each row contains a favorable or mixed result, a null, adverse, or limiting result, and a stronger conclusion that cannot be inherited. A footer requires population, comparator, timeframe, measurement, implementation, and harms for every row.

Two examples show why the last three cells must remain distinct. An integrated workplace and graded-activity program for workers with chronic low-back pain shortened time to sustainable return to work and improved function, while pain did not differ.[^28-20] Participation and disability changed without a corresponding pain result, and the multicomponent design does not isolate an ergonomic mechanism.

In another trial involving people with work disabilities, a participatory workplace intervention did not improve sustainable employment, mental-health scores were slightly worse, and delivery was low because the workplace component generally could not begin until employment had already been obtained.[^28-21] The result does not argue against accommodation or disability inclusion. It shows how program logic and implementation can fail before a desired participation outcome is reached.

Recurrence requires its own baseline and event definition. In a randomized trial of adults recovered from nonspecific low-back pain, an individualized progressive walking-and-education program delayed activity-limiting recurrence, while lower-extremity adverse events were more numerous in the intervention group and the contributions of walking and education could not be separated.[^28-22] This is evidence for that intervention and that recurrence endpoint. It is not an instruction to walk, a universal dose, primary prevention, or evidence for a preferred body configuration.

An honest prevention narrative can therefore end in several ways. A proposal may change the intended outcome. It may change an early exposure while leaving later outcomes null. It may improve one outcome and worsen another. It may be sound in principle but delivered too weakly to test. It may transfer demand or burden to another person or part of the system. Or it may add no value compared with simpler existing practice. Those endings are information, not inconveniences to be hidden behind a broad claim of benefit.

The figure deliberately does not add a generic disease cell. A disease-prevention claim would require a condition-specific causal and intervention chain, including biological, psychological, social, developmental, environmental, and medical alternatives appropriate to that condition. It cannot be manufactured by extending a favorable exposure or symptom result upward. Population benefit would add another layer: reach, distribution of benefit and harm, cost, adoption, sustainability, and the consequences of displacing other programs. Naming those higher burdens preserves the ambition without pretending that the present studies have met it.

## Access, control, and the cost of awareness

The practical option space depends on who controls the conditions. Disability, pregnancy, aging, chronic illness, pain, fatigue, body diversity, language, culture, job security, caregiving, finances, digital access, and safety can change both the feasible strategies and the meaning of an outcome. A design that increases theoretical choice while requiring money, disclosure, unpaid time, or unavailable assistance has not necessarily increased realistic options.

Participation is an outcome in its own right. It is not a proxy for symptom relief, tissue state, independence, or conformity to one movement strategy. Assistance, rest, sitting, stable specialization, and external support can be capable solutions. A person should not have to display or correct a body to earn access.

Participatory design is valuable as a way of discovering needs and sharing authority; it is not an efficacy guarantee. Review must ask who chose the outcome, who could refuse, who controlled resources, which proposed changes were implemented, and whose costs increased. An average benefit can coexist with exclusion or harm in a subgroup.

The distinction among universal design, accommodation, and assistance helps keep responsibility distributed. A broadly accessible baseline may reduce the number of barriers many people encounter. It will not eliminate every need for an individual modification or a particular support. Accommodation responds to a person's actual relation with a task and setting. Assistance can be part of an effective configuration rather than a temporary concession on the way to unsupported performance. The three approaches overlap in practice, but treating them as interchangeable can hide whose needs remain unmet.

Institutional control also changes the ethics of advice. A suggestion that is low burden for someone with flexible time and private space can be impossible for a worker whose pace is monitored, a student who cannot leave class, or a caregiver who cannot pause a transfer. Asking such a person to manage the exposure personally can create guilt without changing the relevant condition. The analysis should move upstream until it reaches a variable that an individual, team, organization, or public body can actually alter.

Monitoring deserves the same scrutiny. Digital systems can help recognize hazards, but occupational-safety guidance also identifies risks involving surveillance, privacy, data ownership, discrimination, algorithmic management, and replacement of collective controls with individual monitoring.[^28-23] Public-health-surveillance ethics adds duties of necessity, proportionality, autonomy, equity, transparency, and engagement.[^28-24] These principles do not make every sensor harmful. They do rule out the assumption that more awareness is automatically benign.

A monitoring proposal should name the hazard and outcome, explain why direct design change is insufficient, identify who owns and can act on the data, and include refusal, correction, deletion, and redress. It should test false alerts, missingness, unequal performance, stigma, vigilance, and whether feedback expands options or commands conformity. A posture alert that makes a worker continuously correct the body while production pace remains unchanged may transfer responsibility without controlling the source.

The same adverse pathway applies to public education. Mechanical language can enlarge agency when it helps people describe demand and request change. It can narrow agency when it teaches them to scan for invisible damage, interpret fatigue as failure, or feel responsible for conditions they cannot control. Comprehension, burden, vigilance, shame, and blame therefore belong among the first outcomes of any mechanical-literacy program.

## What belongs to development, not personal correction

Book I can responsibly offer a descriptive language and a set of design questions. It can argue that duration, repetition, variability, support, capacity, recovery, and control deserve explicit attention. It can show that environments alter boundary conditions and that prevention claims must name their outcomes. These are substantive claims, but they do not complete the applied program.

Individual tests, correction cues, posture prescriptions, equipment specifications, movement doses, exercise progressions, posterior-engagement instruction, force-line imagery, breathing practices, bandhas, traditional correspondences, and self-experimentation belong to later development and later books. So do therapeutic use and condition-specific prevention. Their preservation matters: deferral is not rejection. It prevents general literacy from acting as unearned evidence for a personal intervention.

The larger institutional ambition also remains alive. Schools, workplaces, communities, professional curricula, health systems, and public agencies are possible sites of development. Work on complex interventions emphasizes context, program theory, stakeholders, uncertainty, refinement, evaluation, and implementation rather than a one-way march from idea to scale.[^28-25] Applied here, the sequence begins with co-defining an audience and problem; testing comprehension, accessibility, and unintended effects; examining feasibility and burden in a bounded setting; comparing the proposal with existing practice; and evaluating only the outcome actually claimed. Revision or withdrawal remains a legitimate result.

Research has a distinct role across that sequence. It can define constructs, compare plain language, test whether observers classify the same task similarly, measure exposure under declared conditions, and examine whether a proposed change reaches the intended endpoint. It can also discover that the framework adds no value, works only in a narrower setting, excludes an audience, or produces an adverse interpretation. Those results should route back to the component that failed. A null comprehension result changes the teaching object; it does not refute all environmental design. A null health result after a successful exposure change weakens the later link; it does not erase the measured exposure result.

Therapeutic development and health-system development require still different records. A therapeutic proposal needs a population, mechanism, dose, comparator, contraindications, adverse events, and patient-valued outcome. A health-system proposal needs governance, workforce, workflow, cost, equity, and comparison with existing services. Chapter 29 will separate those tracks so that a promising educational result cannot be used as unearned support for treatment or system change.

Return to the shared computer station. Mechanical literacy does not reveal one correct arrangement. It makes the system legible enough to ask better questions: which task phase matters, who can use the support, what can be adjusted, what cannot, which demand moves elsewhere, and what outcome will show whether the change helped. One response might alter the environment. Another might provide assistance or accommodation. Another might leave the arrangement alone because it already works for the person and task. None requires a hidden diagnosis.

The present contribution is a vocabulary for demand and options, a systems boundary for design, and an outcome-specific discipline for prevention. Its strongest claim is not that education or ergonomics will produce health. It is that a serious program must keep comprehension, behavior, exposure, injury, symptom, participation, and system outcomes from silently substituting for one another. Chapter 29 inherits the next question: how should the separate research, measurement, education, therapeutic-development, implementation, and health-system tracks be organized so that each can fail, learn, and advance without borrowing another track's result?
