Low delivery limits interpretation, and the result does not argue against accommodation, disability inclusion, supported employment, or participation in general.

[^28-22]: Natasha C. Pocovi et al., “Effectiveness and Cost-Effectiveness of an Individualised, Progressive Walking and Education Intervention for the Prevention of Low Back Pain Recurrence in Australia (WalkBack): A Randomised Controlled Trial,” *Lancet* 404, no. 10448 (2024): 134–144, [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00755-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00755-4). The trial does not isolate education, test primary prevention, validate a universal movement dose, or establish a preferred configuration.

[^28-23]: European Agency for Safety and Health at Work, *Smart Digital Monitoring Systems for Occupational Safety and Health: Uses and Challenges—Summary* (Luxembourg: Publications Office of the European Union, 2022), [official PDF](https://osha.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/Smart-digital-monitoring-systems-uses-challenges-summary_EN.pdf). The guidance identifies governance risks and possible benefits; it does not determine the effect of every monitoring system.

[^28-24]: World Health Organization, *WHO Guidelines on Ethical Issues in Public Health Surveillance* (Geneva: World Health Organization, 2017), [official publication](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512657). The guidance supplies general ethical duties, not workplace-specific legal advice or proof that a selected program is effective.

[^28-25]: Kathryn Skivington et al., “A New Framework for Developing and Evaluating Complex Interventions: Update of Medical Research Council Guidance,” *BMJ* 374 (2021): n2061, [doi:10.1136/bmj.n2061](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.n2061). The framework does not endorse this program or prescribe one mandatory development sequence.

# Chapter 29 — Building the research and development program

## One pathway, six different questions

Chapter 24 followed a focal relation in which surrounding anatomy and a later arterial state could be observed together, while the repeated deformation proposed to connect them remained reconstructed. That missing interval is not merely an imperfection in one narrative. It is a productive object of work. The question is what kind.

A mechanics study could ask whether a declared boundary condition deforms the wall during a specified task. A measurement study could ask whether that deformation can be acquired reliably and whether the signal represents the intended construct. An education study could ask whether learners distinguish surrounding demand, wall response, lumen, flow, symptom, and diagnosis. Therapeutic development could ask whether changing a declared boundary condition improves an outcome that matters to patients and whether the proposed intermediate changes with it. Implementation research could ask whether a sufficiently mature method can be delivered with fidelity, access, and acceptable burden. Health-system development could ask whether the accumulated component adds enough value to justify changes in training, workflow, financing, or policy.

Those are six different questions. Their answers can inform one another, but none contains the others. A reproducible deformation does not create a clinical measure. A reliable measure does not identify a diagnosis. A well-understood explanation does not improve health by comprehension alone. A beneficial intervention does not prove the mechanism proposed for it. Successful delivery does not establish benefit, and widespread adoption does not establish system value.

The framework developed in this book therefore needs more than a list of promising studies. It needs a development architecture in which every project earns a declared output and in which the limit of that output travels with it. Existing research frameworks already reject a simple one-way march from idea to implementation. Updated Medical Research Council guidance treats development, feasibility, evaluation, and implementation as iterative work shaped throughout by context, program theory, stakeholders, uncertainty, refinement, and economic considerations.[^29-01] The National Institutes of Health Stage Model likewise permits recursive movement among intervention generation, mechanism work, efficacy, effectiveness, and implementation rather than prescribing one irreversible sequence.[^29-02] Neither framework supplies the exact architecture used here. They establish the more general point: different kinds of maturity can develop, fail, and return upstream without rising together.

This chapter organizes the project into exactly six tracks: research, measurement, education, therapeutic development, implementation, and health-system development. The tracks form a network, not a staircase. The aim is not to reduce ambition. It is to let the program become more ambitious without allowing one attractive result to carry claims it never tested.

## A portfolio, not a staircase

Each track has a distinct immediate question, output, and stopping condition. A project can occupy more than one track, but only when its aims and results remain separable. A study might measure both patient outcomes and delivery fidelity, for example. That combination does not turn one outcome into evidence for the other.

> **Figure 29.1 — Six independently gated tracks [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Track | Immediate question | Immediate output | Example stop or return |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **1. Research** | Does a declared relation occur under stated conditions? | bounded finding, estimate, model comparison, or revised pathway | relation absent, opposite, nonunique, or local only |
> | **2. Measurement** | Can a construct be acquired and interpreted for one declared use? | qualified measure with uncertainty and use limit | reliable but nonspecific, reactive, burdensome, or not decision-relevant |
> | **3. Education** | Does teaching change a selected learning or communication outcome safely? | audience- and outcome-specific educational result | liked but inaccurate, fear-inducing, exclusionary, or no better than existing language |
> | **4. Therapeutic development** | Does a candidate help a named population on a declared outcome with acceptable harms? | staged feasibility, safety, efficacy, effectiveness, or mechanism result | no benefit, excess harm, mechanism discordance, or a better existing option |
> | **5. Implementation** | Can a sufficiently mature object be delivered in a real setting? | setting-specific reach, fidelity, access, cost, and sustainability result | poor delivery, inequitable reach, excessive burden, or loss of core function |
> | **6. Health-system development** | Do mature components add enough value to justify durable institutional change? | transparent training, workflow, financing, or policy decision | duplication, low-value care, worsened access, or no system benefit |
>
> ```text
> established mechanics ───────────────> education
>         │                                  │
>         v                                  v
> research <──────────────> measurement    implementation
>         │                       │          │       ^
>         v                       └──────────┘       │ return for redesign
> therapeutic development ──────────────────────────┘
>         │
>         v   only when the proposed use is mature
> health-system development
>
> Every node can revise, stop, retire, or re-enter. No arrow is automatic.
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The six tracks coordinate through conditional handoffs. Education can develop from established material without a novel measure; a research measure need never become clinical; implementation can return a mature object upstream. Placement in the network does not establish readiness.
>
> **Text alternative.** A six-row table gives research, measurement, education, therapeutic development, implementation, and health-system development separate questions, outputs, and stopping conditions. A network beneath it shows several optional forward and return paths rather than one ascending pipeline.

The matrix makes two kinds of dependency visible. Some are necessary. Implementation requires an object mature enough to deliver, and health-system development requires components whose benefit, burden, and intended use have been characterized well enough to compare with existing practice. Other dependencies are merely useful. Education can teach established distinctions before a new sensor exists. Measurement can qualify a quantity for research even if no intervention follows. Research can disfavor a proposed mechanism while an independently supported educational tool remains useful.

For that reason, the program has no single maturity score. Readiness always completes a sentence: ready to describe under one protocol, ready to compare groups, ready to test a mediator, ready to teach to one audience, ready to evaluate for benefit, ready to deliver in one setting, or ready to inform a system decision. The same object can be mature for one use and immature for another. A motion estimate might be adequate for comparing two laboratory tasks while remaining too reactive or nonspecific for clinical interpretation. A plain-language explanation might be ready for a comprehension study while the underlying authorial hypothesis remains untested. Recording those unequal states is more informative than placing the project on one ladder.

Multi-track projects need the same discipline. Their aims should be declared separately, their methods assigned to the outputs they can support, and their stopping conditions applied independently. If one component fails, the others do not inherit failure automatically; if one succeeds, the others do not inherit success. A combined design is useful when shared recruitment, timing, or context improves the questions. It becomes dangerous when logistical proximity is mistaken for causal or evidentiary unity.

An output should be judged by the decision it was designed to inform. A precise instrument can fail as a clinical tool and succeed as a laboratory measure. A curriculum can improve causal-language accuracy without changing behavior. A beneficial intervention can be worth preserving after its proposed mediator fails. This use-specific account of success is the organizing principle for all six tracks.

## Track 1: Research

Here, the research track has the narrower job of testing proposed physical and causal relations; every other track also requires research methods appropriate to its own question. This track begins with one declared relation along the book's causal chain: task and environment, configuration and available paths, external demand and internal distribution, local exposure, material or biological response, and a later finding, symptom, function, participation, or outcome. A study should state which link it observes, which it measures or calculates, which it represents with a model, and which it leaves open.

The six adverse-organization families developed in Part III generate concrete questions. Does a change in geometry redistribute a defined force or moment? Does an interface concentrate stress or strain under a stated condition? Does a segment fail to maintain a relation during a task? Does timing alter a handoff between named carriers? Does an imposed boundary maintain deformation or reduce excursion? Does a compensation shift exposure, preserve performance, or do both at different times? These are candidate relations, not generic searches for proof that biomechanics matters.

Design follows the relation. Anatomical and material studies can establish that a structure or property exists without establishing clinical importance. Perturbation and within-person studies can compare distribution under declared tasks without recovering a complete internal route from surface motion. Longitudinal observations can place exposure before response while leaving causal alternatives. Simultaneous multiregion measurement can test a proposed carrier; adjacency or shared timing alone cannot. A prospective comparison can ask whether mechanical history adds information beyond an existing model, but association and added information remain different from decision value.

Exploratory work belongs in this program. So does confirmatory work. The distinction should be recorded before interpretation rather than reconstructed after an appealing result. Preregistration can help separate planned tests from exploratory analyses, although it cannot repair an invalid construct or poor execution.[^29-03] The aim is not procedural purity. It is to prevent an observation that generated a hypothesis from reappearing as if it had independently confirmed it.

A good research question also says what would lower its priority. If predicted redistribution is absent across an adequate range, the relation should narrow or retire within that domain. If several configurations produce equivalent selected outcomes, the result is nonunique; it does not select one route. If a local change is observed but no regional carrier is measured, the result stops locally. If compensation lowers rather than raises exposure, the model must retain that protective result. An unmeasured hidden whole-body mechanism cannot become the default destination for every null.

Nonsignificance alone is not evidence of equivalence. Equivalence testing requires a substantively justified range of effects small enough to treat as unimportant and a design precise enough to test that range.[^29-04] The program should therefore distinguish a negative result within a prespecified meaningful range from an inconclusive result caused by poor precision, inadequate exposure, missing data, or a weak construct. “Further research” becomes useful only when the unresolved quantity and the next discriminating design can be named.

The research track succeeds when it makes the causal chain more specific. That success can be positive, negative, mixed, nonunique, or local. Its product is a better-bounded relation—not an automatic measure, diagnosis, intervention, or institutional claim.

## Track 2: Measurement

Measurement turns a proposed quantity or construct into an inspectable acquisition and interpretation problem. The first question is not whether a device produces a number. It is what that number is meant to represent, within which system, at what scale and phase, under which protocol, and for what use.

At least seven claims should remain separate. The signal can be acquired. Its disagreement and error can be estimated. It represents the intended construct. It distinguishes relevant states or changes when the construct changes. The change is interpretable relative to error and a meaningful reference. Using it improves a declared decision. Its burden and reactivity are acceptable. A project may support one claim and fail the next.

Measurement science offers established distinctions without supplying a ready-made load-routing instrument. The COSMIN taxonomy separates reliability, measurement error, validity, and responsiveness while also treating interpretability and feasibility as distinct concerns.[^29-05] Reporting guidance for reliability and agreement studies requires the sample, observers, repetitions, measurement process, and estimates to be explicit; repeatability is not truth.[^29-06] The living FDA–NIH BEST glossary makes context of use central and distinguishes biomarkers, clinical outcome assessments, endpoints, validation, and clinical utility.[^29-07] These frameworks arose in particular measurement domains. Their distinctions transfer more readily than their thresholds.

A minimum record for a mechanical measure names the construct, unit, direction, boundary, scale, phase, and time. It declares whether the intended use is description, comparison, state tracking, mechanism testing, prognosis, diagnosis, decision support, or outcome measurement. It specifies acquisition, calibration, preprocessing, missingness, reference, known confounds, error, generalizability, and decision consequence. It also asks whose bodies, tasks, devices, assistance, and settings were represented.

Burden is part of validity for use. A sensor can alter the movement it intends to observe. Repeated imaging can impose cost and access barriers. A monitoring system can change attention, behavior, privacy, and power. A composite score can conceal incompatible quantities behind an apparently simple result. Digital precision should never substitute for a defined construct.

This chapter does not create a whole-body efficiency score, a misrouting score, a diagnostic threshold, or a treatment-selection instrument. Those objects first require an operational state, a comparison class, transformation rules, measurement properties, and disfavoring evidence. A measure can mature for one narrow research use without becoming a proxy for the framework or the person.

## Track 3: Education

Chapter 28 proposed mechanical literacy as a way to describe task, support, duration, repetition, variability, recovery, control, options, and uncertainty. The education track asks whether a selected audience actually learns or communicates something better through that language. It does not use assent to the framework as an endpoint.

The first record names what is taught, to whom, compared with what, for which direct outcome, over what interval, and with which possible harms. Public audiences, patients, clinicians, movement professionals, engineers, researchers, and educators cannot be treated as interchangeable. Health literacy is shaped by organizational resources and social conditions as well as individual knowledge and competencies; responsibility for intelligibility and access therefore belongs partly to the system providing information.[^29-08]

Educational outcomes form no automatic chain. Satisfaction, recall, comprehension, reasoning accuracy, communication, behavior, clinical outcome, and system outcome are separate. Medical-education research has usefully distinguished studies that describe what occurred, compare whether an approach worked, and investigate how or why it worked.[^29-09] A memorable phrase can fail an accuracy test. Accurate classification can fail to change communication. Changed communication can fail to affect care. Each result remains valuable at the level it measured.

For this project, candidate direct outcomes include whether learners distinguish task from configuration, external demand from internal distribution, and local exposure from symptom or diagnosis. Another study could test whether they identify a missing carrier in a body-wide account, ask a better load-history question, calibrate uncertainty, or stop a mechanical explanation when it adds little. These are educational questions about the framework, not evidence that the framework's untested mechanisms are true.

Adverse outcomes belong beside benefit. Teaching can increase fear, pain vigilance, shame, body surveillance, jargon burden, professional overconfidence, or the belief that one body shape is correct. It can exclude disabled or assisted movement, erase useful discipline-specific language, or shift responsibility from an institution to an individual. A well-liked program that does not improve accuracy is an educational null. A program that improves knowledge while increasing fear is mixed or adverse. Either result changes the curriculum, audience, or claimed use; neither decides the underlying mechanics.

Education can therefore move early and independently. Established mechanics, evidence-state distinctions, and person–task–environment reasoning can be taught without waiting for a novel measure or therapy. What cannot move with them is an unearned promise of behavior change, clinical competence, health benefit, or prevention.

## Track 4: Therapeutic development

The wider project contains a range of assessment and practice ideas. Preserving them as development objects is different from presenting them for use. Therapeutic development begins only after a candidate has a declared population, purpose, comparator, provider, outcome, time horizon, and safety burden. Book I supplies no examination sequence, corrective cue, exercise, breathing practice, movement system, protocol, diagnosis, or treatment recommendation.

The first task is to make the candidate reproducible enough to evaluate. TIDieR asks authors to describe why an intervention is proposed, what it contains, who provides it, how and where it is delivered, when and how much is given, how it is tailored or modified, and what fidelity is achieved.[^29-10] Complete description does not establish benefit. It prevents an intervention name from hiding several materially different objects.

Prospective trial protocols and complete reports have their own obligations. SPIRIT requires the intended questions, methods, outcomes, analyses, oversight, and registration of randomized trials to be specified transparently.[^29-11] CONSORT requires corresponding clarity in reports, including participant flow, outcomes, analyses, protocol information, and deviations.[^29-12] Neither standard can turn an unsuitable design into good evidence, but both make it harder for the tested object or endpoint to change silently after results appear.

Benefit and harm must be sought with comparable seriousness. Updated CONSORT harms guidance emphasizes planned ascertainment, analysis, and reporting, including how recurrent and serious events were handled.[^29-13] “No harm observed” is interpretable only in relation to how harm was elicited, how many people were observed, and for how long. Access, cost, disability, language, cultural fit, professional scope, co-interventions, adherence, and the burden of repeated attention also belong to the candidate's record.

An outcome effect and a mechanism effect are different objects. Process evaluation separates delivery, mechanisms of impact, and context.[^29-14] Causal mediation analysis adds assumptions about how a proposed intermediate and outcome are related; measuring both before and after an intervention is not sufficient by itself.[^29-15] If function improves while the proposed mechanical mediator does not, the benefit should be retained and the mechanism claim weakened. If the mediator changes while a patient-important outcome does not, the mechanical result remains and therapeutic use remains unsupported.

Study purpose also affects what can be inferred. PRECIS-2 asks designers to align eligibility, recruitment, setting, organization, delivery, adherence, follow-up, outcome, and analysis with a more explanatory or pragmatic aim.[^29-16] A tightly controlled study can ask whether a candidate produces a change under selected conditions without establishing ordinary-care effectiveness. A pragmatic study can estimate performance in a real setting without isolating a mechanism. The useful design is the one fitted to the immediate question.

Therapeutic development is therefore not the track where a plausible mechanical idea becomes advice. It is where the proposed object becomes specific enough to fail. Feasibility, safety, efficacy, effectiveness, mechanism, comparative value, and scope can then mature independently.

## Track 5: Implementation

Implementation begins with a sufficiently mature object and asks what happens when it enters a real setting. The object might be an educational module, a research or clinical measurement procedure, an environmental design, or an intervention. The implementation strategy is separate: training, facilitation, documentation, reminders, financing, staffing, workflow redesign, or another means of delivery must be named rather than folded into the object.

Implementation outcomes are not clinical outcomes. A widely used taxonomy distinguishes acceptability, adoption, appropriateness, feasibility, fidelity, implementation cost, penetration, and sustainability from service and patient outcomes.[^29-17] RE-AIM separately draws attention to reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, maintenance, and the representativeness of both participants and settings.[^29-18] CFIR organizes possible determinants across the intervention, outer setting, inner setting, people, and implementation process.[^29-19] These frameworks help organize questions; completing one does not prove successful or equitable delivery.

The implementation record asks who is offered the object, who is excluded, which settings adopt it, what core function is preserved, what form changes, who controls adaptation, what resources are required, whose workload increases, and whether effects persist. It compares the proposal with the actual existing workflow, not with an imagined system that contains no mechanical reasoning. It also examines unintended effects: surveillance, stigma, data extraction, professional boundary conflict, low-value follow-up, displacement of effective care, and unequal access.

Effectiveness and implementation questions can be examined in one prospectively designed study. Hybrid designs formalize that possibility while retaining separate aims and outcomes.[^29-20] If an effective object has poor reach or fidelity, implementation can return it for redesign without erasing the efficacy estimate within its tested domain. If delivery is strong but patient outcomes are null, adoption cannot rescue effectiveness. If benefit appears despite low measured fidelity, the definition of fidelity, the theory of the object, and alternative contributors all require review.

Equity is not a late subgroup table. The Health Equity Implementation Framework places recipients, providers, the encounter, organizational context, and wider social conditions inside the implementation problem.[^29-21] For this project, that means asking who defined the target, whose movement was treated as the reference, who can refuse monitoring, who bears time and financial costs, who has access to alternatives, and who controls the resulting data and decisions.

An implementation failure is information about a relation among object, strategy, setting, and people. It does not automatically disprove the underlying mechanism. Successful implementation is equally bounded. It shows that something was delivered under stated conditions, not that it should be adopted everywhere or that it produced system value.

## Track 6: Health-system development

The project's institutional ambition is direct: medicine may eventually benefit from a more coherent account of demand, routing, exposure, capacity, recovery, and person–task–environment relations across existing disciplines. That horizon is not permanently limited to a minor adjunct. Its present posture is additive and comparative because durable change must show what it adds, duplicates, displaces, or worsens.

Health-system development begins with mature components rather than with allegiance to a doctrine. Possible objects include a shared vocabulary that improves a declared reasoning outcome, a measure qualified for a particular decision, an intervention with favorable benefit and harm relative to alternatives, or an implementation strategy that reaches its intended population without disproportionate burden. No single specialty, device, assessment, therapy, traditional system, or preferred-state model needs to own the field.

Decision frameworks make the additional burden visible. GRADE Evidence-to-Decision work for health-system and public-health questions considers effects, resources, equity, acceptability, feasibility, and implementation while making the basis of judgments explicit.[^29-22] The World Health Organization describes health-technology assessment as a multidisciplinary evaluation of direct and indirect consequences for policy decisions.[^29-23] Such frameworks structure judgment. They do not fill missing evidence, choose society's values, or favor this project in advance.

A system proposal must therefore address opportunity cost. Training consumes professional time. Documentation can displace attention. Measurement infrastructure creates financial, privacy, and maintenance burdens. A new label can trigger unnecessary follow-up. A service can fragment care or duplicate work already performed well. An apparently equitable program can distribute benefit, inconvenience, risk, and decision power unevenly.

*Overdiagnosis* has a narrow meaning: a condition is identified correctly but would not have caused symptoms or harm during the person's lifetime. It should not be used as an umbrella for every project risk.[^29-24] False positives, misdiagnosis, detection of inconsequential variation, overtreatment, surveillance burden, and low-value care should be named separately when those are the actual concerns.

System development can begin incrementally. Shared language, research infrastructure, data standards, or interdisciplinary questions may warrant evaluation before disease-specific prevention or reimbursement claims. Later milestones might include improved histories, validated measures, effective and equitable interventions, better coordination, justified design changes, and cumulative evidence strong enough to revise broader medical models. Each milestone is a new empirical and normative question, not a reward granted for completing the previous track.

The overhaul ambition survives precisely because it has stopping conditions. A component that adds no value over existing care should not displace it. A system that expands low-value measurement, worsens access, or imposes more burden than benefit should narrow or stop. Institutional scale must be earned by system outcomes.

## Provenance must travel

The six tracks prevent one kind of result from becoming another. A second control prevents a result from losing its history during a legitimate handoff. Every claim, model, measure, curriculum, candidate intervention, implementation strategy, and institutional proposal needs a compact provenance record.

> **Figure 29.2 — The cross-track provenance record [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> ORIGIN
> direct authorial formulation | prior internal formulation | theoretical extrapolation | traditional correspondence
> embodied observation | external evidence | mixed
>       |
>       v
> NORMALIZED OBJECT + DOMAIN
> exact proposition or construct | population | anatomy | task | state
> scale | setting | endpoint | time | intended use
>       |
>       v
> METHOD + EVIDENCE STATE
> observed (OBS) | measured (MEAS) | calculated (CALC) | modeled (MOD)
> inferred (INF) | hypothesized (HYP) | manipulated | taught | delivered
> positive | negative | mixed | inconclusive | method-limited | not tested | retired
>       |
>       v
> ALTERNATIVES + STOP + SAFETY + ACCESS + GOVERNANCE
>       |
>       v
> LICENSED OUTPUT ──────────────── PROHIBITED INFERENCE
>       |
>       v
> OPTIONAL HANDOFF TO A NAMED TRACK
> receiving question + retained uncertainty + new stopping condition
> ```
>
> **Caption.** A favorable result changes the evidence state of the tested object. It does not erase the object's origin, upgrade an earlier source retrospectively, or authorize a stronger use that was not tested.
>
> **Text alternative.** A vertical record begins with source origin, then names the exact object and domain, method and evidence state, alternatives and obligations, licensed output, prohibited inference, and an optional handoff. Every handoff carries uncertainty and a new stopping condition.

Origin matters without fixing destiny. An embodied observation can generate a task or construct for measurement. If a later experiment finds a reproducible relation, the measured relation gains external support; the original experience does not become a direct measurement of anatomy or force. A traditional correspondence can motivate a comparison without serving as proof of mechanics. A theoretical extrapolation can be corrected, formalized, and tested, but the initial extrapolation does not become a scientific source. Favorable evidence upgrades the tested proposition, not everything upstream of it.

A handoff should therefore read like a compact contract between tracks. It names the result being transferred, the domain in which it was obtained, the uncertainty that remains, the stronger inference still prohibited, and the new question the receiving track will ask. Measurement might receive a task-specific mechanical relation from research and ask whether a proposed quantity represents it. Therapeutic development might receive a qualified measure and use it only as a mediator, not as a diagnostic label. Implementation might receive evidence of benefit for a named population while retaining uncertainty about another setting. Health-system development might receive a mature component while reopening cost, access, opportunity cost, and governance. At each crossing, the receiving track adds a burden; it does not erase the burden already carried.

Scientific-data stewardship is one part of this record. National Institutes of Health policy requires prospective planning for data management and appropriate sharing, including standards, repositories, and justified limits.[^29-25] The wider provenance record also needs versions, materials, code, analysis plans, deviations, conflicts, consent, cultural and community governance where applicable, and a route for negative findings. Data availability alone does not guarantee interpretability or responsible reuse.

Retirement also requires a record. A candidate can re-enter after new evidence, a materially revised construct, or a demonstrated method failure. It cannot re-enter merely because the same null has been redescribed at a more abstract level. Preserving an idea in the program keeps its history and possible route forward; it does not endorse it.

## The maintained-deformation pathway through the network

The pathway from Chapter 24 can now move through all six tracks without its weakest arrow becoming stronger. Surrounding anatomy and a current wall or luminal state may be observed. The proposed cumulative deformation and material-state transition between them remains reconstructed unless directly tested.

> **Figure 29.3 — One maintained-deformation pathway, six questions [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> declared boundary condition or applied force
>       -> wall deformation, excursion change, or lumen/space change
>       - -> reconstructed cumulative material-state transition
>       -> endpoint-specific physical consequence
>       -> finding, symptom, function, or clinical interpretation
>
> 1. RESEARCH: Does the declared relation occur, and what alternative produces the same state?
> 2. MEASUREMENT: Which local quantity can be acquired for which use, with what error?
> 3. EDUCATION: Can learners keep demand, wall response, lumen, endpoint, and diagnosis separate?
> 4. THERAPEUTIC DEVELOPMENT: Does changing the boundary condition improve a patient-important outcome,
>    and does the proposed intermediate change?
> 5. IMPLEMENTATION: Can a mature object be delivered with fidelity, access, and acceptable burden?
> 6. HEALTH-SYSTEM DEVELOPMENT: Does the mature component add enough value to justify institutional change?
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The same candidate pathway creates six different development objects. The dashed cumulative transition remains reconstructed. No local measure, educational result, intervention effect, or delivery result automatically fills that arrow or creates a diagnosis.
>
> **Text alternative.** A four-link physical pathway contains a dashed reconstructed transition between wall deformation and a retained material state. Six numbered questions sit beside the pathway in the required track order, each with a different immediate output and none with authority to complete the unmeasured arrow.

Suppose research demonstrates a reproducible task-specific change in local geometry. That result supports the local relation under its tested conditions. Suppose the measurement is reliable but poorly specific to symptoms. It can remain useful for description or mechanism research without becoming diagnostic. Suppose an educational module improves learners' separation of geometry from diagnosis. That is an educational success, not confirmation of the pathway. Suppose an intervention improves function but the proposed geometry does not change. The benefit remains; the mediation claim weakens. Suppose the intervention is effective in a selected study but cannot be delivered with adequate reach or equity. The efficacy estimate remains bounded while implementation returns the object upstream. Suppose a mature component adds no value over existing care. The system track stops even if earlier results remain sound.

The reverse is also possible. A careful research study might find no declared deformation across the relevant task range. That result can retire one route without erasing the general concept of constraint-maintained deformation in other structures and conditions. A local mechanism can fail while the wider load-routing framework remains useful. The project does not need every hypothesis to survive in order to develop.

## Negative results are program results

A disciplined program does not treat every unfavorable result as the same kind of failure. The destination depends on which claim was tested and why the result was negative, mixed, or inconclusive.

> **Figure 29.4 — Productive result routing [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Result | Immediate action | What remains unavailable |
> |---|---|---|
> | Predicted redistribution absent with adequate construct, range, and precision | narrow or retire the declared relation | hidden redistribution as the default rescue |
> | Several routes fit the selected outcome | retain a nonunique result or compare additional costs and states | one preferred route from that outcome |
> | Local change without a measured regional carrier | stop locally or design a bridge study | body-wide transmission |
> | Repeatable signal with poor construct specificity | relabel, constrain, revise, or retire the measure for that use | diagnosis or treatment selection |
> | Educational program liked but no gain in accuracy | revise language, audience, comparator, or stop | educational success or truth of the theory |
> | Benefit without change in the proposed mediator | retain benefit and test alternatives | proof of the proposed mechanism |
> | Mediator change without patient-important benefit | retain the mechanical finding; stop therapeutic promotion | recommendation or clinical value |
> | Effective object with poor reach, fidelity, equity, or sustainability | redesign strategy or setting | routine delivery or system readiness |
> | Mature component adds no value over existing practice | do not integrate or displace current care | institutional overhaul claim |
> | Precision or construct too weak to discriminate | name the failure and next decisive design, or stop | positive, negative, or equivalence conclusion |
>
> **Caption.** Results update the proposition and track that generated them. Negative, nonunique, mechanism-discordant, implementation-failure, no-added-value, and inconclusive findings have different destinations.
>
> **Text alternative.** A ten-row table maps distinct unfavorable or noncorresponding findings to revision, local stopping, retirement, alternative-mechanism testing, implementation redesign, or no integration. The third column names the stronger claim each result still forbids.

Mixed results deserve the same specificity. An education program can improve accuracy and increase fear. An intervention can improve one outcome and worsen another. An implementation strategy can increase adoption while reducing access. A system change can help one group and transfer cost or surveillance to another. The correct response is not to average these into an overall impression but to retain each outcome, its importance, and its distribution.

An inconclusive result also needs a cause. The method may lack precision. The construct may not have been valid. The exposure range may have been too narrow. Attrition or missingness may have changed the comparison. Outcomes may conflict. Two models may be observationally equivalent. The next project should target that uncertainty specifically—or the program should stop spending effort on an object that cannot yet be made discriminating.

This result grammar protects the project's breadth. A null does not have to destroy the entire series, so it can be accepted without rhetorical rescue. A positive result does not validate the entire series, so it can be used without inflation. The program advances by changing the exact proposition tested.

## Ambition through division

Book I has produced more than a general request for further study. It has defined relations worth testing: how task and configuration alter distribution; how local exposure depends on carrier, geometry, direction, dose, state, and time; how maintained deformation, instability, handoff, and compensation can be observed without becoming diagnoses; how tissue response and whole-person context modify clinical meaning; and how education and environmental design can be evaluated without promising a universal correction.

The six tracks turn those questions into a durable program. Research earns bounded relations. Measurement earns qualified quantities for declared uses. Education earns audience- and outcome-specific learning results. Therapeutic development earns separate feasibility, safety, benefit, harm, mechanism, and comparative results. Implementation earns setting-specific delivery evidence. Health-system development earns institutional decisions based on mature components, added value, opportunity cost, equity, governance, and burden. Each output can move only through an explicit handoff, carrying its provenance and limits.

This architecture also gives stronger future hypotheses somewhere honest to live. Preferred configuration, signed whole-body modes, traditional correspondences, breath and pressure geometry, embodied observation, and practice can enter research, measurement, education, therapeutic-development, implementation, or system programs appropriate to their actual claims. Inclusion does not validate them. It prevents their preservation from being confused with recommendation and their ambition from being confused with readiness.

The result is a program capable of genuine revision. A pathway can narrow. A measure can remain descriptive. A curriculum can be withdrawn. A beneficial intervention can survive a failed mechanism. An implementation strategy can return upstream. An institutional proposal can stop for lack of added value. None of those outcomes requires denying the mechanical dimension of life or forcing unrelated parts of the project to compensate.

The final chapter can now state the wider series hypothesis directly. Its task is not to borrow authority from this development architecture. It is to distinguish what Book I has already earned from what the preferred-configuration, coordinate, breath, and practice programs must still define, compare, measure, and risk losing.

# Chapter 30 — The wider series hypothesis: *The Back Goes Backwards*

## Return to the object

At the beginning of this book, a person moved an object from one support to another and carried it across a room. Nothing about the task required one body, one technique, or one internal route. The person could stand or sit, use an assistive device, share the object with someone else, change the environment, pause, change hands, or choose not to move it at all. Yet every completed version had a mechanical history. External contacts and body configuration shaped the available paths; active, tensile, skeletal, compliant, sliding, and pressure-mediated structures divided the demand; and the distribution changed from first contact to release.

That ordinary event can now carry three different propositions.

The first is the foundation established in this volume: living bodies must manage material demand, and tracing how that demand was distributed can improve an account of exposure, response, function, and possible medical meaning. The second is a bounded organizing lens: posterior structures form a substantial anatomical and functional system, so anterior–posterior distribution deserves explicit attention alongside other relations. The third is a stronger authorial hypothesis: human anatomy may possess a preferred body-wide organization in which demand is resolved through three signed generalized modes and posterior participation is necessary but insufficient.

These propositions are nested, but their dependence runs in one direction. The stronger hypothesis uses the foundation. The foundation does not require the stronger hypothesis to be true. That separation allows the series title to be direct about its destination without turning destination into proof.

> **Figure 30.1 — Three nested propositions [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> OUTER:  preferred-configuration research hypothesis
>         may use the posterior lens and Book I foundation
>                         |
>                         v
> MIDDLE: posterior organizing lens
>         uses the Book I foundation
>                         |
>                         v
> INNER:  durable Book I foundation
>         stands on its own evidence
>
> If the outer proposition fails:
>     revise or retire the outer proposition
>     review, but do not automatically erase, the inner propositions
> ```
>
> **Caption.** The nesting represents logical dependence, not anatomical location or certainty by size. The wider hypothesis can depend on the posterior lens and the general foundation; independently supported foundation claims do not become false merely because the wider hypothesis is disfavored.
>
> **Text alternative.** Three nested levels descend from an outer preferred-configuration hypothesis through a middle posterior organizing lens to an inner Book I foundation. Arrows point inward to show what the stronger propositions use. A separate failure branch says that rejection of the outer proposition requires revision of that proposition and review, but not automatic erasure, of the inner levels.

The research and development tracks in the previous chapter make this separation practical. A definition can fail while an anatomical observation survives. A measure can work while a proposed interpretation fails. An intervention can change an outcome through a mechanism different from the one expected. The close of Book I therefore does not promise that later books will confirm the title. It states what the title means now, what the later series proposes, and what evidence would require the proposal to change.

## The foundation does not need a preferred route

A living body is a changing material system. Geometry, contact, activation, pressure, material state, capacity, and boundary conditions vary as the body acts. Force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, work, power, dose, and recovery describe different parts of that history. Continuum mechanics provides a disciplined way to declare a system, its boundary, configuration, deformation, forces, stresses, material relations, and balances. It does not by itself reveal how a living body shared an internal demand or which share mattered clinically.[^30-01]

The same restraint applies to measurement. A change in visible shape is not automatically a measurement of stress. Estimating stress in living tissue requires some relation among geometry, material behavior, force, imaging, sensing, and a model. Each method observes or infers only part of that relation.[^30-02] A load path is therefore a bounded account of distribution among named candidate carriers. It need not be one cable, one serial handoff, or one directly visible line running through the body.

The hard/soft polarity gives that distribution a relational vocabulary. A hard role is comparatively shape-preserving, path-establishing, constraining, or structurally resolving in a declared direction, scale, phase, and task. A soft role is comparatively form-receiving and shape-conforming. It remains available to yield, glide, contain, expand, buffer, respond to pressure, or change local shape. Either role can transmit substantial force; transmission alone does not decide the role. The distinction is motivated by traditional Chinese medicine's hard/soft and Yin/Yang concepts. The mechanical translation is not claimed to be definitionally identical to those traditional categories.

This is the meaning of the project's compact intuition:

> Load wants to travel through the hard body so that the soft body can remain soft.

The sentence personifies load to make a division of labor memorable. It does not claim that compliant structures should carry no force. Tendon, muscle, ligament, fascia, cartilage, a pressurized cavity, and an external support can carry substantial demand while serving different roles in different directions or phases. The proposal is that gross structural demand should be resolved through capable, sufficiently continuous relations while form-receiving structures retain the freedom their functions require. Any technical use must still name the demand, scale, carriers, receiving freedom, comparison, and observable.

Mechanical description becomes medical reasoning only through additional links. The recurring sequence has been:

> task and environment → body state and configuration → available paths and internal distribution → local force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, or excursion → tissue or system response over time → function, finding, possible symptom, and clinical interpretation

Every arrow is a proposition. A causal diagram can expose assumed paths, alternatives, confounding, and mediation, but drawing an arrow does not establish it.[^30-03] Whole-person reasoning adds body functions and structures, activity, participation, health conditions, personal relations, and environmental context without pretending that one classification supplies an individual's causal ranking.[^30-04] Pain, inflammation, fatigue, fear, illness, disability, resources, and environment can change later mechanics as well as follow from them.

This foundation is affirmative. Mechanical histories are real. Configuration and time change possible distributions. Local exposure differs from tissue response, and both differ from symptom, diagnosis, function, and outcome. Capacity and recovery alter what a given exposure means. The six families developed in Part III—geometric redistribution, local concentration, instability, failed or changed handoff, constraint-maintained deformation, and compensatory rerouting—make candidate histories more inspectable. None becomes a diagnosis simply by being mechanically coherent.

A reader can stop at this level and retain the complete contribution of Book I: an explicit way to ask how material demand entered a living system, how it was divided, what exposure may have reached a receiver, what changed through time, what the body or person preserved, and where the inference must stop. No preferred configuration is needed for those questions to improve inquiry.

## The posterior system in its earned sense

The posterior chain is not an imaginary invention, and it is not one cable. It is a practical name for a layered regional and functional grouping that extends through the feet and posterior legs, hamstrings, gluteal region, pelvis and hips, paraspinal region, thoracolumbar relations, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, shoulder girdle, posterior neck, and the joints, tendons, fasciae, contacts, and active control with which those structures work.

Several muscles in that grouping are large by ordinary anatomical measures. Whole-body magnetic-resonance imaging can support careful comparison of muscle volumes, but volume is not physiological cross-sectional area, force, moment, activation, or task contribution, and large muscles outside the posterior grouping remain essential comparators.[^30-05] Size makes a structure available for consequential work. It does not specify the work performed in a particular phase.

Anatomical continuity also requires scale. Reviews of proposed myofascial chains find morphological support for some continuities while describing functional force-transfer evidence as limited, heterogeneous, and often adjacent or indirect.[^30-06] A named attachment or local transfer can be real without proving that the entire posterior body behaves as one mechanically dominant chain.

Task evidence gives the posterior grouping its strongest ordinary meaning. Musculoskeletal simulations of walking estimate changing contributions from gluteal, hamstring, plantar-flexor, vasti, and other structures across speed and gait phase; the estimates depend on the model and do not uniquely solve internal force sharing.[^30-07] Dynamic lifting estimates likewise depend on the object, motion, asymmetry, muscle activity, and model assumptions rather than one visible spinal shape.[^30-08] During perturbed walking, healthy adults can use several direction-dependent recovery strategies rather than one universal balance response.[^30-09]

These results support a substantial but bounded account. Posterior structures participate in stance, gait, propulsion, lifting, deceleration, balance, transfer, reaching, and recovery from perturbation. Their contribution changes with phase, task, body, assistance, and environment. Anterior, lateral, deep, pressure-mediated, and external supports can dominate a selected relation or make the posterior contribution nondiscriminating.

An external carrier makes the last point especially clear. In one small lifting study, changing an exoskeleton's lumbar-to-hip support ratio altered modeled loading, active moments, movement, and perceived hindrance.[^30-10] The device changed the available distribution. That does not establish that the resulting distribution was globally preferred, clinically superior, or appropriate for every user. It shows why strong posterior participation cannot be sufficient: a posterior contribution can be present in several organizations with different costs, constraints, and outcomes.

The title's first meaning is therefore earned. The back goes backwards by coming back into the mechanical account. Posterior anatomy is not merely a surface noticed after pain or a passive remainder behind the structures that appear to lead a task. It has its own architecture, capacity, timing, and substantial participation. The title's second meaning is an organizing choice: anterior–posterior distribution can sometimes expose a relation missed by a purely local account. Neither meaning establishes one preferred direction for every force or movement.

## The stronger proposition the series investigates

The wider series makes a more specific proposal:

> We propose that human anatomy may possess a preferred body-wide organization associated with a real, still-to-be-defined relation of whole-system mechanical efficiency. In that organization, gross structural demand would be resolved coherently through capable skeletal, tensile, active, and pressure-mediated support while form-receiving structures remained sufficiently free to yield, conform, glide, contain, expand, and recover.

*Preferred* does not mean visually straight, symmetrical, comfortable, statistically common, minimally active, or fixed in one pose. It requires a declared system, task, population, state, comparison class, period, and criterion. The preferred object could turn out to be a family of configurations, a task-dependent region, a phase-dependent bias, a viable routing regime, or a return tendency rather than a single configuration.

Nonuniqueness is not a technical nuisance. Redundant actuation permits multiple internal solutions to satisfy the same external task; modeled feasible activation sets provide a bounded example of how broad that solution space can be.[^30-11] Development, morphology, disability, training, pain, fatigue, skill, assistance, and environment can change which solutions are available and what they preserve. A theory of preference must compare those solutions rather than treating variation as noise.

The word *efficiency* is also provisional. Candidate manifestations include strain distribution, active or metabolic cost, stability, resilience, reserve, adaptability, repeatability, preserved excursion, and return behavior. They may conflict. A strategy can reduce active cost while reducing reserve; another can use more cocontraction while better resisting a perturbation. Even a task-specific relation among tendon mechanics, work, and apparent efficiency does not establish a global health or preference measure.[^30-12]

Book II must decide whether efficiency is one objective, a constrained combination of objectives, a Pareto family, a viability condition, an attractor property, or an umbrella that should eventually be replaced. The hypothesis becomes stronger, not weaker, when those alternatives are stated before a result is interpreted.

The author's current expectation is that mechanically meaningful posterior participation will prove **necessary but insufficient** within the eventual domain of the preferred organization. *Necessary* means that a fully expressed instance inside that domain would not occur without the relevant posterior participation. *Insufficient* means that posterior participation alone could appear in organizations that are costly, mistimed, constrained, unstable, or otherwise outside the preferred relation. This expectation is not derived from the posterior anatomy reviewed above. It is a direct design commitment for the next investigation.

The three meanings of the title can now remain distinct:

1. **Anatomical:** posterior structures form a substantial system with important participation in ordinary tasks. Book I has earned this statement at bounded scales.
2. **Organizing:** anterior–posterior distribution can improve a comparison when it changes a prediction, measurement, or interpretation. Book I offers this as one lens among several.
3. **Preferred-direction:** the later series investigates whether preferred organization includes necessary-but-insufficient posterior participation. This is an authorial hypothesis, not a Book I result.

The title is therefore neither a hidden conclusion nor an instruction to pull, arch, lean, or route every force backward. Its strongest meaning is direct, consequential, and permitted to fail.

## Three modes, not three Cartesian arrows

The proposed reduced description begins with three generalized modes, each carrying two signs:

- an **axial mode**, currently signed toward downward resolution as Yang and upward resolution as Yin;
- an **opening or rotational mode**, currently signed toward external or opening organization as Yang and internal or closing organization as Yin; and
- an **expansive or lateral mode**, currently signed toward outward expansion as Yang and inward contraction as Yin.

The current preferred-direction candidate combines downward axial resolution, external or opening rotation, and outward expansion. It may later be called an all-Yang organization. The label names the proposed signs. It does not make Yang equivalent to healthy, posterior, hard, active, exterior, or mechanically established.

These modes are not three orthogonal Cartesian force vectors. The candidate set contains two translation-like or shape-like relations and one rotation-like relation. A generalized coordinate reduces a system's possible configurations or motions to a declared degree of freedom. Its conjugate generalized load follows from virtual work and may appear as a force, moment, pressure-related resultant, or another integrated quantity, depending on the coordinate and boundary.[^30-13] The sign of a configuration does not automatically determine the sign of its velocity, acceleration, external action, internal force share, or return tendency.

Local frames are unavoidable. Outward on the left and outward on the right can point in opposite directions in a room-fixed frame while expressing the same bilateral expansive sign. A curved spine, rotating pelvis, scapula, limb, and changing ground contact each require a local reference and a rule for transformation. Book II must define left and right, local and global, open and closed chains, contact changes, coupling, respiratory phase, and task phase before a body-wide sign can become a measurable proposition.

Orthotropy may help model a selected tissue or region whose material behavior differs along three symmetry directions. It is optional and local. The body is not assumed to be a homogeneous orthotropic material, and orthotropy neither creates these generalized modes nor proves their preferred signs.

> **Figure 30.2 — Terms that must not collapse [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> | Term family | What it names | A noncorresponding case |
> |---|---|---|
> | Posterior / anterior | Region or distribution relative to a declared frame | A posterior muscle can lengthen and receive form; an anterior structure can preserve a skeletal relation |
> | Exterior / interior | Relative location, surface, depth, or containment | Deep posterior and superficial anterior structures prevent identity with posterior/anterior |
> | Hard / soft | Changing shape-preserving and form-receiving roles | Tendon can sustain tension while bending or sliding; pressure can help a deformable assembly preserve shape |
> | Axial / opening / expansive | Candidate generalized modes | A mode is not an anatomical region, permanent tissue class, or room-fixed arrow |
> | Yang / Yin | Proposed signs and traditional relations | A Yin-directed phase can be required inside a viable movement; Yang does not mean healthy by definition |
> | Preferred / nonpreferred | Comparison under an eventual efficiency or viability relation | A strong posterior contribution can occur in an organization that does not satisfy the preferred relation |
>
> **Caption.** Region, relative location, mechanical role, generalized mode, traditional sign, and evaluative hypothesis can be related only after each has been defined and measured at the relevant scale. No row can substitute for a force, moment, pressure, displacement, strain field, task result, or clinical outcome.
>
> **Text alternative.** Six rows distinguish posterior/anterior region, exterior/interior location, hard/soft role, three generalized modes, Yang/Yin signs, and preferred/nonpreferred evaluation. Each row includes a counterexample showing why it cannot be identified with the others.

The project proposes that posterior, exterior, hard, and Yang may coincide or correlate in important phases. It does not define them as the same thing. They may align in one task, alternate by phase in another, or separate entirely. A vocabulary that makes every observation confirm the same category would not be a model. It would be a way of avoiding measurement.

## Traditional coordinates, breath, geometry, and practice

The hard/soft polarity disclosed earlier was motivated by traditional Chinese medicine. A later part of the research program asks whether the mechanical modes correspond meaningfully to Yin/Yang, the Six Divisions, paired channels, and embodied observations. The current authorial mapping is:

- **axial (Shaoyin–Taiyang):** Kidney/Bladder and Heart/Small Intestine;
- **opening or rotational (Taiyin–Yangming):** Lung/Large Intestine and Spleen/Stomach; and
- **expansive or lateral (Jueyin–Shaoyang):** Pericardium/Triple Warmer and Liver/Gallbladder.

A related gross projection weights the legs and feet toward axial support, the arms and hands toward expansion, and rotational organization toward coordination between upper and lower systems. That projection does not reassign every local hand or foot channel. The author's reported Kidney 1–Pericardium 8 relation is an embodied observation of felt coordination or a force-line-like continuity between foot and hand, especially salient in the beginning and closing phases of a Yang-style Tai Chi sequence. It motivates questions. It does not measure a carrier, force, moment, stress, anatomical cable, channel, or clinical effect.

Book III owns the historical and textual reconstruction, the Six-Division and channel terminology, the relation among mapping scales, the embodied phenomenology, and independent tests of mechanical correspondence. The traditional map does not validate the modes merely by resembling them, and the mechanical proposal does not replace the traditional system by translating it.

Pressure-mediated support already belongs to the Book I foundation. Bounded models of lifting can show how intra-abdominal pressure, posture, coactivation, and assumptions change estimated spinal loading and stability.[^30-14] Such a model does not establish that breath drives a preferred body-wide organization or that one breathing practice should be prescribed.

Book IV takes up the stronger possibilities. Breath may drive, organize, modulate, reveal, accompany, or add little to the proposed state. The diaphragm, rib cage, abdominal wall, pelvic floor, hyoid, respiratory phase, tensegrity, toroidal geometry, and other representations remain candidate parts of that comparison. A torus is an additional model, not a replacement imposed on the coordinate, posterior, or hard/soft accounts. The hyoid is an anatomical node or suspended structure, not a fourth spatial dimension. A materially different routing regime may provisionally be called a state transition; it should not be called a topological transformation unless a defined invariant and discontinuity warrant the term.

Book V receives observations, tests, cues, drills, strength and coordination work, breathing practices, bandhas, yoga, Tai Chi, teaching methods, professional applications, and personal exploration. Their place downstream is deliberate. Embodied experience can identify a phenomenon and generate a hypothesis. A useful practice can work through a mechanism different from the one proposed. Neither experience nor usefulness bypasses construct validity, reliability, comparison, contraindications, adverse events, accessibility, or professional scope.

Book I therefore ends without a corrective routine. The reader is not asked to find a hidden line, adopt the proposed signs, change posture, breathe in a particular way, or diagnose a failure of preferred organization. The later programs remain present in full view, but they carry no evidentiary weight backward.

## A hypothesis that is allowed to fail

Imagine that the next stages of work produce a coherent negative result. Several organizations prove equally viable or efficient within the same declared task. No stable whole-system efficiency relation can be recovered. The proposed Yang signs reverse under reasonable local-frame or phase definitions. Posterior participation is common but not necessary. Another coordinate reduction predicts measured mechanics better. The traditional correspondences are partial, metaphorical, historically discontinuous, or absent. Breath proves a local modulator rather than a global organizer, toroidal geometry adds no discriminating prediction, and candidate practices work through unrelated mechanisms or do not work.

That result would disfavor the wider hypothesis. It would require the series to revise or retire a general preferred-configuration model, posterior necessity, the present three-mode reduction or its signs, the proposed correspondence with the Six Divisions or paired channels, breath- or torus-led organization, and assessments or practices derived specifically from those claims. The title's strongest directional meaning would need to change.

The result would not show that living structure lacks a mechanical history. It would not erase the distinction among force, moment, pressure, stress, strain, deformation, dose, and response. It would not make hard/soft role exchange incoherent, make posterior anatomy disappear, or turn concentration, interrupted handoff, maintained deformation, instability, compensation, and scale transition into meaningless questions. It would not collapse tissue response into symptoms or remove biological, psychological, social, developmental, and environmental context.

This is the rejection test that keeps the series cumulative rather than circular. Later claims are not protected by redefining preferred after every unfavorable observation. Earlier claims survive only where their own evidence supports them.

> **Figure 30.3 — The Book I–II seam and rejection path [text-native first-draft figure]**
>
> ```text
> BOOK I INHERITANCE
> definitions | role distinctions | posterior anatomy
> adverse-organization families | causal and medical boundaries
>                         |
>                         v
> BOOK II NEW WORK
> preferred object | efficiency relation | frames and transformations
> three signed modes | posterior-necessity test | alternatives
>                         |
>          +--------------+--------------+
>          |              |              |
>          v              v              v
>       favored         mixed         disfavored
>       refine          revise        retire or replace
>       domain           coupling      stronger model
>          |              |              |
>          +--------------+--------------+
>                         |
>                         v
> independently supported Book I foundation remains available
> ```
>
> **Caption.** Book II can favor, revise, or disfavor its stronger propositions. Every branch returns to review of the inherited foundation; none treats Book II as inevitable confirmation or rejection as erasure of independently supported claims.
>
> **Text alternative.** Book I definitions, role distinctions, posterior anatomy, adverse-organization families, and medical boundaries feed into new Book II work on preference, efficiency, frames, modes, posterior necessity, and alternatives. Three equally presented result branches—favored, mixed, and disfavored—lead respectively to refinement, revision, or retirement of the stronger model, while the independently supported Book I foundation remains available.

## What Book II inherits—and what it must earn

Book II assumes this volume has been read. It inherits the distinctions among mechanical quantities; the discipline of declaring systems, boundaries, tasks, frames, phases, and scales; load path as a bounded distribution model; changing hard and soft roles; cooperative skeletal, joint, active, tensile, compliant, sliding, and pressure-mediated support; posterior anatomy; capacity and recovery; the six adverse-organization families; the exposure-to-outcome causal chain; whole-person alternatives; and the separate research and development tracks.

It does not inherit a preferred route.

Book II must introduce bilateral reference symmetry and skeletal-primary routing as first-order modeling assumptions rather than Book I conclusions. It must define the preferred object, population and task domain, comparison class, reference configurations, efficiency or viability relation, axial, opening/rotational, and expansive generalized coordinates, conjugate loads, local frames, left/right and local/global transformations, mode coupling, contact and phase dependence, and the difference among an instantaneous state, recurring bias, routing regime, attractor, and return tendency.

It must also test the all-Yang combination rather than infer it from names. It must define what counts as posterior participation, which quantity carries the claim, at what scale and phase necessity is expected, which examples show strong posterior participation without preferred organization, and which candidate preferred examples appear to have little posterior participation. Multiple optima, redundancy, variation, disability, assistance, task dependence, and alternative coordinate reductions remain live comparisons. Orthotropy can enter only where a selected regional material model earns it.

The seam can be stated in one paragraph:

> Book I has established a working language of mechanical demand, configuration-dependent routing, changing hard and soft roles, posterior support, adverse exposure, tissue response, compensation, and whole-person interpretation. Book II inherits that foundation without inheriting a preferred route. It asks the stronger question directly: whether human anatomy has a preferred body-wide routing organization, whether three signed generalized modes can describe it, and whether posterior participation is necessary but insufficient within it.

This is not a request for Book II to repeat the medical argument. It is a requirement that the stronger mechanical proposition add discriminating definitions, observations, and failure conditions beyond what ordinary anatomy and load-capacity reasoning already explain.

## The mechanical history remains

Return one last time to the person and the object. Book I does not tell that person how to stand, what to feel, which muscles to recruit, or whether the transfer displays a preferred configuration. It gives the observer a better sequence of questions. What was the task and boundary? What configuration and contacts were available? Which structures preserved relations, and which received form? How was demand divided? What local exposure followed? What changed with repetition, state, assistance, and recovery? What did the strategy preserve? Which links were measured, modeled, inferred, or left open?

Those questions form the durable foundation. They are enough to make mechanics a more coherent participant in accounts of function, exposure, tissue state, symptoms, recovery, and health without making it the master explanation for a person.

The posterior lens adds a bounded emphasis. The back is a large, active, layered part of support and movement, not a passive remainder. Anterior–posterior distribution can matter, and the back goes backwards first by returning to view.

The wider series then names its stronger possibility without disguising it as a result: human structure may have a preferred body-wide organization, provisionally signed toward downward axial resolution, external or opening rotation, and outward expansion, with posterior participation necessary but insufficient. That hypothesis can now be developed, formalized, compared, and rejected without weakening the reason this book was worth writing.

Book I ends with a complete lens and one exact question for Book II: can preferred organization and efficiency be defined well enough that axial, opening/rotational, expansive, posterior, and return-behavior predictions become discriminating rather than retrospective?

This first-draft bibliography consolidates the annotated source records documented in the chapter endnotes. Where the same record appears in more than one chapter, one complete entry is retained here. Composite records remain intact, so an individual source may appear again when its annotation or source grouping differs. The chapter notes preserve each proposition-specific use and limit. Publication editing will normalize house style and recheck metadata without changing the evidentiary job of a source.
